Center: Floor cleared deliberately. Original furnishings (shattered pedestals, broken braziers) pushed to walls. Circular depression in swept floor — nest shape, formed by repeated use by something large. Edges built from broken furniture and torn fabric. Currently empty. Radiates warmth and a sense of presence.

Hidden door (east wall): Stone-framed, flush with surface, seam filled with centuries of grit. Accessed via a 5 ft wide, 20 ft long secret hallway. Opened by pressing the bronze disc against a specific carved scale in the dragon-frieze border. Leads to the head priest's private chamber (15 ft wide × 20 ft deep — never entered since the order fell).

  • The Surviving Scroll — sei-lacquer identification (DC 13 Arcana)
  • The Scroll's Hidden Thread / Sei Conduit Filament (DC 16 Arcana, or DC 14 if lens already found; DC 14 Sleight of Hand to extract) (Observatory component #5)
  • Breaking the Wards — analysis (DC 15 Arcana — shadow-aspected, Kokuryu)
  • The Hidden Door to Jushoku no Ma (DC 15 Perception, or automatic if searching walls; bronze disc opens)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Kinjiro's Journal (in bronze box, DC 16 Thieves' Tools or disc as key)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Kinryu no Chikara Mandate (in bronze box)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Operational Ledger (in bronze box)
  • Jushoku no Ma — Kinjiro's Remains
  • The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen (found on Zasu's body after encounter; see zasu-ritual-scrolls.md)
  • Hoko (secret door S wall behind dresser — contents TBD)

The Surviving Scroll: The preserved scroll of Kinryu in flight is worth 800gp as an antique, more to the right buyer. More importantly, the sei-lacquer preserving it is still active — a character who examines it closely (DC 13 Arcana) identifies the preservation technique as Golden Dragon order craft, and notes that the same technique was almost certainly used on the most important records kept in this temple. Records preserved this way would survive in far better condition than anything else here. This is a subtle pointer toward the Scriptorium — the same preservation technique was used on the order's most important records, and they are still legible. The Scriptorium is on this floor, off the south side of the E-W corridor.

The Scroll's Hidden Thread: DC 16 Arcana (or DC 14 for a character who has already identified a projection lens elsewhere in the temple) reveals something additional: woven into the scroll's decorative border is an impossibly fine golden filament — not thread, not wire, something between the two. It carries a faint, steady sei charge, distinct from the preservation enchantment. This filament is a sei conduit — a transmission line designed to carry magical resonance between connected systems. Removing it without destroying the scroll requires DC 14 Sleight of Hand or Tinker's Tools; on failure, the scroll's preservation enchantment collapses and the image fades to nothing within minutes (the scroll is destroyed, but the filament is recovered). On success, both the scroll and filament are preserved intact. (Observatory component: sei conduit filament. Connects the orrery's mechanical output to the arcane projection system. The scroll was stored in the sanctum because the conduit needed to remain within the temple's foundational magic field to retain its charge — the sanctum sits well within the field.)

Breaking the Wards: The magical seals on the door were broken from outside. The magic used to break them — DC 15 Arcana — is shadow-aspected. Kokuryu tradition. The infiltrators unsealed this room during the order's fall, gaining access to the sanctum's contents. Whatever was in here, they took it or destroyed it.

The Jushoku no Ma (Abbot's Chamber): Behind the rubble on the east side of the room, almost invisible unless the party is actively looking (DC 15 Perception, or automatic if they are searching the walls), is a section of wall that is actually a door — stone-framed, flush with the surface, its seam filled with centuries of grit. The locking mechanism is a pressure sequence on specific carved scales in the dragon-frieze border; the bronze disc from the sealed dormitory room, when pressed against a specific scale, triggers the release. The room beyond — the head priest's private chamber — has never been entered since the order fell.

What Is In The Jushoku no Ma: A small, very austere room (15 ft wide × 20 ft deep). A sleeping platform against the west wall with a dresser beside it. A writing desk with a locked bronze box (DC 16 Thieves' Tools or the disc again as a key). Inside the box: three documents, each sealed separately.

  1. The personal journal of Head Priest Kinjiro — final entries. The journal is personal, written in a direct hand that does not match the formality of the other documents. The final entries describe the order's disintegration — not the external pressures (those are in the ledger) but the internal experience of watching a community fracture. Kinjiro names no traitors. The journal's emotional weight is in what it does not accuse.

  2. The Kinryu no Chikara mandate — a sealed tube containing a formal document conferring specific authority within the temple to named individuals. The mandate is blank on the recipient line, left that way deliberately — Kinjiro did not know who would find it and chose to leave it open. A character who performs the short ritual described in the journal (10 minutes, spoken in any language, a genuine statement of intent to protect rather than exploit what lies within) can inscribe their name. The mandate grants its bearer advantage on all Charisma checks within the temple and allows passage through one magically sealed door elsewhere in the structure.

  3. The operational ledger of the hub — a formal record of network activity kept by the head priest. Each significant entry logs the full operational cycle: distress signal received, acknowledgement authorized and sent, dispatch ordered, field report on findings. The ledger records both inbound signals and outbound responses — a complete cycle document, not a record of actions alone.

Ledger physical condition: Sei-lacquered selectively in the same technique as the surviving sanctum scroll. Routine entries written in ordinary ink have faded to illegibility. Entries the head priest considered significant were lacquered and remain fully readable. Which entries were treated is itself information about what the head priest considered to matter.

Standard entry format: Prior entries from the order's functional period are complete. Signal received, response sent, investigator dispatched, findings returned and summarized. These entries establish the template clearly. The party understands what a finished cycle looks like before they reach the entries that are not finished.

The fall-period entries — what is absent: The distress signals sent by @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} at the fall of 13088 are not recorded in the ledger. No entry exists for either signal — not the incoming alert, not an acknowledgement, not a dispatch, not a field report. The ledger's last entries are whatever completed operational cycles preceded the fall. Then the record ends. The absence is not by design — distress signals appear in prior entries. Kaze and Sora are simply not there because the collapse overtook the record-keeping.

Sora acknowledgement gap: The acknowledged state exists in the network (visible on Tapestry III). It does not exist in the ledger. Possible explanations: a monitor acting independently during the chaos; the head priest sent it but was interrupted before recording; someone who didn't survive sent it; or the entry was among those that faded. The document cannot close the gap.

Kaze in the ledger: Whether Kaze was ever acknowledged cannot be determined from the ledger. The signal is absent from the record entirely.

Placement note: The journal is personal. The mandate confers authority. The ledger is institutional memory. Together they represent what the order chose to preserve when everything else was falling.

The Remains: On the sleeping platform, partially covered by a threadbare blanket that has largely disintegrated, lie the skeletal remains of Head Priest Kinjiro. The posture is deliberate — hands folded across the chest, body aligned with the room's cardinal orientation, head turned slightly toward the writing desk. He went to his bed and did not rise. The bones are undisturbed. Nothing in this room has been touched since the door sealed.

  • @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.monsters.Actor.cRhrQ7TL3vVUKO75]{Nagaji Zasu} (Inner Sanctum lair — currently patrolling; returns periodically)
  • Head Priest Kinjiro's @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.monsters.Actor.I8CGFyd6dUeRizU2]{Bōrei} (Jushoku no Ma — manifests when bronze box or remains touched)

Kinjiro's Spirit: The head priest did not move on after death. His spirit persists in this chamber as a protector — bound not by curse or unfinished personal business, but by the weight of institutional obligation. He was the last keeper. No one relieved him of the duty. The spirit is dormant until the chamber is entered; it manifests when someone touches the bronze box or the remains.

Manifestation: Not aggressive by default. The spirit appears as a translucent figure seated at the writing desk — the posture of someone still working, still keeping records. Cold fills the room. The torchlight dims but does not go out. Kinjiro does not speak first. He watches. His expression carries exhaustion rather than menace.

Peaceful Resolution: A party that approaches with respect — speaks to the spirit, identifies themselves, or demonstrates they are not here to loot — can engage Kinjiro in limited communication. He cannot speak freely (the binding is too old, his connection too frayed), but he can answer direct questions with gestures, single words, or by directing attention to specific objects in the room. He knows the temple's layout, the purpose of the documents in the box, and the broad shape of what went wrong. He does not know the current state of the Nagaji — he died before the transformation. If the party undertakes to cleanse the temple (removing the corruption, restoring order to the sacred spaces), and succeeds, Kinjiro can finally release. His departure is quiet — the cold lifts, the translucence fades, the bones settle slightly as whatever held them together withdraws.

Combat Resolution: If the party acts aggressively — drawing weapons in the chamber, attempting to force the box open without care, or showing clear intent to desecrate — the spirit defends. Use Revenant (MM p.259) as a base, adjusted: Kinjiro is not pursuing vengeance but defending a post. He fights to drive intruders from the chamber, not to kill. If reduced to 0 HP, he reforms in 24 hours (as Revenant) unless the party has cleansed the temple, in which case he passes on regardless.

Reward: TBD — see Obsidian/dm/plot-threads.md for open decision. Consider: direct knowledge that shortcuts a discovery elsewhere in the temple, a blessing granting advantage on a specific check type within the temple, or a narrative reward connected to the Kinryu no Chikara mandate (the priest confirming the ritual, or adding weight to the inscription).

The Hoko (Storehouse): A secret door on the south wall of the Jushoku no Ma, west side — behind the dresser, west of the bed. Completely concealed. Contains the priest's and the temple's most sacred items. This room has been left entirely untouched since the order fell — sealed within a sealed room within a hidden chamber. The deepest-hidden space on the first floor. (Contents: TBD — see Obsidian/dm/plot-threads.md)

The Zasu's Scrolls: When the Zasu is defeated, the party finds a cracked leather scroll case lashed to its midsection with strips of torn formal silk bearing the Gekkō mon. Contains seven documents in varying states of preservation — the transformation ritual research the chief seimaster gathered before performing the ritual on himself. Full details: zasu-ritual-scrolls.md

The Occupant: A Nagaji Zasu (MM p.308) has made this space its lair — a Nagaji of particular power, one of the original senior members of Clan Gekko, transformed more completely than the others. This individual was once Gekko's chief seimaster — the architect of the failed ritual. The transformation has cost them nearly everything, but not quite. Deep within the abomination, fragments of the original person remain: a scholar, a leader, someone who made a catastrophic decision trying to protect their clan. They are not in the sanctum when the party first arrives (they patrol the temple), but they will return.

Atmosphere: The nest radiates residual warmth and something harder to name — a sense of presence, of being watched, even in an empty room. The cleared center of the room feels deliberately territorial. Players with high Passive Perception (14+) notice that the debris pushed to the walls has been sorted — materials of value (intact objects, sealed containers) are in one pile; pure refuse in another. Whatever lives here is not mindless.

pages.name: The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen

text.content:
Found on or near the @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.monsters.Actor.cRhrQ7TL3vVUKO75]{Nagaji Zasu}'s body after the encounter in the Inner Sanctum (Room 6). A bundle of documents carried by the creature — some rolled tightly inside a cracked leather scroll case lashed to the body with strips of torn silk, others loose and partially crushed beneath its coils.

Physical Description:

The scroll case is lacquered hardwood, once fine, now split along one seam and discoloured by sustained contact with scaled flesh. It is lashed to the Zasu's midsection with strips of silk torn from what was once a formal obi — deep indigo fabric with a barely visible mon: a crescent moon above still water.

Inside: seven documents in varying states of preservation. Not a single unified text — a collection, assembled from multiple sources over time. Some are written in the same hand. Others are not.

The Bundle:

  1. Three intact sheets — Heavy mulberry paper, brushwork in formal seimaster notation. Dense. Technical. Written in a dialect of Classical Kagekunian that predates the current era by centuries. Not a language any living scholar would read fluently, but structural elements are recognizable to anyone trained in arcane or historical study.

  2. One large diagram — Folded repeatedly and worn soft at the creases. Ink faded at the edges but the central image is clear: a human figure enclosed in concentric rings of notation, with lines radiating outward to seven points. The figure's outline blurs at the extremities — the arms taper, the legs merge, the head elongates. Whether this depicts a process or a result is not immediately clear.

  3. Two damaged pages — Charred along one edge, as though pulled from a fire before the damage was complete. The surviving text is fragmentary. Diagrams of something anatomical — bones? Muscles? The proportions are wrong for a human body. Marginal annotations in a second, more hurried hand.

  4. One loose leaf — Thinner paper, different ink, different hand entirely. A list or index of some kind — short entries, each followed by a location reference and a symbol. Several entries have been circled. One has been crossed out with a single deliberate stroke.

  • Identify the scroll case's origin (DC 12 Investigation)
  • Identify the obi fabric and mon (DC 13 Investigation or DC 11 History with Gekkō knowledge)
  • Read the intact sheets — surface meaning (DC 14 Arcana)
  • Read the intact sheets — deeper understanding (DC 17 Arcana)
  • Interpret the large diagram (DC 13 Arcana or DC 14 Medicine)
  • Read the damaged pages (DC 15 Arcana; DC 13 if diagram already interpreted)
  • Interpret the loose leaf index (DC 14 Investigation)
  • Identify the crossed-out entry (DC 16 History or DC 14 with Ko'jiri's Golden Dragon advantage)
  • Recognize the reversal reference (DC 18 Arcana; DC 15 if intact sheets already read at deeper understanding)

The Scroll Case — DC 12 Investigation: The case itself is seimaster's equipment — purpose-built for transporting documents that carry active sei residue. The interior is lined with a thin copper-leaf layer designed to insulate the contents from ambient magical interference. This is not a general-purpose scroll case. It was made for carrying something dangerous, or at least something that interacted with sei in ways that required containment.

The Obi and Mon — DC 13 Investigation (or DC 11 History with prior Gekkō knowledge): The silk is from a formal obi — the width, weave, and indigo dye are consistent with dress worn by clan leadership or senior retainers during official functions. The mon embroidered into the fabric is a crescent moon reflected in still water. Any character who has encountered Clan Gekkō's heraldry — or studied the independent clans — recognizes this as the Gekkō clan crest. The Zasu was carrying documents bound to its body with a strip of its own formal clothing.

The Intact Sheets — DC 14 Arcana (Surface Reading): The notation system is recognizable as seimaster technical writing — the equivalent of a magical research language. The three sheets describe a process. Something is being channelled through a living subject. The terminology is archaic but the structural grammar matches transformation magic — not illusion, not transmutation in the temporary sense, but permanent alteration of a living form. References to "the vessel" and "the shape beyond" appear repeatedly. The tone is clinical. There is no ethical framing anywhere in the text — no discussion of consent, consequence, or reversal. It reads like instructions, not philosophy.

The Intact Sheets — DC 17 Arcana (Deeper Understanding): At this level of comprehension, specific details emerge. The transformation described is not a single event but a cascading process — once initiated in one subject, it propagates through sei-bonded individuals in proximity. The ritual was designed for a group, not an individual. The source tradition is not Golden Dragon — the foundational theory, the sei-alignment patterns, the structural logic all point to Kokuryu. Onyx Dragon magical tradition. A character who knows anything about the dragon clans understands immediately: this was never Kinryū's work. Someone found Kokuryu research and tried to use it.

The text also references a prerequisite — a "site of origin" where the sei conditions are correct for the initial casting. The site is not named. But the geographic and environmental markers described (acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, hollow stone formations) do not match any location the party has visited. They match somewhere else. Somewhere in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} Province.

The Large Diagram — DC 13 Arcana or DC 14 Medicine: The figure at the center is human. The process depicted moves outward through the concentric rings — each ring representing a stage. The outermost ring shows a form that is no longer human. Limbs have fused. The spine has elongated. The skull has narrowed and stretched. A medical eye (DC 14 Medicine) recognizes that this is not artistic abstraction — the anatomical transitions are rendered with the precision of someone who understood exactly how a human body would need to change to arrive at the depicted result. The seven radiating points correspond to sei meridian nodes in the body — the same points targeted in advanced healing magic, but inverted. Whatever this process does, it rewrites the subject at the level of their sei architecture. There is no "off" described anywhere on the diagram.

The Damaged Pages — DC 15 Arcana (DC 13 if diagram already interpreted): Fragmentary, but enough survives to understand: these pages describe what happens after the transformation. Behavioral changes. Cognitive deterioration over time — described not as a flaw but as a known parameter. The phrase that survives most completely translates roughly as: "the mind narrows to the form." A character who has already interpreted the diagram understands: the transformation was known to degrade rational thought. Whoever designed this ritual documented the cognitive cost and included it anyway. The annotations in the second hand — more hurried, less formal — appear to be someone's attempt to calculate timelines. How long before the subject loses coherent speech. How long before decision-making capacity degrades below functional thresholds. The numbers are partially burned away, but the progression described is measured in months, not years.

The Loose Leaf Index — DC 14 Investigation: A reference list. Each entry consists of a short descriptor (a place or a thing, not a person), a location reference using a coordinate system the party does not recognize, and a symbol from a set of about a dozen recurring glyphs. The format is consistent with a research index — a scholar's shorthand for tracking source materials across multiple sites. Several entries have been circled in the same ink as the intact sheets. One entry — near the bottom of the list — has been crossed out with a single, deliberate horizontal stroke. The ink used for the strike-through is different from everything else on the page. Newer.

The Crossed-Out Entry — DC 16 History (DC 14 with Ko'jiri's Golden Dragon Clan advantage): The struck entry's descriptor translates loosely as "the golden restoration" or "the golden counter-work." Its location reference, while in the same unrecognized coordinate system as the rest, includes a secondary notation that uses directional language consistent with mountain-interior positioning. A character with knowledge of the Golden Dragon Clan's history (Ko'jiri) recognizes the phrasing: "counter-work" is a term used in Golden Dragon magical tradition for a specifically developed countermeasure to another clan's magic. The crossed-out entry refers to a Golden Dragon response to whatever this ritual represents. It exists — or existed — somewhere. And whoever crossed it out knew it was there and chose to mark it as eliminated, completed, or irrelevant.

The Reversal Reference — DC 18 Arcana (DC 15 if intact sheets already read at deeper understanding): Buried in the technical language of the intact sheets, between two passages describing sei-channel alignment during the transformation's second phase, is a parenthetical notation — almost an aside. It translates approximately as: "Restoration of original form requires inversion at the site of origin, using the counter-work of the golden tradition, during a convergence of the three lights." Three components. A location (site of origin — wherever the ritual was first performed). A method (the Golden Dragon countermeasure — the crossed-out entry on the index). A timing condition (convergence of the three lights — a celestial alignment involving Kagekuni's three stars). The notation is not a guide. It is a footnote — an acknowledgement that reversal is theoretically possible, recorded with the clinical detachment of someone cataloguing edge cases, not someone who expected it to matter.

Why the Zasu carries these: The chief seimaster gathered these documents before performing the ritual on himself — the last to undergo it, trying to maintain enough awareness to lead his transformed people. He kept them because some fragment of the scholar he was still compels him to. The scrolls are lashed to his body the way a drowning person holds a rope. He cannot read them anymore. He cannot remember why they matter. But he will not let them go.

The obi: The strip of formal clothing binding the case to the Zasu's body is a detail that should land quietly. This creature dressed itself. Or — more precisely — something that was becoming this creature took the time to secure these documents to its body using a piece of its own ceremonial clothing before the transformation completed. The crescent moon mon is facing outward. Whether that was intentional is unknowable.

Narrative function: These scrolls serve three purposes simultaneously:

  1. Dot-connection for the Gekkō investigation. The Gekkō mon on the obi, the transformation ritual in the sheets, and the Nagaji the party has been fighting begin to form a single picture. The party doesn't need to reach the full conclusion here — but they should leave this encounter with a growing unease that the Nagaji are not what they assumed.

  2. Breadcrumb toward the Order of the Black Lily. The "site of origin" referenced in the reversal notation — with its acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, and hollow stone — describes a location in Kaze Province. The party doesn't know that yet. When they reach Kaze and encounter those geographic features, the scrolls become a key that unlocks a door they didn't know they were carrying.

  3. Breadcrumb toward the Golden Dragon countermeasure. The crossed-out entry on the index tells the party two things: a reversal exists (or existed), and someone — the Zasu, before the transformation — knew about it and struck it from the list. Whether he crossed it out because he believed it was destroyed, because he had already looked for it and failed, or because he wanted to ensure no one pursued it, is deliberately ambiguous. The party may interpret this differently depending on their read of the Zasu — as a warning, a surrender, or a sabotage.

What the scrolls do NOT reveal:

  • They do not name Clan Gekkō, Masota Gekkō, or any individual
  • They do not explain why the ritual was performed
  • They do not describe where the "site of origin" is (geographic markers only — no place names)
  • They do not confirm that the Nagaji the party has fought are transformed people (the connection is inferential, not explicit)
  • They do not provide enough information to perform the reversal — only to know that one theoretically exists and requires three components the party does not yet have

Ko'jiri's unique position: Ko'jiri's advantage on Golden Dragon History checks makes him the most likely party member to identify the crossed-out entry's significance. This is by design — the con artist who faked Golden Dragon expertise is now the person whose genuine research matters most. If Ko'jiri is the one who identifies the "golden counter-work" reference, the narrative irony completes: the knowledge he built to deceive is the knowledge that may save an entire clan.

Timing and pacing: The scrolls are meant to be studied, not instantly decoded. Encourage the party to examine them over a short rest or between encounters. The check DCs are set so that a single character is unlikely to extract everything in one pass — this is a puzzle that rewards collaboration. The fighter won't read the Arcana. The sorcerer won't catch the History. The druid might notice the Medicine angle on the diagram. Everyone has something to contribute, and the full picture only emerges when they share what they've found.

Read-Aloud — The Star Shrine

The hallway that leads here is unmarked — no carvings, no script, no alcoves. Just stone, ten feet wide, stretching sixty feet ahead of you with the narrowing sense that you are going somewhere set apart.

The room at the end is broad and still — forty-five feet across, thirty-five deep, the ceiling rising into shadow above you. The floor is polished obsidian, black and seamless, still reflective despite the centuries — you see your own feet in it, blurred, moving just behind you. At the center, a low stone dais sized for a single seated figure, unadorned.

Then you notice the ceiling.

Thousands of small holes, each one no wider than a finger, pierce it in an arrangement that is clearly deliberate — too consistent for accident, too complex for simple decoration. Through a narrow shaft in the outer northwest wall, moonlight enters the chamber and passes through the holes, each one casting a single pinprick of shadow down onto the obsidian below.

The shadows together form the sky.

Not an approximation of it. Not a simplified rendering. The actual night sky above this latitude, mapped in negative across the reflective floor: the constellations of Seizan, the positions of the four moons, the dim stellar clusters between the named stars. The room is holding the sky in place.

Sound arrives at the threshold and stops. Whatever you carried in from the hallway — footsteps, breath, the creak of armor — becomes, within a step, nothing.

The dais has been used recently. The dust on it is disturbed: a circular impression, the shape of something large and coiled, pressed into the surface more than once.

Northwest wing, accessible via the west end of the E-W hallway.

Physical Description:

Accessed via a 10 ft wide, 60 ft long unmarked hallway extending north from the west wing of the E-W hallway. Room is 50 ft wide × 40 ft deep, high ceiling. Complete sound suppression at the threshold — all external noise ceases on entry.

Magical Darkness: The rear two-thirds of the room is consumed by magical darkness — a clean circular boundary approximately 20 ft radius centered on the dais. The entrance third remains lit. Light sources stop precisely at the boundary and do not spill inward. Darkvision does not function within the darkness. The boundary is visible and investigable from the entrance before committing.

Floor: Polished obsidian, black and seamless, still reflective. Functions as the projection surface for the star map (currently inactive — obscured by darkness).

Ceiling: Thousands of finger-width holes piercing the dome in a precise arrangement. A narrow shaft in the outer northwest wall admits moonlight, which passes through the holes and casts pinprick shadows onto the obsidian floor — reproducing the actual night sky at this latitude (constellations of Seizan, four moons, stellar clusters). Full map renders under Kagetsu (largest moon). Currently inert while darkness persists.

Dais: Low stone platform at center (within the darkness), sized for a single seated figure. Shows recent use — dust disturbed, circular coiled impression pressed into the surface repeatedly. A cursed urn sits on the dais, radiating the darkness.

Permanent etching: A fixed star configuration carved into the obsidian floor (not projected) depicting the Great Aphelion — all three stars and four moons at maximum distance from Seizan. Partially visible in the lit entrance third; full configuration only visible once darkness lifts.

  • The Darkness — source identification (DC 12 Arcana or Perception; DC 13 Arcana curse aura; DC 16 Arcana protective ward)
  • The Purification Rite (DC 18 Religion or second floor hidden archive)
  • How It Works — star map mechanism (DC 10 Arcana for navigator check) (requires darkness to be lifted)
  • The Dais Impression — @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.monsters.Actor.OGA1LtjRQuabbHHR]{Nagaji Kannushi} attunement
  • Relic Collection (DC 14 Investigation — once darkness lifts)
  • Meditation Benefit (short rest on dais during moonlight) (requires darkness to be lifted)

Source Identification:

Check DC Result
Arcana or Perception 12 Identifies the urn on the central dais as the epicenter of the darkness
Arcana 13 Confirms curse aura on the urn
Arcana 16 Identifies curse as a deliberate protective ward, not corruption — can be unwound
Religion 18 Reveals the purification rite to lift the darkness

Purification Rite: One action, both hands on the urn's surface, spoken invocation to Kinryū. Lifting the darkness does not damage the urn. The rite can also be learned from the hidden archive on the second floor.

If the party lifts the darkness mid-combat: The darkness collapses instantly. The Kannushi loses concealment.

The shaft in the outer northwest wall is angled precisely to admit moonlight at specific lunar positions. Under Kagetsu (the largest moon), the full star map renders on the floor. Under Ryugetsu, certain star positions shift slightly — reflecting that moon's complex orbit — creating what the order called the "Dragon's Compass," a subtle pattern within the map pointing toward celestial events of significance. A seimaster or character with proficiency in Arcana or Navigator's Tools who studies the map for 10 minutes can extract one piece of information about current celestial alignment (DM's discretion based on current campaign date — Aki season, Kugatsu 1).

The circular coiled impression in the dust was left by the Nagaji Kannushi who inhabits this space. It was not meditating in the conventional sense — it was drawn here, instinctively, by something in the stone that resonates with its transformed nature. The Nagaji connection to Kokuryu's shadow rituals creates a faint attunement to certain sei-charged spaces. The Kannushi has been tidying the space — making it a meditation chamber.

The Kannushi gathered and preserved these objects from elsewhere in the temple:

  • Three intact ceremonial incense burners (gold-inlaid bronze; functional; 120gp each as antiques)
  • A silk-wrapped bundle of seven prayer slips in Old Imperial script — celestial observation function
  • A cracked but sealed lacquer box containing brass astronomical instruments — grant advantage on celestial Navigation checks
  • A carved jade medallion bearing Kinryū's clan sigil — devotional; radiates faint warmth; worth 200gp
  • Tsukuyomi projection lens — deep red crystal, warm to the touch; moved here by the Kannushi from elsewhere in the temple (Observatory component #4 — originally hidden in the mess hall sealed jar by a priest during the fall; the Kannushi found and relocated it)

The full ceiling becomes visible and active once darkness ends. Silver and gemstone inlay responds to current celestial date. DC 14 Arcana or Nature (10 minutes study) reveals current celestial alignment and sei implications.

A character who spends a short rest seated on the dais (during a moonlit period, darkness lifted) receives the benefits of the Calm Emotions spell upon completing the rest, and has advantage on their first Wisdom saving throw before their next long rest. This is a one-time benefit per creature per visit.

  • Nagaji Kannushi (present and meditating on the dais when party arrives; fully hostile once triggered; has Devil Sight)
  • Present when the party arrives — meditating on the dais within the darkness; may have heard the party and chosen stillness
  • Devil Sight — sees in the darkness as bright light to 120 ft; is not imposed on by the darkness she created
  • Trigger: Loud noise, light spells directed toward her, or anyone crossing the darkness boundary
  • No non-combat resolution — she is fully hostile once triggered
  • Fights to protect the dais and urn — does not abandon them aggressively
  • If the party reaches the urn mid-combat and succeeds on DC 18 Religion: darkness collapses instantly

The Kannushi cursed the urn deliberately as a guardian measure — her intent is protective. She created the darkness to shield the space she has claimed. This is a ward, not corruption.

Relc's Vision: When the darkness lifts and the star map activates, green luminescence briefly appears in one constellation matching Solas's letter sigil — visible to Relc only, for a moment only. Pass note to player directly.

Relc's Moment (Dais): This is a meaningful space for Relc specifically. The Sacred Grove and the Golden Dragon Clan had a historical relationship — both traditions understood the sky as a living text. When Relc stands on the dais, Solas's next vision arrives: not words, not instruction — just the image of Solas in the grove above @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.glkgG2E8eJWrxCrm]{Koriwara}, one hand on a standing stone, dawn light striking it from the east. The vision lasts three seconds. It is quiet. It is pointing him home, after this is done.

The Last Observation — The Great Aphelion: The star map contains a fixed reference configuration etched into the obsidian floor — not projected by moonlight but carved permanently. It depicts all three stars (Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi) and all four moons at their maximum distance from Seizan: the Great Aphelion (formal in-world name TBD). This configuration appears to be the last documented celestial observation made by the temple's order. No subsequent observations were recorded, suggesting the temple fell at approximately the same time as this event. A character proficient in Arcana, History, or Navigator's Tools who studies this etching (DC 16) recognizes it as an extreme astronomical configuration — one that would occur only on cycles measured in millennia. A seimaster or Ancient Guard member would understand its potential connection to the sei drought. The party is unlikely to grasp the full significance without outside expertise, but the etching stands as physical evidence linking the temple's abandonment to a cosmic event.

What Was Taught Here: This room was the order's primary space for sei study linked to celestial alignment. Dragon-priests would sit for days on the dais, mapping the movements of the star shadows as the moon tracked across the shaft, correlating them with sei fluctuations they could feel in the mountain stone. The knowledge developed here fed into the Golden Dragon Clan's deep understanding of Kinryu's transformation-reversal work — the idea that sei corruption can be unmade through precise celestial timing. That insight is relevant to the Gekko situation, and a character who meditates here and succeeds on a DC 14 Arcana or History check intuits it: the stars matter. Whatever is broken, the sky must be right when it is mended.

Moral Weight: When the darkness lifts, the party sees what the Kannushi was guarding — the tidied floor, the arranged relics, the straightened shelf. She was not protecting a threat. She was tending a sanctuary. This lands without narration.

pages.name: The Mess Hall and Kitchen — Shokudo

text.content:
Read-Aloud — The Mess Hall and Kitchen

The hallway turns — south, then east — and the smell finds you before the room does. The fire was a long time ago. The smell of it is still here.

Not a fresh smell — old char, baked into stone so thoroughly it has become part of the stone.

The passage opens into a broad space — fifty feet across, fifty deep. Long low tables run the length of it. The ones nearest the kitchen archway to the west are charred down to their legs. The ones farther away have simply rotted, their surfaces caved in over years of neglect. Ceramic bowls are scattered across the floor, cracked and blackened, lying where they fell.

One bowl is upright. Intact. Set on the floor near the far wall as if someone placed it there.

Dark stains mark the stone in places. The occasional fragment of bone, scattered, has been here long enough to look like part of the room.

Through the kitchen archway to the west, the damage is worse. The ceiling there is black, scorched to a depth that centuries of stillness have not touched. The great central hearth has partially collapsed inward; the iron crane that hung above it is bent at an angle that suggests heat far beyond anything a cooking fire would produce. In the far wall, a section of mortar gave out — from the heat, from the cold, from something — leaving a ragged gap that lets in a thin blade of mountain air, clean and sharp against everything else in the room.

In the far corner of the kitchen, a larder door stands half-open. Inside, shapes on shelves that might have been preserved goods — jars, sacks, something — have collapsed into uniform grey dust.

Southwest wing, accessible via L-shaped hallway from the south side of the west E-W hallway.

Physical Description:

Accessed via an L-shaped hallway (10 ft wide) from the south side of the west wing — south 35 ft, then east 45 ft into the mess hall. No direct line of sight from the main corridor. Pervasive old char smell baked permanently into the stone. Draft of clean mountain air from a gap in the kitchen's west wall.

Mess Hall (50 ft × 50 ft): Long low tables running the length of the space. Tables nearest kitchen charred to legs; farther tables rotted, surfaces caved in. Cracked and blackened ceramic bowls scattered on the floor. Dark stains on stone. Scattered bone fragments. One ceramic bowl upright, intact, placed (not fallen) near the far wall — recently wiped clean of grime.

Kitchen (35 ft × 35 ft, west side of mess hall): Ceiling scorched black to significant depth. Great central hearth partially collapsed inward. Iron crane above hearth bent by extreme heat (far beyond normal cooking fire — this was a deliberate blaze). Gap in west wall mortar admits outside air and thin natural light.

Larder: Far corner of kitchen, door half-open. Shelved goods collapsed into uniform grey dust. Contains a sealed double-fired ceramic jar with intact wax seal (magical preservation).

  • The Intact Bowl (DC 13 Investigation)
  • The Sealed Jar — inscription (DC 14 Investigation) (Handout: "They are already inside. Hiroki knows.")

The Intact Bowl: The single upright, unbroken bowl is a small mystery with a simple answer — it was placed there by a Nagaji. They found it intact in the larder rubble and set it on the floor for reasons even they could not articulate. An instinct toward ritual. A faint echo of the person they used to be. DC 13 Investigation to notice the bowl has been wiped clean of grime, recently.

What Can Be Found: DC 14 Investigation in the larder reveals, beneath the uniform dust and decay: a sealed ceramic jar, double-fired with a wax seal that has held. Inside — preserved vegetables, technically still edible though profoundly unpleasant (the preservation is magical in nature, a minor kitchen enchantment common to the order). More importantly, scratched into the inside of the jar's lid in hasty characters: "They are already inside. Hiroki knows. The gate will not save us." This is a message from a priest who died in this room, writing in the moment of understanding. It is a handout. It confirms that the order's destruction came from within, not from outside assault.

Note: The Tsukuyomi projection lens was originally hidden in this jar by a priest during the fall. It has since been found and moved by the @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.monsters.Actor.OGA1LtjRQuabbHHR]{Nagaji Kannushi} to the Star Shrine (Okuden), where it now resides among the Kannushi's collected relics. The jar contains only the inscription and preserved vegetables.

  • 4 Yaminezumi (闇鼠 — "Darkness Rats"; nest in collapsed west wall section of kitchen; not aggressive unless cornered; carry Kegare no Yamai)

Yaminezumi (闇鼠 — Darkness Rats): Four Swarms of Rats (MM p.339) that have lived in the dark corruption of the temple long enough to have changed. They have nested in the collapsed section of the west wall. Not aggressive unless cornered. Their presence means something edible was here recently — they have been feeding on the Nagaji's food stores, which are stashed in the larder area. Carry Kegare no Yamai: On a successful hit, target makes a DC 12 Constitution saving throw or gains one stack of Kegare no Yamai (see floor-1/kegare-no-yamai.md).

The Fire: The kitchen fire was deliberate — set by the Akaryu/Kokuryu infiltrators as part of the final assault on the order. It was intended to drive the priests out of this wing and into the Grand Hall, cutting off retreat to the southern entrance and funneling the defenders. It worked. The conflict that killed most of the order happened in the dormitory corridor and the Grand Hall, not here.

Atmosphere: The room smells of old char and cold stone. The draft from the gap in the west wall carries mountain air — clean, sharp, a relief from the closed smell of the rest of the temple. Sound behaves normally here, unlike the shrine.

pages.name: Kegare no Yamai — Disease of Defilement

text.content:
Type: Curse (not disease)

Reflects kegare as spiritual pollution — a Shinto concept of ritual impurity — not physical illness. Removal requires Remove Curse (3rd level spell), not Lesser Restoration.

Transmission

Vector: Yaminezumi (闇鼠 — Darkness Rats) bite

On a successful hit, the target makes a DC 12 Constitution saving throw. Failure: gains one stack of Kegare no Yamai.

Effect

Each stack reduces Wisdom by 1.

  • Stacks accumulate — multiple failed saves = multiple stacks = increasing Wisdom reduction
  • Affects Insight, Perception, Wisdom saving throws, and spellcasting for Wisdom-based casters

Removal

  • Remove Curse spell removes all stacks
  • The restorative pools in the Grand Hall auto-cleanse on entry — 1 charge per stack removed

Read-Aloud — The Dormitories

A long corridor, wide enough for two people to walk side by side, with doors branching left and right. Most of the doors are open. At the far ends of the corridor, larger chambers.

The doors that are open were not left that way. The frames are splintered — forced inward, or outward, depending on the door. Several bear scoring at shoulder height, the kind left by edged weapons. Inside the cells: sleeping pallets collapsed into their own decay. Personal effects on hooks or shelves, long since fallen — a sandal, a cloth, a small painted tile lying face-down in the dust.

In the southern shared chamber, the evidence is heavier. Furniture was moved — pushed against walls, pushed away again, the drag marks visible in the grit. Impact marks at various heights. On the floor near the far wall, the stone itself is damaged: a starburst pattern, cracked outward from a central point.

The northern shared chamber is different. Its door has a bar, and the bar is in its brackets. This door was never forced. You lift the bar yourself and push the door open.

The air inside is old in the way only sealed places can be — still, and slightly too dry, as if the room has been holding its breath. The pallet inside holds a complete skeleton. They are facing the wall. They lay down on their own.

On the floor beside the pallet: a small bronze disc on a cord. An ink-block, dried to nothing. A sealed scroll case.

East wing — a long corridor with cells branching left and right, plus larger shared quarters at the north and south ends.

Physical Description:

East wing, 120 ft from center intersection. Dormitory complex connects to both the north and south sides of the E-W hallway. Colder than the Grand Hall — an unnatural cold associated with accumulated violence, not mountain temperature.

North-side dormitory (accessible): Long corridor, two-person width, with eight individual cells — four west (Cells 1, 3, 5, 7), four east (Cells 2, 4, 6, 8). Most doors forced open — frames splintered inward or outward, some bearing edged-weapon scoring at shoulder height.

South-side dormitory (entrance collapsed — sealing kept it intact): The entrance from the E-W hallway was deliberately collapsed by the priests during the fall, and the rubble has done its job. The wing beyond is relatively pristine — the collapse spared it the looting, defacement, and weather-rot that have worn the rest of the temple over the intervening millennia. Doors still on their hinges. Personal effects still on shelves where they were left. No Nagaji ever reached it. Access requires clearing the rubble (hours; loud) or an alternate route via the second floor or the cavern system below; the wing is a time capsule of the order's last day, preserved by the very act of sealing.

Sealed room (Senior Priests' Quarters): Heavy wooden door, barred from inside; bar visible through gap at base. Beyond: 20 ft × 20 ft; four sleeping platforms, each occupied by skeletal remains. Remains are deliberate — hands folded, bodies oriented toward room's center. They chose this. On the writing desk: scroll case (Last Record of Priest Tomohiro) + bronze disc — left in plain sight, meant to be found.

Cell Layout

Cell Side Notable Feature Onryō
1 West Faded star chart drawings on wall Yes
2 East Single intact ceramic cup, upright, perfectly centered on shelf Yes
3 West Starburst damage — scorched walls, cracked floor, platform obliterated Yes — most volatile
4 East Personal effects scattered; sandal near doorway as if left mid-step Yes
5 West Swept clean — deliberately tidied after the fall; platform scrape marks No
6 East Nagaji-searched — contents pulled, platform overturned No
7 West Small devotional Kinryū carving still upright on shelf No
8 East Door frame scorched — caught edge of Cell 3 discharge No
  • Cell 3 — Starburst Damage (DC 14 Arcana; DC 17 Arcana for reconstruction)
  • Cell 5 — Swept Clean (intentionally unresolved)
  • Cell 6 — Planetary Gear Assembly (DC 13 Investigation) (Observatory component #2)
  • The Sealed Room — Priest Tomohiro's remains (DC 12 Thieves' Tools to open scroll case) (Handout: Last Record of Priest Tomohiro)
  • The Bronze Disc — orbital engravings (DC 13 Investigation) (Observatory component: calibration disc)
  • Evidence of the Nagaji — searched cells
  • DC 14 Arcana: identifies sei discharge as cause — magical energy released suddenly without control
  • DC 17 Arcana: reconstructs the attempt — a priest tried to weaponize their own sei reserves in a single concentrated release against something already in the corridor; discharge was too large and uncontrolled; killed the priest and damaged Cell 8 through the shared wall

Someone tidied this cell after the fall — older than the Nagaji's arrival. Platform moved deliberately, replaced; nothing beneath it now. Intentionally unresolved — possible connection to Tomohiro.

DC 13 Investigation locates the planetary gear assembly — seven interlocking bronze rings of graduated size, partially disassembled, discarded in debris under overturned platform. The rings are nested concentrically, each engraved with tiny orbital notations in Old Imperial. The outermost ring is bent but not broken. A character proficient in Tinker's Tools, Smith's Tools, or Navigator's Tools recognizes this as a precision gear mechanism — a planetary drive designed to model multiple simultaneous orbital periods through a single input rotation. DC 14 History (DC 11 for Ko'jiri) connects the orbital notations to the seven known planets of the Miyosai system. (Observatory component: planetary gear assembly. The Nagaji found it, examined it, could not understand it, and discarded it.)

The priests who sealed themselves in were not hiding — they were staying. They had made their peace and chose not to participate in the violence. Four sleeping platforms, each occupied by skeletal remains — hands folded, bodies oriented toward the room's center. The sealed room has been untouched since their death.

Breaking the door: AC 15, 40 HP. Alternatively, the bar can be lifted through the gap at the base (DC 12 Thieves' Tools or Dexterity check).

On the writing desk: The scroll case (DC 12 Thieves' Tools or carefully broken open) contains a last account — a personal record of the final days, from Priest Tomohiro's perspective. This is a major handout (see Handout: The Last Record of Priest Tomohiro) detailing how the infiltrators were discovered too late, who gave the order to seal the inner sanctum, and the name of the head infiltrator — a detail that, with a DC 17 History check, connects to a lineage that still exists in present-day Kagekuni.

The bronze disc is a formal order seal, granting the bearer recognition as a member of the Golden Dragon order — useful as a key within the temple for certain sealed areas (specifically the Jushoku no Ma hidden door).

The Bronze Disc — Additional Detail: The reverse face of the disc bears fine engravings invisible without close examination (DC 13 Investigation or automatic if studying the disc under good light). Concentric rings scored into the bronze correspond to orbital tracks, with seven small notches along the outer edge and four along an inner ring. A character who has found the planetary gear assembly recognizes the match immediately — the disc is designed to seat into a mechanical device as a positional reference. (Observatory component: calibration disc. When seated in the orrery's control interface, it establishes the reference date from which the mechanism can advance or rewind. The order seal and calibration key were the same object — the person authorized to operate the observatory was, by definition, a member of the order.)

Two of the individual cells (including Cell 6) show recent disturbance — the dust displaced, a pallet dragged aside to reveal the floor. The Nagaji have been searching these rooms. What they were looking for is unclear, but the cells they searched belonged (per the scroll case record) to the two most senior non-priest scholars of the order. Whatever those scholars possessed or knew, something is looking for it.

  • 4 Uragiri no Onryō (裏切りの怨霊 — "Vengeful Spirits of Betrayal"; Specters, MM p.279 — Cells 1, 2, 3, 4)

Corrupted priests who were the infiltrating force that destroyed the order from within. Named to reflect the specific sin that defines them — not just evil, but betrayers of the order they swore to serve. Each haunts a specific cell — emerge when the corridor is disturbed.

Trigger: Corridor disturbed (loud noise, running, light brought close to an occupied cell, combat vibration from elsewhere in the temple)

Initial state: Confused and territorial — emerge from cells, move erratically, cannot fully perceive the party. Window of non-hostility.

Escalation to hostility: Party attacks any of the four, OR the sealed room is interfered with disrespectfully (forcing door loudly, attempting to break it).

Respectful entry (picking the bar, asking permission aloud, moving quietly) does not trigger escalation.

Cell 3 spirit: Manifests first if party lingers near Cell 3 without triggering combat. Most volatile. Use Specter (MM p.279) with maximum HP and one additional action option.

De-escalation: A character who speaks to them calmly in any language (the intent reads through, even across the language barrier) and succeeds on a DC 14 Persuasion check can quiet one Onryō; it dissipates with a sound like a long exhale.

Atmosphere: The dormitory wing is colder than the Grand Hall. The cold is not mountain cold — it is the specific cold of places where violence has accumulated. Even mundane characters should feel uneasy here without knowing why.

Entrance deliberately collapsed by the priests during the fall — and the seal protected what lay behind it. The south wing is relatively pristine: no Nagaji incursion, no ambient looting, no weather damage, no later defacement. Furniture remains where it was set down. Personal effects (sandals at the door, a folded robe across a bed, an inkstone with the cake of dried ink still on it) sit as if their owners stepped out for a moment. The dust is heavy but undisturbed. The bodies of those who did not make it to the sealed senior chamber lie where they fell — most along the corridor, a few in their own cells, posture suggesting flight rather than resistance.

The contents inside are still being designed; treat the wing as a preservation goldmine when access opens — intact ritual implements, clothing, personal scrolls, household objects from the order's daily life that survive nowhere else in Hokori. Specifics: TBD before the party gains access. Establish them in response to the path the party takes to get in (clearing rubble vs. cavern approach vs. floor 2 descent), since the manner of arrival shapes which corner of the wing they reach first.

  • Tomohiro's scroll — contents to be drafted (significant handout; bridges dormitory and Jushoku no Ma)
  • South dormitory contents — establish before party gains access; the wing is intact and preservation-rich, so the canon answer can be generous
  • Cell 5 swept clean — decide whether to connect to Tomohiro or leave unresolved

"The Celestial Ring" — the ring corridor that surrounds the great aperture above Hiroba.

Physical Description:

The stairs from the first floor — both west and east — emerge onto a broad ring corridor 20 ft wide that surrounds a circular aperture roughly 80 ft across, open to the Grand Hall below. The aperture is unrailed at the inner edge except for a low stone parapet, waist-high, set back two feet from the lip. The parapet is the offering wall.

Through the aperture: Kinryū rises. The statue's coiled body fills the lower half of the opening; the great head and forelimbs lift through the upper half into the space of the second floor itself, the inlaid amber eyes now level with whoever stands at the parapet. Looking up at the statue from Hiroba is one experience. Standing eye-to-eye with it is another. The warmth that radiates within thirty feet of the statue on the first floor reaches here too — stronger, more present, the way standing near a hearth differs from standing near its smoke.

The Offering Plates — Seven Around the Ring:

Set into the parapet at seven positions around the ring are shallow stone offering plates, each roughly the size of a soup bowl, recessed into the stone so the plate lip sits flush with the parapet's upper surface. Six of the seven are equidistant — spaced 51.4° apart around the ring. The seventh, at true north, is anchored to the cardinal point and is distinct: larger, raised slightly above the parapet line, framed in a halo of inlaid gold leaf. The other six are bronze, plain, mounted at the cardinal and intercardinal points around the remaining ring.

Each plate corresponds to one of the seven Progenitor dragons. Going clockwise from north:

Position Progenitor Plate condition
N (anchor) Kinryū (Golden) Raised, gold-leaf halo intact, polished — the only plate the dust does not seem to settle on
NE Akaryū (Crimson) Bronze; soot-blackened, edges scorched; appears to have been struck by fire long ago — but untouched by chisel or hammer
E Aoryū (Azure) Bronze; verdigris-green, salt-pitted; faint blue patina blooms outward across the parapet stone
SE Midoryū (Emerald) Bronze; rim overgrown with dry moss; thin root tendrils have crept up the parapet from somewhere below
SW Kokuryū (Onyx) Bronze; pristine — no soot, no decay, no vandalism; the metal is dark but bright, as though recently cleaned
W Ginryū (Silver) Bronze; tarnished but mirror-bright in spots; pinprick star-patterns etched into the rim catch torchlight
NW Murasakiryū (Amethyst) Bronze; defaced — the dragon's name and any identifying glyphs have been chiseled out, the surrounding stone gouged. Not battle damage. Methodical, single-purpose work, done with patience. The chisel marks are not the same age as the rest of the temple's deliberate desecrations.

The Shrine — South Wall:

Directly opposite the Kinryū plate, set into the south wall of the ring corridor at the inner edge, is a small shrine — a recessed alcove, three feet wide, four feet deep, six feet high. Inside: a single carved kneeling stone before a low altar of dark lacquered wood. Above the altar, a relief carving of Kinryū descending — head lowered, forelimbs extended, the same posture as the great statue. No incense burner. No offering vessels. The shrine is for prayer, not for objects. The altar itself is unblemished.

The South Wall — Portal Frame:

Flanking the shrine on the south wall is an arched opening sealed by a flat plane of polished stone — no door, no seam, no hinge. The arch frame is inlaid with a band of gold script in old liturgical Draconic, running unbroken around the perimeter. The script is dim. The stone within the frame is solid — testing it confirms it is not a door but a wall. (When activated, the plane becomes a portal.)

The North Wall — Scorch Marks:

The entire north wall of the ring corridor — fifty feet of stone — is blackened with scorch patterns. Concentric blast rings, dozens of them, overlapping. The damage is old; the stone has not crumbled. Something held the wall together against blasts that should have demolished it. The scorch marks are external — they happened to the wall, not from it. A character standing close can still smell, faintly, the burned-air scent of long-spent fire magic. Beyond this wall: the Hidden Archives. The wall does not yield. It has not yielded for thousands of years.

The Northeast Doorway — Orrery:

A single tall doorway in the NE quadrant of the ring opens into a circular domed chamber — the Hoshikagami no Ma, the Chamber of the Star Mirror. The doorway has no door; it is open. The dome is visible from the threshold.

The Northwest Doorway — Brood Sanctum:

In the NW quadrant, a heavy wooden door — bronze-banded, closed, intact. Old. Whatever is behind it has been kept behind it. The door is not locked but it is not loose; opening it requires deliberate effort.

Lighting:

Gold sconces ring the corridor at the same seven-foot spacing as the South Entrance. Most still burn — the cold blue-white of the temple's foundational enchantment. Light falls clearly across the parapet and the offering plates. The aperture is bright. The shadows are at the corners of the ring corridor, where the sconces cannot reach.

  • The Aperture and the Statue (passive — automatic)
  • The Offering Plates — Pattern of Damage (DC 12 Investigation)
  • The Two Untouched Plates (DC 14 History or Religion; DC 11 for Ko'jiri)
  • The Defaced Amethyst Plate (DC 15 History or Investigation)
  • The Shrine — Function (DC 13 Religion)
  • The Sealed Portal Frame (DC 14 Arcana)
  • The Activation Ritual (multiple paths — see below)
  • The Scorch-Marked North Wall (DC 12 Arcana for damage age; DC 15 Arcana for the wall's resistance)
  • The Anti-Teleport Wards (DC 16 Arcana)

The Aperture: Looking down through the opening, the party stands eye-to-eye with the statue's head. Anyone with a connection to the statue (Ko'jiri, primarily) feels the connection more strongly here than they did in the Hiroba — closer, more present, the way meeting someone's eyes differs from seeing them across a room. Ko'jiri may experience an involuntary moment of recognition. The amber eyes have been waiting at exactly this height for a very long time.

The Offering Plates — Pattern of Damage: A character who examines the plates around the ring (DC 12 Investigation) registers that the damage is not uniform — most plates show wear, decay, or deliberate harm consistent with the rest of the temple, but two plates (NE Crimson, SW Onyx) show no sign of vandalism. Crimson is fire-damaged but the damage is environmental, not directed. Onyx is essentially untouched. This is anomalous. Other plates (Murasakiryū particularly, but also others) bear chisel marks and gouges that the Crimson and Onyx plates do not.

The Two Untouched Plates — DC 14 History (DC 11 for Ko'jiri): A character with knowledge of the Golden Dragon order's fall recognizes what the absence implies. The temple was infiltrated by agents of two specific Progenitor lines: the Akaryū (Crimson) and Kokuryū (Onyx) clans. Those agents would not have desecrated the offering plates of their own patrons. The pattern of damage on this ring is a record of who did the damage, not who was damaged. The party now knows, with reasonable certainty, that the temple's fall was an inside job carried out by Crimson and Onyx infiltrators. (This is information the temple's first-floor canon supports through the tapestries and head priest's records — the offering ring confirms it spatially.)

The Defaced Amethyst Plate — DC 15 History or Investigation: The vandalism on Murasakiryū's plate is different from the temple's other deliberate desecrations. The temple's general defacement (pillar carvings, head-priest tapestry face) is consistent in tool, technique, and approximate age — done during or shortly after the fall, ~13088. The chisel marks on the Amethyst plate are newer. The cuts are sharper, the edges of the gouges less weathered. Someone returned to this temple, possibly long after the fall, specifically to erase Murasakiryū's name. The work was careful and singular — only the Amethyst plate was touched. A character who notices the age discrepancy may ask who, and when, and why. The temple does not answer. (DM: see DM Notes for sealed context.)

The Shrine — Function: DC 13 Religion identifies the shrine as a personal-prayer alcove dedicated to Kinryū — the kind of recessed shrine common to Golden Dragon temples for direct supplication. The absence of incense burners or offering vessels is intentional: this shrine accepts the prayer itself, not material offerings. The relief above the altar mirrors the great statue's posture — the supplicant kneels and offers their prayer to the same form they can see, alive in stone, through the aperture behind them. The architecture is a single integrated devotional act.

The Sealed Portal Frame: DC 14 Arcana on the gold-script arch reveals it as a teleportation gate frame, currently inert. The script is in old liturgical Draconic and reads, approximately: "By honor offered to the seven, by prayer offered to the one, the path opens." The Arcana check confirms the gate is keyed — it requires a specific activation sequence, not raw magical force. Brute-force attempts (Dispel Magic, Knock, etc.) on the seal do nothing visible.

The Activation Ritual: The full sequence is discoverable through several paths:

Path Method DC
Direct interpretation Read the gold-script inscription DC 16 History (DC 13 with Comprehend Languages)
Religious knowledge Recognize the Golden Dragon's "sevenfold tribute" rite DC 16 Religion (DC 13 for Ko'jiri)
Trial and experimentation Place a coin in any plate; observe response Automatic (see below)
Hidden archive (after entry) The rite is documented in full Automatic — but circular: the archive is what the gate leads to

The activation sequence:

  1. A gold coin (1 gp value or higher; the metal matters, not the denomination) must be placed in each of the seven offering plates. The order does not matter. Each coin placed produces a faint warm hum from the plate that receives it; partial completion (one through six plates) does nothing further.
  2. Once all seven plates hold gold, a prayer must be offered at the south shrine — kneeling on the prayer stone, hands together, prayer offered aloud to Kinryū. The prayer's content does not matter; the act of supplication does. The shrine recognizes sincerity, not script.
  3. On completion of the prayer, the gold-script around the south arch warms to bright gold, the stone within the arch becomes translucent, and the portal opens. The portal is a one-way teleport: stepping through transports the supplicant into the hallway leading to the Hidden Archives (see rm-hidden-archives). Multiple supplicants can pass through in sequence; the portal remains open for ten minutes after activation, then seals again. The gold coins remain in the plates and are not consumed — they may be retrieved after the ritual completes, but doing so closes the portal immediately.

The Scorch-Marked North Wall — Damage Age: DC 12 Arcana confirms the blasts were fireball-class evocation, multiple casters, sustained over time. The carbon scoring carries trace sei residue old enough that it predates everything the party has seen elsewhere — fall-period damage, ~13088. The attackers did not breach.

The Wall's Resistance — DC 15 Arcana: The wall is not merely thick. A skilled arcanist registers that the wall consumed the magical energy of the blasts — absorbed them rather than resisted them. The damage on the surface is residual heat and physical scoring; the magical force was diverted, drained, or dissipated by the wall's own enchantment before it could do structural harm. This is foundational magic, not battle warding — the same construction-level enchantment that powers the sconces and preserves the great statue. The temple's builders anticipated that someone would try this. They built the archives wall to last forever.

The Anti-Teleport Wards — DC 16 Arcana: A character who probes the wall, or who attempts teleportation magic anywhere on this floor, registers a layered warding field that extends through the floor, ceiling, and outer walls of the second floor's northern half. The field nullifies inbound and outbound magical teleportation specifically targeting the archives or its approach hallway. Misty step, dimension door, teleport, plane shift — all fail with no visible effect except a faint chime in the spellcaster's ears. The south-wall portal is the singular exception: it is woven into the warding rather than penetrating it, an authorized exit built by the same hands that built the wards. There is no other way in.

(No combat encounters in this room under normal circumstances. The Nagaji have not reached the second floor — the western and eastern stairs are undisturbed, per rm-central-hallway. Should the Nagaji track the party up, this is an open arena with deadly fall hazard: an unwitting enemy pushed over the parapet drops ~30 ft to the Grand Hall floor, taking 3d6 falling damage and likely landing among the offering debris near the statue's base.)

Tactical features if combat occurs:

  • The aperture is a falling hazard for anyone within 5 ft of the parapet. Shove (Athletics contest) or forced movement effects can push targets into the void. Falling onto the statue itself (within the 30 ft warmth radius on the way down) does not heal but does reduce cold damage by 1d4 per the statue's passive effect.
  • The ring corridor is 20 ft wide — wide enough for melee but narrow enough that ranged combatants cannot easily flank.
  • The two unactivated doorways (NE to orrery, NW to Brood Sanctum) provide cover and retreat options. The NW door is heavy and slows passage; the NE doorway has no door at all.
  • The shrine alcove is a tight defensive position (3 ft wide × 4 ft deep) — one defender at the threshold, no flanking possible. A combatant who occupies it is hard to dislodge.

The Two Untouched Plates — Confirming The Inside Job: This is the spatial confirmation of what the tapestries and head priest's journal already imply. Crimson and Onyx infiltrators desecrated everything they could reach but spared their own progenitors' plates. A party that picks up on the pattern (DC 12 Investigation, then DC 14 History) gains certainty that the temple's fall was a Crimson+Onyx joint operation. This dovetails with [Tapestry II — Rite of the Golden Flame] (which catches an infiltrator in the image) and the operational ledger from [Jushoku no Ma] (which records the order's inability to identify all the traitors before the end).

The Defaced Amethyst Plate — The Sealed Layer: This is the campaign's most subtle Murasakiryū breadcrumb. The defacement is not contemporary with the temple's fall. Someone returned, much later, specifically to erase Murasakiryū's name from this ring. Two readings, both true, both sealed:

  1. The Order of the Ancient Guard has been working — across centuries — to suppress public memory of Murasakiryū as a Progenitor. The Amethyst defacement is one of many small acts of erasure across Kagekuni. The Guard's working theory (still unproven to themselves) is that Murasakiryū's awareness can be partially insulated by removing focal points of devotion. Whether this works at all is unknown; they continue regardless.

  2. The deeper, more dangerous reading: Murasakiryū herself, working through cultists or compromised individuals, has been quietly removing references to her existence as a Progenitor — because being acknowledged as Murasakiryū interferes with her ongoing masquerade as Kokuryū. If the world remembers there is a seventh dragon, the world might start asking which one it actually has.

The party will not resolve this here. The defacement is a quiet question they carry forward. If they later encounter similar defacements at other shrines, the pattern may resolve.

Pristine Onyx Plate — The Layered Trap: The Kokuryū plate's pristine condition reads to the party as evidence that Onyx infiltrators spared their patron. That reading is correct — and incomplete. What the party does not know is that honoring the Kokuryū plate (by placing a gold coin during the ritual) channels supplication through the Onyx position to the dragon currently occupying that domain in mortal awareness — Murasakiryū. The activation ritual, performed in good faith by the party, briefly registers their honor in Murasakiryū's awareness. This does not harm them and produces no immediate visible effect. It is a flag the dragon has noticed. Whether and how this matters in the campaign is a long-game thread — file under "Murasakiryū has now seen them" rather than under "trap."

Activation Without All Seven Plates: A creative party may attempt to skip a plate (e.g., refuse to honor Kokuryū). The ritual does not activate with six. The frame remains inert. There is no penalty for trying — the system simply does not engage. This is a choice the party can make; it costs them access to the archives. They may find another way (none currently exists; the wards are absolute), or they may choose to honor all seven and accept the cost. The honest framing for the table: "the rite is the rite, and the rite asks for all seven."

The Scorch Marks — Whose Fireballs: The fireballs that did not breach were cast by the infiltrators, after they had killed or transformed most of the surviving order. They knew what was in the archives and they tried to take it by force. The wards held. The infiltrators left. The archives still hold what they were trying to take. (What they were trying to take is the Vigil-Oath dismissal rite for Akiyo and the full Gekkō-reversal documentation — the same documents that would, in modern hands, allow the party to release Akiyo and reverse the Nagaji transformation. The infiltrators were trying to permanently sever both lifelines.)

Pacing: This room is the second floor's hub. Most floor-2 activity returns here — to enter the orrery, to enter Brood Sanctum, to attempt the archives. Treat it as a recurring waypoint, not a destination. The first-time entry should land the dragon's eye-level moment (Ko'jiri especially), the parapet's ring of plates, and the silence of the scorch-marked wall. Subsequent visits should feel different in tone — the party knows where it is going.

Connected entries: rm-orrery-chamber (NE), rm-brood-sanctum-approach (NW), rm-hidden-archives (N, accessed via south portal), rm-central-hallway (stairs down), rm-grand-hall (visible through aperture).

pages.name: Hoshikagami no Ma — Chamber of the Star Mirror

text.content:
The orrery chamber. NE doorway off the Tenkairō.

Detailed mechanics — repair sequence, component checklist, projection states across the Great Aphelion timeline, and tapestry activation propagation — live in the supplement rm-observatory-repair-mechanics. This room file covers the physical chamber and its current state. Refer to the supplement for everything else.

Physical Description:

A circular domed chamber, 60 ft across, ceiling rising 35 ft to the apex of the dome. The dome's interior is etched with constellation guides — pinpoint engravings filled with traces of silver leaf, faded but still legible where the lacquer has held. The floor is polished obsidian, similar to the Star Shrine on the first floor but oriented differently — concentric rings inlaid in dark bronze radiate outward from the central plinth.

At the chamber's heart: the mechanical-arcane orrery. A vertical spindle rises from the center of the floor to the dome's apex; around it, fourteen bronze armatures of varying length and inclination orbit in a frozen tableau — three for the stars, four for the moons, seven for the planets. Each armature terminates in a mounting cradle. Six cradles are empty. Three hold projection lenses still in place — Amaterasu (golden, central, cracked), and two minor planetary mounts. Four lunar armatures are missing entirely from their slots.

The central spindle is bronze, intricately geared, seized — the mechanism has not turned in millennia. Dust and grit have settled into the gear track. A control interface ring at the spindle's base shows a recessed circular slot for a calibration disc and a row of small push-rods that look like date inputs.

The chamber is silent. The acoustic dampening of the dome is so complete that the sound of the party's breath returns slightly and slowly, as though through deep water.

Lighting: Two cold-flame sconces flank the doorway. The chamber's primary lighting was always meant to be the orrery itself — projection light filling the dome from within. With the mechanism dormant, the chamber is mostly dark. Beyond the sconces' reach, the dome and its constellation etchings are visible only as suggestions.

Current State

What is in this chamber as the party enters:

  • The orrery, dormant. The Amaterasu lens (component #6) cracked but still mounted. The stellar drive (component #7) seized. Both are repairable in place.
  • The dome's constellation etchings, intact.
  • The control interface, awaiting the calibration disc.
  • No loose components in this room. Components #8 (lunar armature set) and #9 (operator's manual) are not here — they were moved to the Scriptorium on the first floor before the temple fell, along with the four lunar armatures already removed from their slots.

See rm-observatory-repair-mechanics for the full repair sequence, projection states, and tapestry-activation effects.

Refer to rm-observatory-repair-mechanics § Stage 1 — Assessment for the entry-point checks (DC 12 Investigation/Arcana, DC 14 History, DC 14 Tinker's/Smith's Tools).

Specific to this room:

  • The Dome's Constellation Etchings (DC 13 Arcana or Navigator's Tools)
  • The Acoustic Dampening (passive)
  • The Empty Cradles (visible)

The Dome's Constellation Etchings: A character with celestial knowledge (DC 13 Arcana or Navigator's Tools) identifies the engraved star map as the fixed sky — the constellations as they appear from this latitude under ideal conditions, independent of the moving stars. The etching is reference, not projection: it tells the operator what should be, against which the orrery's projection plays out what is. With the orrery operational, the projected stars and the etched stars overlay; deviations — like the Great Aphelion's withdrawal — are visible as an absence against the fixed background.

The Acoustic Dampening: The dome's geometry is acoustically engineered. Sound made within the chamber returns as a faint, slightly delayed echo. Sound from outside the chamber — including the Nagaji moving on the first floor, including any combat in the Tenkairō — does not carry into this room at all. The chamber is, effectively, a sealed acoustic environment. This is intentional: an operator working the orrery needed to hear the mechanism, not the temple.

The Empty Cradles: Six of the fourteen mounting cradles are empty. A DC 12 Investigation identifies which: Susanoo and Tsukuyomi (stellar projection lenses, both first-floor components — see rm-grand-hall and rm-star-shrine), and four of the lunar armatures (currently in the first-floor Scriptorium). The remaining two cradles are minor planetary mounts that did not require lenses originally. The orrery's design is legible: a competent operator could read the room and know what is missing.

(No combat encounters. The chamber's acoustic isolation makes it a safe-haven for short rests, provided the party has secured the Tenkairō behind them. The orrery itself, if disturbed clumsily, can produce mechanical hazards — a falling armature, a snapped gear chain — but these are repair complications, not creatures.)
