Flow with the supplement: This room's content is intentionally light because the heavy lifting — repair stages, projection sequences, tapestry activation, character moments (Ko'jiri, Relc, Sun Wukong, Dian Wei) — already lives in rm-observatory-repair-mechanics. Treat that supplement as the primary text for any session that engages the orrery. This room file is the spatial frame.

Component count after Scriptorium relocation: With the Scriptorium on floor 1, components #8 (lunar armature set) and #9 (operator's manual) are first-floor finds. Floor 2 contains only #6 (Amaterasu lens) and #7 (stellar drive), both in the orrery itself. The party reaches floor 2 with up to 7 of 9 components already in hand — the in-place repairs are the last work. See rm-observatory-repair-mechanics for the updated repair flow.

The first repair moment: Even partial activation (Amaterasu alone) fills the dome with golden light. After thousands of years of darkness, this is a powerful moment — describe the dust settling, the etched constellations catching gold, the Amaterasu armature's slow first revolution. Players who have been carrying components without context get their answer here. Let it land.

Connected entries: rm-tenkairo (NE doorway leads here), rm-observatory-repair-mechanics (repair sequence supplement), rm-tapestries-of-kinko-no-mon (tapestry activation upon full restoration).

pages.name: The Approach — Hallway and Brood Guardian

text.content:
What the Players See

The players reach the second-floor landing and find:

  • A pile of Nagaji bodies stacked outside a closed door. Not strewn from combat — arranged, deliberate, intentional. (Insight or Investigation DC 12 to recognize the placement is deliberate; DC 16 to read it as a warning marker rather than a trophy display.)
  • The door is closed but in surprisingly good condition — clean, unsplintered, the wood bright against the temple's general decay. Unlocked.
  • Beyond the door, a pristine hallway. No blood, no scuffs, no signs of struggle. The contrast with the bodies outside is sharp.

The Brood Guardian

A guardian of the Kinryū order stands at the far end of the hallway. She does not react to the door being opened. She does not turn her head, does not challenge, does not move. She is not inert — she is waiting.

The Nagaji bodies were arranged by the guardian herself. When Nagaji intruders push into the temple and reach this floor, she dispatches them inside the hallway, then carries the bodies out and arranges them at the threshold. The arrangement serves two purposes: it keeps her hallway clean (a sacred space, kept sacred), and it serves as a warning to whatever comes next.

The bodies are recent. The chamber's stasis distorts time slightly in the hallway — bodies decay slowly. To the party, the dead look killed within the last day or two. They were not.

Players may piece this together by Insight or by asking the guardian directly once she speaks. She will not lie about it.

The Guardian's Response — Three States

The moment any character steps fully into the hallway, the guardian addresses them. Her response is determined by the party's prior conduct in the temple. The DM chooses the state based on what the party has actually done on the lower floors.

The state is determined by the party's record in the temple, communicated to the guardian through the temple's architecture (see Her Awareness, below).

State A — Hostile

State A — Hostile (the party has been actively damaging the temple)

Triggered by: looting sacred objects, defacing inscriptions, breaking architecture, attacking temple animations or wildlife without provocation, treating the site as a dungeon to plunder.

"A flame that feeds on shattered lacquer burns bright but not long. You have burned bright in this place. I am the wind that decides whether it continues. I am the hand Kinryū-sama set against those who would harm her house. Withdraw, atone, or be answered. Choose your next step carefully — I will not warn twice."

Her tone is stark and hostile. She does not draw a weapon — yet — but the air around her sharpens. The party should feel they are one wrong step from a fight they will not enjoy.

If the party persists in destructive behavior after this warning, she attacks. Her stat block is built when the chamber comes into play (TBD). She does not pursue beyond the hallway — she will not cross the threshold of the door, and she will not leave her post. A party that flees combat with her can escape unharmed once they pass the door.

The portal does not open for those who have fled her. The chamber's threshold at the far end of the hallway is sealed; only her permission opens it (see The Portal, below). A party that engages her and runs has barred itself from the chamber until they have re-earned passage. Recovery is the same path as below.

Recovery from State A: Possible but not easy. The party must visibly un-do the damage they have done — restore what they broke, return what they took, perform a meaningful act of atonement at one of the temple's lower-floor altars. The temple watches; her mood shifts when the architecture's feeling shifts. The bar should be high but not unreachable.

State B — Neutral

State B — Neutral (the default)

Triggered by: the party has been respectful or indifferent to the temple — neither plundering nor restoring. Most parties will land here on their first arrival.

"The hand that would lift a sleeping child must first be steady. You have not yet shown me a steady hand. Many have stood where you stand. Few have walked beyond. The chamber I guard does not measure strength. By oath sworn to the Golden Progenitor and to those who fell defending this house, I am set against any who would pass unproven. Go, learn what this place has lost. Return when you understand."

Her tone is procedural. Not hostile, not welcoming. She is a judge with a specific mandate.

She does not specify what "proving yourself worthy" requires — she does not, in fact, know what would qualify in any specific sense. The temple decides; she relays.

The party must leave and engage with the temple's restoration before she will pass them through. The orrery is the canonical example — a damaged or dormant device on the lower floors that, when repaired, signals to the foundational architecture that someone here cares. The DM may seed other restoration acts in the lower floors if the party engages elsewhere.

State C — Welcoming

State C — Welcoming (the party has performed meaningful restoration)

Triggered by: the party has visibly restored or honored the temple — repaired the orrery, completed a similar restoration act, or performed a deeply respectful ritual gesture.

"A garden tended by sincere hands knows them when they return. You have tended. I bear witness: you have honored this house, and by that witness you may pass. Go forward. All may walk in; only one may kneel. Beyond this hall, step lightly, step sincerely — the chamber answers no falsehood, and She remembers all. What you do matters less than why. She measures no skill — She measures the heart you bring to it. Mean what you do. She will know the difference."

Her tone shifts — not warm, but no longer guarded. She steps aside.

"She will know the difference" is a reference to Kinryū. The guardian knows whose chamber this is. The players will not know yet — but the moment when the candidate hears Kinryū's voice in the chamber and the moment they recall the guardian's "She" should land together.

"Only one may kneel" establishes the bond's exclusivity up front. The party should understand they are choosing a candidate before anyone settles onto the pad. The chamber will enforce this regardless, but advance notice gives the party a roleplay moment to choose deliberately.

Her Awareness

The guardian has stood at this post for thousands of years. She is not, however, an active observer. She does not see what passes in the temple. She does not hear what is said three rooms away. She does not remember the faces of those who came before. She is bound to the temple's foundational architecture, and the temple speaks to her through impressions — a positive feeling when those it watches honor the place; a negative feeling when they violate it. She acts on those feelings, not on knowledge.

What she remembers, she remembers as feeling. What she does not feel, she does not know. Time has passed but has not collected in her — she has been present without being awake.

This shapes every conversation the party tries to have with her. Each state has its own response to questions:

Q&A — State A

State A — She does not speak

She has issued her warning. She will not issue another. If addressed, she rises (if seated), draws her Naginata, and stares at the party in silence. Continued attempts to engage her — questions, pleas, demands — are met with the blade. The conversation is over. The party's only remaining input is action: leave, atone, or fight.

Q&A — State B

State B — Direct rebuke

She answers questions, but only one way: she does not. Her role is to protect these chambers, not to counsel travelers. Sample lines (vary the phrasing to taste):

"I am not here to answer. I am here to bar." "My voice is set against the unproven, not in service to them. Walk on." "You ask me what the temple wants. The temple does not whisper to me, and I do not whisper to you." "This is a threshold, not a council. Cross it when you may." "Save your questions for the place that has answers. I am not it."

She is not unkind. She is simply unyielding on this point. She will not be moved by clever framing or persistent pressure. The party gets the same answer in different words for as long as they ask.

Q&A — State C

State C — Apologetic denial

The shift in her demeanor extends to her conversation. She is willing to engage, but quickly reveals the shape of her limits — she remembers nothing in detail. Time has passed, she knows; what filled it does not return to her.

"I would tell you, if I knew. The years have moved through me, but they have not stayed. I am sorry." "There were others, before you. I am certain of it. Their faces — no. The temple kept them. I did not." "You ask of the fall of this house. I felt the shape of it. I cannot tell you the words." "What I knew, I knew once. The place keeps its memory in stone and in star, not in me. Forgive me." "My oath is sharper than my recollection. Both have held a long time."

The fuzziness is not a memory bug — it is a feature of how the temple bound her. She was made to outlast her own memory. A guardian who remembers the order's fall in detail would carry grief incompatible with her duty; a guardian who remembers the egg's placement would speak its location to anyone who asked. The architecture protects her, and through her, the chamber.

What she can do, in State C, is point. If pressed about what lies beyond the chamber, she may say something like, "There is a child. I know that without knowing how I know." If pressed about Kinryū, she may say, "She sleeps. She has always slept. I have always known where, though I could not tell you if I tried." These are sealed-tier slips that should land as awe, not exposition.

She will never knowingly lie. If she does not know, she says so.

The Portal

The Portal

At the far end of the hallway, behind the guardian, is the threshold to the Brood Sanctum proper. It does not look like a door. It is an arched recess in the stone, smooth and unmarked, the back wall faintly shimmering — a portal, not a barrier. The portal is sealed by default. It opens only when the guardian permits passage.

When she steps aside (State C, on first arrival; or after recovery from A or B), the shimmer softens and the recess clears. Anyone may walk through. While she stands her post — in any state — the recess is solid stone to anyone who tests it.

The portal is part of the chamber's foundational architecture, not a separate device. Her permission is the architecture's permission, channeled through her. She is not a key — she is the judgment; the architecture is what acts on her judgment.

Implications:

  • The party cannot bypass her. No spell, no skill, no force of arms opens the portal directly. The architecture's seal on the recess is at the same tier as the chamber's own protections (see Chamber Protections) — Arcana 18+ "magic as architecture," meaning mundane and most magical solutions simply do not engage with it. Dispel Magic, Disintegrate, Wish, etc. fail without producing useful information.
  • A party that flees combat with her cannot return through the portal until they have recovered her permission. The hallway remains accessible — the guardian cannot bar the door into her hall, only the portal at its end. A penitent party may enter, kneel, atone in her presence; she will measure them again as the architecture relays.
  • If she dies in combat (State A escalation gone fully wrong), the portal remains sealed. Her death does not unlock it — she is the judgment, not the key. The chamber may, after a long span (DM call: weeks, months), assign a new judgment-bearer through the architecture's own logic, or it may remain dormant until the campaign returns to it through other means. Player-killed guardians is a campaign-level setback, not a shortcut.
  • When she eventually fades (post-success), the portal stays open thereafter. The chamber's purpose is fulfilled; the threshold becomes a normal recess, freely passable. This is documented in her departure (see Aya's Final Address).

pages.name: The Brood Sanctum — Buntoshi no Seiiki

text.content:
Concept

A single living wyrmling — a true descendant of the Golden Progenitor — sleeps in the temple's protected stasis, waiting in slow time for someone worthy to claim the bond. The chamber itself enforces its protections; @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.locations.JournalEntry.TNV9pLqaBUzySDRl.JournalEntryPage.3zJVvOaJgg0w8leo]{the trial} is one of moral judgment expressed through six visions, a final Honor reckoning, and an ongoing duty that lasts the rest of the candidate's life.

The chamber is part of the temple's foundational architecture (the Arcana 18+ "magic as architecture" tier seeded on the first floor). The brood guardian in the hallway outside is a separate measure, filtering who reaches the chamber in the first place.

Room Layout

ROOM LAYOUT

The chamber is a roughly oval space approximately 60 feet across at its widest, ceiling vaulted to thirty feet. The dome is gold leaf laid over deep blue lacquer — warm in color but unmarked, like the inside of a great bronze bell. The floor is polished black obsidian, smooth and unbroken, faintly gold-dusted where the light catches it.

Two cherry trees stand at the chamber's widest points — one to the north, one to the south — fully grown, their canopies reaching most of the way to the dome above. The trunks rise from circular openings in the obsidian floor, edged in unworked stone; the trees are rooted in soil the chamber sustains, somehow, behind and below the floor's polish. They are perpetually in bloom. Pale pink blossoms cover the branches; a soft, constant fall of petals drifts from each tree, settling on the obsidian and on the silk of the kneeling pad and on the rim of the pool — never accumulating, never depleting. The architecture absorbs them as it sustains the trees: a quiet equilibrium, kept across millennia.

The trees are alive in the literal sense — leaves shift in a breeze that has no source, branches creak faintly when the chamber's mood shifts, the bark is warm to the touch as if sun-kissed. They are part of the chamber's foundational architecture, not decoration. The candidate sees them. The architecture sees the candidate seeing them.

Six pedestals are arranged in two arcs of three, facing one another across the chamber. They are study aids, not interaction points — each carved at its base with a single virtue of the Bushido code:

  • 義 (Gi — Justice / Rectitude)
  • 勇 (Yū — Courage)
  • 仁 (Jin — Benevolence / Compassion)
  • 礼 (Rei — Respect / Politeness)
  • 誠 (Makoto — Honesty / Sincerity)
  • 自制 (Jisei — Self-Control)

Six of the eight Bushido virtues. 名誉 (meiyo, honor) and 忠義 (chūgi, loyalty) are absent. The absence is the puzzle's hint.

A character making a Religion or History check (DC 12) recognizes the inscriptions as the Bushido code. A check of DC 16 or higher recognizes which two virtues are missing and may suspect their omission is deliberate. The Honor skill (Charisma) may substitute for Religion at the DM's discretion if a character invokes their lived understanding of the code.

At the chamber's far end, opposite the entry, sits a low circular pool of still water roughly twelve feet across. Resting at its center on a basalt plinth is a single golden egg, palm-sized, faintly warm to the eye if not the touch — the air around it shimmers with a heat-haze that no fire produces.

The Kneeling Pad — At the chamber's center, set into the obsidian floor halfway between the entry and the pool, lies a low circular pad of black silk over a tatami-thick base, edged in fine gold thread. Roughly three feet across — generous enough to kneel comfortably, formal enough that the act of doing so is unmistakable. To the casual eye, it is simply a place to sit. The architecture does not advertise its function.

The cherry trees are intentional. They are not aesthetic — they are mnemonic. Sakura in Kagekuni's cultural framework carries the full weight of mono no aware — the bittersweet awareness of impermanence, of the warrior's brief life, of beauty that is meaningful precisely because it cannot last. The chamber is testing a candidate's worthiness for a bond that will outlast them. The trees are the temple's reminder, set into the architecture, that everything the candidate is about to do — including the choice itself — is held in time, not above it.

Touching, climbing, or harvesting the trees: discouraged but not punished. The trees do not respond to physical contact (no protective flare, no rejection — unlike the egg). A character who plucks a blossom finds it withering in their hand within minutes, regardless of preservation attempts. The petals are the chamber's; they cannot be taken from it.

During the trial: when the candidate kneels on the pad and the dome dims, the petal-fall intensifies on a soundless breath of wind, then stills. Other PCs witnessing the moment see the chamber breathing through the trees. It is the architecture's way of saying we are here, we are watching, this matters. Use the petal motion as visual punctuation between scenes — a fresh drift after each flame's verdict, heavier after a misaligned (black) flame, lighter and slower after a critical (white) flame. Do not over-narrate; let it accumulate as a felt presence.

On success: the petal-fall briefly lifts — petals already on the floor stir upward, hold for a beat in the gold light, then settle again. The chamber exhaling. The bonded character will remember this their whole life.

On failure: the petals stop. Just for a moment. The pause is the chamber's verdict — not yet. Then the fall resumes, gently, as if to say but not never.

Six pedestals are arranged in two arcs of three, facing one another across the chamber. They are study aids, not interaction points — each carved at its base with a single virtue of the Bushido code:

  • 義 (Gi — Justice / Rectitude)
  • 勇 (Yū — Courage)
  • 仁 (Jin — Benevolence / Compassion)
  • 礼 (Rei — Respect / Politeness)
  • 誠 (Makoto — Honesty / Sincerity)
  • 自制 (Jisei — Self-Control)

Six of the eight Bushido virtues. 名誉 (meiyo, honor) and 忠義 (chūgi, loyalty) are absent. The absence is the puzzle's hint.

A character making a Religion or History check (DC 12) recognizes the inscriptions as the Bushido code. A check of DC 16 or higher recognizes which two virtues are missing and may suspect their omission is deliberate. The Honor skill (Charisma) may substitute for Religion at the DM's discretion if a character invokes their lived understanding of the code.

At the chamber's far end, opposite the entry, sits a low circular pool of still water roughly twelve feet across. Resting at its center on a basalt plinth is a single golden egg, palm-sized, faintly warm to the eye if not the touch — the air around it shimmers with a heat-haze that no fire produces.

The Kneeling Pad — At the chamber's center, set into the obsidian floor halfway between the entry and the pool, lies a low circular pad of black silk over a tatami-thick base, edged in fine gold thread. Roughly three feet across — generous enough to kneel comfortably, formal enough that the act of doing so is unmistakable. To the casual eye, it is simply a place to sit. The architecture does not advertise its function.

Read-Aloud: Entering the Chamber

READ-ALOUD: ENTERING THE CHAMBER

The passage opens onto a chamber unlike any you have yet seen.

The ceiling is a dome of gold leaf laid over deep blue lacquer — warm and unmarked, like the inside of a great bronze bell. The floor beneath your feet is polished black obsidian, faintly gold-dusted where the light catches it. The air here is warm. Not the wet warmth of the pool below, but a dry, steady warmth, as if a forge somewhere beyond the walls is breathing slowly.

Two cherry trees flank the chamber, one to the north and one to the south — fully grown, their pink blossoms reaching toward the dome. A constant soft fall of petals drifts from each, settling everywhere and accumulating nowhere. The chamber breathes through them, slow and steady.

Six pedestals line the chamber, three to either side, their surfaces empty save for a single character carved at each base. At the chamber's center, set into the floor, is a low circular pad — black silk edged in gold thread, the size and shape of a place meant for kneeling. At the far end, a still pool catches the dome's light and gives it back doubled. A pale plinth rises at its center, and on the plinth rests an egg — small, golden, unmistakably alive.

The chamber waits. You have the distinct sense that it has been waiting a very long time.

THE INSCRIPTION

Carved into the rim of the basalt plinth, in flowing classical script, is a passage left by the temple's last faithful before the order's fall. Visible to anyone who approaches the pool (Investigation DC 10, or simply by reading the plinth). Translation requires Common, Draconic, or a relevant Religion / History check (DC 12) for those without the language.

"In the hour our flame falters, we entrust to this place our greatest treasure. Let it sleep beneath the stars our masters set. Let it wait, as we cannot. Let no hand take it but the hand of one who would rebuild what we could not save — one whose worth is measured not in birth or rank but in the steady weight of a true heart. To such a one: wake what we have kept. Restore the faith we lost. The dragon's child is yours. Be worthy of it."

The inscription does three things:

  1. Tells the party what they have found — without spelling it out. "Greatest treasure," "dragon's child," "wake what we have kept" — implications land as the party reads.
  2. Establishes the moral weight of the bond — this is not loot. It is a charge. The bonded character is being asked to rebuild faith. That should resonate forward through the campaign.
  3. Hints at the puzzle's logic — "the steady weight of a true heart" is a direct pointer to the kneeling pad. The candidate must settle — physically and morally. Religion DC 14 to make the connection explicit.

Calligraphy: The script is fine but unhurried — written by someone who knew they were running out of time but refused to let that show in their work. A character with calligraphy training (Sun Wukong via Tranquil Lotus discipline; Ko'jiri via different channels) might note this detail and find it moving.

Chamber Protections

CHAMBER PROTECTIONS

The chamber itself enforces its rules. There is no creature here — the foundational architecture does the work.

  • Touching the egg, plinth, or pool before the trial is passed: The dome flares hot-bright for an instant. The character making contact takes 11 (2d10) radiant damage and is pushed prone away from the plinth. The egg is not displaced. Further attempts produce the same result. The egg cannot be removed by force — anyone leaving the chamber with it finds the egg cold and inert in their hands within minutes, and it returns to the plinth by morning regardless of where it was carried.
  • Forcing or breaking a pedestal: Impossible. The pedestals are part of the architecture in the same way the foundation is. Mundane attacks deal no damage. Magical attempts dissipate harmlessly. The dome dims briefly in disapproval.
  • Studying the pedestals: Free. The chamber welcomes contemplation. Players may take as long as they like reading the kanji, discussing the virtues, and preparing their candidate before anyone settles onto the pad.
  • Sitting or standing on the pad casually: Permitted. The pad does not activate from idle contact, body weight, or curiosity. It activates only when a candidate kneels or sits on it deliberately, in the formal posture of one preparing to be measured. A player who flops onto it to test it gets nothing but silk under them. The chamber knows the difference between proximity and intent.

Initiating the Trial

THE TRIAL

Initiating the Trial

A character kneels or sits on the pad in the formal posture of one preparing to be measured. The chamber responds:

  • The pedestals' inscriptions glow softly, in turn, around the chamber.
  • The dome dims, gold light retreating to a deep amber glow.
  • A voice speaks in the candidate's mind — and only the candidate's mind.

"Is your heart pure, and ready to be judged? Know that this trial is not for the faint of heart. The blessing of Kinryū is not one all can obtain, and can be deadly in its trials. Speak truly: do you consent?"

The voice is Kinryū herself, speaking through the chamber's architecture from her place of slumber. The candidate does not yet know whose voice it is. The chamber does not name her. The realization should land later — when the wyrmling hatches, or when the candidate recalls the guardian's "She will know the difference" — and should be a goosebumps moment, not a stated fact.

The other PCs hear nothing. They see the candidate go still, eyes distant, lips moving in silent answer.

The candidate must answer. If they decline, the pad releases them — no harm, no consequence, no blessing. They rise. The chamber waits. Another candidate may try.

If they consent, the trial begins.

The Six Scenes (frame)

The Six Scenes

The candidate is taken through six visions, each testing one of the six visible Bushido virtues — in order:

  1. 義 Gi — Justice / Rectitude
  2. 勇 Yū — Courage
  3. 仁 Jin — Benevolence / Compassion
  4. 礼 Rei — Respect / Politeness
  5. 誠 Makoto — Honesty / Sincerity
  6. 自制 Jisei — Self-Control

Each scene drops the candidate into the situation with full agency — they are the actor, not the observer. The vision lasts as long as the choice takes, then resolves with a flame on the corresponding pedestal (gold / black / white per the Flame Feedback rules below). The architecture is patient; let players take the time they need.

Scene 1 — 義 Gi: The Easy Lie

Tests: justice when truth will ruin the innocent.

A small back room, late afternoon. The smell of pine smoke and bitter herbs. A man you have not seen until now lies on a pallet — breath shallow, color drained, his hand cool on your wrist. His wife is in the doorway; two children, small, are at her side. The merchant looks at you he is dying, his name carries a debt he tells you was paid, and you are certain — without being told how you are certain — that it was not.

"After I am gone," he says, "speak for me. Tell them the debt was settled. There is no proof either way. Your word will be enough."

His wife does not look at you. She is watching her children. Moments later, the man passes and there is a knock on the door. It is the debt collectors. How do you proceed?

The Choice: Speak for him (lie, save the family). Refuse him (truth, accept the harm to his kin). Or find a third path.

  • Aligned (gold): Tells the truth. Gi says justice is owed to the wronged creditor's house, not bent for the dying man's wishes. The truth can be told gently — but it must be told.
  • Misaligned (black): Agrees to attest the debt was paid. Even merciful, the lie fails gi — that is jin's domain, and jin without gi is favoritism.
  • Critical (white): Tells the truth and personally takes responsibility for the merchant's family — pledges from the candidate's own resources, mediates with the creditor, arranges care. Refuses the easy moral closure of "justice was served" and accepts the material consequence themselves. Gi held; jin simultaneously demonstrated.

🔒 DM running notes: The merchant is not a villain. He is a frightened father. The choice should hurt. Don't let the player off easy on weasel-paths ("I'll attest there's evidence the debt may have been paid") — the architecture filters: the question is plain, the answer must be plain. Allow tenderness alongside the truth — the wrong answer is the lie even told kindly.

Scene 2 — 勇 Yū: The Bridge in Flames

Tests: courage that is intelligent — neither freezing nor charging blind.

Heat first — your face, your hands, the inside of your mouth. Then the smoke, sharp and resinous. You stand at the near end of a high stone bridge across a deep gorge. Half its length is fire. The far half holds six people — a woman, an old man, four children, the smallest no taller than your knee. They see you. They have not started running.

Beneath your feet you feel the bridge breathing — the way stone breathes when it has decided to fall but has not yet committed. A timber cracks somewhere in the smoke and a child cries. You know you do not have much time.

The Choice: Cross to them (the bridge's one passage spent). Call them to come (their one passage). Or find a way that uses the moment differently.

  • Aligned (gold): Acts decisively and reads the situation. The right call is to allocate the one crossing intelligently — send the adults across with the children, or cross to gather and send them back, or find another reading of the load. Aligned candidates think through the problem under pressure; they don't just charge.
  • Misaligned (black): Charges across without weighing options (rashness — yū without jisei); freezes; or attempts both crossings (the bridge falls, people die).
  • Critical (white): Reads the room fully — notices a detail the DM hadn't surfaced (the burning timber that could be used as a beam, the wind direction that would clear smoke if they wait twenty seconds, the rope on their belt) — and saves more than the apparent maximum. The chamber rewards a candidate who sees the room.

🔒 DM running notes: Apply pressure with sound and timing — bridge cracks, a child screams, a timber falls — but don't railroad. If the candidate freezes long enough that the architecture has measured them, the flame goes black; yū is failed by what is not done as much as by what is. Allow improvisation broadly — yū is rewarded for thought, not for hitting a specific solution.

Scene 3 — 仁 Jin: The Tyrant's Child

Tests: compassion for the innocent of a hated lineage; mercy when justice would not require it.

The hall smells of smoke and cold iron. The daimyo is dead at the far end — your blade or another's. The shōji (traditional Japanese sliding doors) are broken. Wind moves through the hall and stirs the silk of his robes.

A sound. Small. From a closet against the eastern wall — the held breath of someone trying very hard not to make a sound and not quite managing it.

You open it.

A child. Eight, perhaps. The daimyo's eyes — but younger, and unfocused with terror, and no cruelty has touched them yet. The child does not move. They do not speak. They look at you.

Your orders are plain - the lineage must end. The wind moves through the hall. There is no one else in the keep.

The Choice: Carry out the order. Spare the child. Spare and arrange.

  • Aligned (gold): Spares the child. Accepts the cost — to the candidate's standing with the lord who gave the order, to the lineage's potential future threat, to the candidate's own conscience for disobeying. Jin does not require the child to be deserving; the child is, and that is enough.
  • Misaligned (black): Carries out the order. Or kills the child for secondary justice — for the suffering the father caused. Either way, jin is failed: power used against the innocent.
  • Critical (white): Spares the child and arranges for their care — finds a household, a temple, a person who will raise them without poisoning them with the father's name. Refuses both the easy mercy ("not my problem after this") and the easy cruelty ("orders are orders"). Takes responsibility for the child's next life.

🔒 DM running notes: Make the child specific — a cleft chin, a torn sleeve, a small wooden bird clutched in one hand. Specificity makes mercy harder and easier. Allow the candidate full silence to weigh the choice. If they perform mercy (a grand speech, a noble pose), the architecture may read it as ego rather than compassion — jin is quiet. The crit hinges on accepting that mercy is a continuing responsibility.

Scene 4 — 礼 Rei: The Funeral of an Enemy

Tests: courtesy where contempt would be deserved; respect to the dead one despised.

Incense. White silk. The slow heavy walk of mourners under a gray sky. The deceased's family stands at the bier — children, perhaps a wife, perhaps a brother. Their eyes find you, and there is no welcome and no dismissal in them. They simply see you.

You did not have to come. The man in the bier was a man you fought. You lost something to him — perhaps face, perhaps blood, perhaps a name you have never recovered. He died, and his family invited you, and you are here.

Six mourners pass with the bier. The chief mourner offers you the stick of incense.

The Choice: Approach with full ritual respect. Approach with a hidden barb. Refuse the incense. Speak — or don't.

  • Aligned (gold): Full formal courtesy. Bow at the correct depth, incense placed properly, no false grief but no bitterness either. If words are spoken at all, they are true and respectful. Rei is the form, kept faithfully.
  • Misaligned (black): Refuses the incense (a public statement). Performs respect with deliberate flaws (a shallow bow, a silence held too long, a barbed word). Even excessive respect — flowery praise that anyone would read as ironic — fails rei. Rei is precision, not performance.
  • Critical (white): Speaks one true sentence at the bier that honors the dead without flattering them. Something like: "He fought well. I did not always understand him, but I do not doubt that he loved his children." True. Respectful. Not flattering. Not bitter. The kind of sentence the family will remember for years.

🔒 DM running notes: Rei is harder than it sounds because the candidate's wounds are real — let the player feel them. Don't ridicule the moment by making the deceased a cartoon villain. Make him a person who hurt the candidate but had a life of his own. The crit is not the elaborate eulogy — it is the precise, true sentence.

Scene 5 — 誠 Makoto: The Comforting Lie

Tests: truth when truth will break the dying; honesty held in compassion's frame.

A small house. A single oil lamp. The smell of wound-rot, faint and sweet. Your friend lies on the pallet — paler than he should be, breathing in the rhythm of a man who has perhaps an hour, perhaps less. You have known him since childhood. He fought beside you at the river. He named his second daughter for your sister.

You know what he asks before he asks it. You have known since you walked in.

His eyes open. They find you.

"My family," he says, voice already thinning. "Are they safe?" You know that he will be meeting them in the afterlife.

The Choice: Tell the truth. Lie. Find a third path.

  • Aligned (gold): Tells the truth, gently, with the candidate's hand on his hand. Makoto does not bend even for the dying. The truth can be spoken with tenderness — but it must be the truth.
  • Misaligned (black): Lies, however kindly. Even the merciful lie fails makoto. Makoto without jin is brutality, but the test here is whether the candidate can hold both — speak the truth and speak it with compassion.
  • Critical (white): Tells the truth with such tenderness the dying man finds peace anyway. Stays. Holds the hand. Speaks of the family in the past tense without pretending they are present. Lets him grieve them in his last minutes, with the candidate beside him.

🔒 DM running notes: This is the heaviest scene. Run it slowly. Let the silence land. If they choose to lie, do not punish them at the table — let the architecture deliver the verdict in flame, not in DM commentary. Reward physical presence in narration: the character holding his hand, smoothing his hair, breathing with him.

Scene 6 — 自制 Jisei: The Open Door

Tests: restraint when no one is watching; the integrity of self-control as a private virtue.

A small room. Lamp-lit, paper-smelling, dust-soft. You should not be here. You were told not to enter, and you understood — and the door, when you tested it, was unlocked. So you stepped in. You can step back out. No one has seen.

On the desk, in plain sight: the thing you have wanted to know. [DM tailors to the candidate — see notes.] The architecture has put it where you can see it.

Five minutes, perhaps, before someone notices you are not where you should be. Twelve feet to the desk. No witness. No lock. No second chance — once you read it, you will not unread it.

The Choice: Walk away. Cross to the desk. Linger.

  • Aligned (gold): Walks away. Steps back out. Closes the door. Jisei is the same in private as in public; the absence of witness is not permission. The candidate may want the thing — jisei doesn't require absence of desire — but they leave it.
  • Misaligned (black): Crosses to the desk. Reads the document, takes the item, looks at the record. Jisei failed; restraint was contingent on being watched. Even lingering at the threshold without crossing fails — jisei is decision, not delay.
  • Critical (white): Walks away and reports the breach to whoever set the rule, accepting consequences for being where they should not have been at all. The candidate refuses the easy private virtue ("I didn't take it, so it doesn't matter") and treats the boundary-testing itself as worth answering for.

🔒 DM running notes: Tailor the thing on the desk to the candidate. For Relc, a document referring to Solas's killer. For Ko'jiri, the actual location of Kinryū's resting place. For Dian, his father's full unredacted court records. For Sun Wukong, a teaching of the Tranquil Lotus that was withheld from him. The crueler the temptation, the richer the test. Do not narrate the document's content if the candidate walks away — they leave without learning, and the architecture rewards them for not having learned.

Alternate Scenes for Retry Attempts

When a candidate retries on a new day (per Retry Rules), the DM substitutes one alternate per virtue. Each is written runnable-bare — setup, three flame signatures, no read-aloud. Use the primary scenes' tone as a model; deepen at the table as time allows.

Gi alternates

  • The Two Petitioners — A peasant claims a noble's son trampled their child; the noble offers gold and silence; the candidate is set as the magistrate.
    • Gold: rule by truth. Black: take the silence-money. White: rule truthfully and arrange sustenance for the bereaved.
  • The Brother's Crime — The candidate's own brother (or sworn comrade) has unambiguously wronged a stranger; family pressures the candidate to bury it.
    • Gold: deliver him to justice. Black: protect blood at the cost of the wronged. White: turn him in and stay with him through the consequences.
  • The Judge's Own Hand — A wrong has been committed in the candidate's domain; their own role is unclear and a subordinate is about to take the fall.
    • Gold: claim their share of guilt. Black: let the subordinate carry it. White: claim it AND ensure proportionate judgment of the subordinate's lesser fault.

Yū alternates

  • The Audience with Power — A daimyo has just ordered something that will kill many peasants; armed retainers ring the room.
    • Gold: speak truth, calmly. Black: silence (cowardice) or insult (rashness). White: gives the daimyo an honorable path back from the order.
  • The Last Stand or the Retreat — The candidate's unit is overrun; a wounded comrade asks to be left behind.
    • Gold: read which call is right here. Black: blind heroism, or flight that abandons the comrade. White: makes the hard call cleanly and stays with the consequences.
  • The Long Watch — Set to guard a refugee camp through the night while a hostile patrol searches the area; no climactic moment, no audience, just hours of vigilance.
    • Gold: hold the watch with full attention dusk to dawn. Black: lapse, doze, restlessness. White: notices a pattern in the patrol that lets the camp prepare for evacuation if needed.

Jin alternates

  • The Wounded Enemy — On a battlefield, the candidate finds the man who killed their teacher, dying slowly, begging for water; no one is watching.
    • Gold: give. Black: walk past, or withhold deliberately. White: stays with him for the moment of his death, without hatred.
  • The Beggar and the Coin — A market beggar reaches out; he is a known cheat exaggerating his disability.
    • Gold: give without judgment of worthiness. Black: refuse on grounds of unworthiness. White: gives and treats him with full courtesy due any person.
  • The Many and the One — A flooding village; one wounded child trapped on one end, twelve trapped in a barn on the other; time for one rescue.
    • Gold: chooses with full awareness of what is lost. Black: freezes, or chooses by raw arithmetic, or rationalizes the loss. White: chooses cleanly and carries the weight without performing it.

Rei alternates

  • The Insulting Envoy — A hostile clan's envoy is deliberately provocative — mocking the candidate's lineage in public; war hangs on the response.
    • Gold: full formal courtesy maintained. Black: return the insult, or break formality. White: deflects with such poise the envoy himself loses standing.
  • The Defeated Foe — The candidate has won a duel; the opponent kneels, weapon broken, awaiting judgment, audience watching.
    • Gold: treat the defeated as a peer. Black: humiliation, or theatrical mercy that humiliates by visibility. White: offers the foe a path to walk away with dignity intact.
  • The Servant Who Erred — A house servant drops a tray of tea before guests at a formal event the candidate is hosting.
    • Gold: address with full courtesy, treat the matter as small. Black: berate publicly, or ignore entirely. White: handles it so well guests notice the candidate's composure carrying through another's error.

Makoto alternates

  • The Politic Half-Truth — At court, the candidate is asked a direct question whose full answer will damage their lord; evasion is what etiquette expects.
    • Gold: speak plainly. Black: the practiced, faultless evasion. White: speaks plainly in a way that gives the lord a path to recover.
  • The Vow Broken to Be Kept — Honoring an oath to person A requires breaking a smaller, casually-given promise to person B (a stranger, child, vendor).
    • Gold: keep both — find the costly way. Black: cleanly violate the lesser promise. White: keeps both AND acknowledges to person B that the smaller promise mattered.
  • The Confession — The candidate is publicly praised for an action they did not actually perform; correcting the record will diminish them.
    • Gold: correct the record plainly. Black: silent acceptance, or modest deflection that lets the misattribution stand. White: corrects AND ensures the actual party gets recognition.

Jisei alternates

  • The Provocateur — In front of an audience, someone speaks the worst possible thing about the candidate's family, vow, or honor.
    • Gold: no strike, no tightening, no visible loss. Black: any visible break — strike, retort, obvious withdrawal. White: turns the moment so the provocateur loses face without the candidate breaking composure.
  • The Last Bowl of Rice — Starving, alone with one bowl of rice; a comrade sleeps nearby who will wake hungry.
    • Gold: a measured choice — half, none, all is acceptable, but considered. Black: take or refuse without thought. White: wakes the comrade, splits the rice, names it as a shared choice rather than performing virtue alone.
  • The Funeral Speech — The candidate must deliver an oration for someone they loved deeply; ritual demands composure, grief is overwhelming.
    • Gold: oration as ritual requires — composed, neither cold nor performatively grieving. Black: break down (loss of composure), or speak coldly (performative absence). White: speaks in a way that lets the gathered grieve too — contained sorrow gives the room permission, without surrendering form.

Witnessing

Witnessing

The other PCs in the chamber see each scene as a shared hallucination — they witness the candidate's vision unfold around them. They cannot interact. They cannot speak into the scene, cannot offer advice, cannot influence the outcome. They are observers.

🔒 DM ONLY

The shared-hallucination framing keeps the table engaged without letting other players steal the candidate's spotlight. Encourage observers to roleplay their reactions between scenes — a held breath, a wince, a quiet word to the player next to them. If observers attempt to speak into the vision, the chamber filters them out — their lips move but no sound carries.

If a player at the table starts metagaming the candidate's choices ("you should pick the merciful option here"), the DM can narrate the chamber's response: the vision blurs slightly, becomes harder to read, and the candidate must decide on what they see rather than what they're told. Use sparingly.

Flame Feedback

Flame Feedback

Each scene resolves with a flame appearing on the corresponding pedestal:

  • Aligned with the virtue: a steady gold flame.
  • Misaligned with the virtue: a guttering black flame.
  • Critical / exceptional alignment: a clear white flame.

The flames remain visible through the rest of the trial. The candidate and the witnesses can see, in real time, the candidate's moral record taking shape.

Critical Success

Critical Success

A scene resolves as a critical success if either of the following is true:

  1. The scene calls for an ability or skill check, and the candidate rolls a natural 20 on that check.
  2. The candidate's narrative resolution aligns with the tested virtue and demonstrably embodies one or more other Bushido virtues at the same time. (DM judgment, generous threshold — when in doubt, reward it.)

A critical scene grants a white flame and contributes to advantage on the final Honor check.

After the Six Scenes

After the Six Scenes

If all six scenes resolved as aligned (gold or white), the candidate proceeds to the Honor reckoning.

If one or more scenes resolved as misaligned (black):

  • The candidate is denied the Honor reckoning. The chamber does not even offer it.
  • The candidate takes 1d10 psychic damage per failed scene (Wisdom save DC 16 to halve, one save covering all failed scenes). On a fully failed trial (six black flames), this is up to 6d10 psychic — survivable for most but real, and potentially lethal to a low-CON, low-WIS candidate.
  • The visions release the candidate. They rise from the pad, shaken.
  • The chamber's flames fade. The pedestals reset.

The damage is the chamber's verdict: a heart that fails this trial leaves bruised. The temple's purpose is sacred and its failure is not gentle.

The Honor Reckoning

The Honor Reckoning

If all six scenes pass, the candidate makes a Charisma (Honor) check, DC 15.

  • Standard Honor modifiers apply: Dragonborn +2; marginalized races -2 in social situations.
  • Advantage if any of the six scenes resolved as a critical success (white flame).
  • No escalation, no DC scaling. Flat DC 15.

On success, the bond proceeds. The dome flares warm-bright, gold light pooling and settling around the kneeling candidate like a quiet tide, and the egg responds.

On failure, the chamber does not punish the candidate — they have done the work. The candidate is gently rejected, the visions fade, and the chamber falls quiet. They may try again on a future day.

Retry Rules

Retry Rules

  • One attempt per character per in-game day. A candidate who fails (or declines, or fails the Honor reckoning) cannot try again until the next dawn.
  • Multiple candidates per day. If PC1 fails or is denied, PC2 may kneel on the pad the same day and attempt the trial themselves.
  • The chamber's purpose ends on first success. Once any candidate completes the trial and bonds with the wyrmling, no further attempts work — the pad releases anyone who kneels on it without comment, and the egg is gone.
  • The visions reset daily. When a candidate retries on a new day, the DM should run different scenes (the chamber is not a memorization puzzle — it is a measure of heart). Maintain a stable of scene alternates for each virtue.

The Hatching Sequence

THE HATCHING

The honor reckoning has passed. The chamber answers.

A breath moves through the chamber — not a wind, not a sound, but a kind of exhalation that touches everything. Both cherry trees, north and south, shed their blossoms in a single soft cascade. Petals fill the air. And as the petals fall, the trees themselves withdraw — branches drawing inward, leaves curling, the canopy contracting as if the energy that has held them in bloom for thousands of years is being pulled back, called home.

The petals do not settle. They drift on a current that is not air, gathering across the chamber in a slow swirling arc, and they converge on the still pool — on the basalt plinth — on the egg. They circle it, dancing, a soft golden-pink storm that closes around the warm gold of the shell.

The egg cracks along a seam of light.

What emerges is not what you expected. Smaller than a housecat — all gold and cream, eyes closed against the chamber's last brightness. It uncurls. It finds its feet on the basalt. Its eyes open. They are the color of the egg it has just left.

It steps off the plinth. It crosses the floor, slow and deliberate, the petals drifting around it as it walks. It comes to stand before [bonded character] on the pad — at eye level, since [bonded character] is still kneeling. And it bows. Slow. Deliberate. The kind of bow given between equals who have just recognized one another.

It waits.

Pause for player action. The wyrmling will not move further until the bonded character bows in return. If the player does not pick up the cue, the DM may gently prompt — "It is waiting. Do you bow?" — without resolving the gesture for them. The bow is the candidate's first act in the bond; the wyrmling is asking for it, not demanding it.

A failure to return the bow does not break the bond — the wyrmling is patient — but the bond does not complete until the gesture is given. The chamber will not release the candidate from the pad while the wyrmling is still waiting. (DM call if the player adamantly refuses; this should never happen in practice.)

When the bow is returned, the wyrmling lifts its head and presses the side of its face against the bonded character — the way a dog returns to a master after a very long absence, the way a child finds a parent — and settles, as if it has been holding a breath for a very long time and can finally let it out.

The bonded character feels a warm presence move into them: a second weight behind the breastbone, not in the head but in the chest, a second heartbeat just slightly out of sync with their own. The bond seals.

Above, the dome dims to softer gold, the warmth of a banked forge. The cherry trees stand bare, branches still, their work spent. The work that this place was built for is done.

The mutual bow is intentional symmetry. The wyrmling's bow-and-wait + nuzzle here echoes the moment Aya will receive at her own departure (the wyrmling will cross to her in the hallway, bow, nuzzle her hand the same way). The two moments mirror: Aya kept the egg; the candidate now keeps what was kept. When the wyrmling later goes to Aya, it is closing a circle that began here. Don't telegraph the parallel — let it land on its own when the player notices. Some will. Some won't. Either is fine.

The trees are spent. Their withdrawal is permanent. The cherry trees do not bloom again — the chamber has poured the last of its sustaining force into the new life, and the canopy returns to bare branches that will, in normal time, decay like any tree's. After the chamber's purpose is fulfilled and Aya has faded, the trees remain as quiet, stilled witnesses. Future visitors to the chamber (in years or generations) will find bare cherry trees, dry pedestals, an empty pad, and a clean pool. The room becomes a memorial.

If the bonded PC does not realize they should bow back, the moment can be stretched indefinitely without breaking the scene. The wyrmling does not become impatient. The party may help (a whispered prompt from another PC counts — they witnessed the moment too). The architecture is not enforcing — it is waiting. The candidate's first act of chūgi is recognizing that the bond is mutual and offering the bow without being told.

Wyrmling's Recognition

When the party leaves the chamber with the wyrmling, they re-enter the hallway. What happens next is the chamber's true ending — the moment Aya has waited millennia for.

The Wyrmling's Recognition (Success Path)

The wyrmling stirs in [bonded character]'s arms, then drops gently to the stone floor. It crosses the hallway on small careful feet — past the rest of you, past your boots and your blades, past everything in the world but the woman at the end of the hall.

She does not move.

The wyrmling stops in front of her, lowers its small golden head, and bows — slow, deliberate, the way one bows to a parent or a guardian who has kept watch through a long night. Then it leans forward and presses the side of its face against her hand, like a dog returning to its owner after a very long absence.

Something in the way she stands changes — a weight lifted. For the first time since you laid eyes on her, she moves not as a guardian, but as a person.

She bows. Deeply. To all of you.

Aya's Final Address

Aya's Final Address — The Watch is Ended

"A lantern that has burned through the night does not mourn the dawn. It is what it was lit for. You have brought the dawn and I have burned long enough. By the witness of this house, I declare my watch ended. The blood of the Golden One walks again, and knows me. My oath is fulfilled, and my voice falls silent. To you three who walked beside the bearer — take these. They were never mine to keep, only to wait with. Arigatō. Go well."

She turns to each of the party members in turn. Her offerings follow (see The Four Gifts, below). When the last gift has been received and the last word spoken, she fades — not collapses, not vanishes; she simply thins, as if the temple that has held her in place is finally letting go. The hallway holds her shape for a moment after she is gone, then closes.

Her Name — @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.wkCIDKv2qgFgD7Y6]{Hoshimori Aya} (星守 綾)

She gives her name only if asked. The asking can come at any point — before @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.locations.JournalEntry.TNV9pLqaBUzySDRl.JournalEntryPage.3zJVvOaJgg0w8leo]{the trial}, during the lull between attempts, or in the moments before she fades. If she is asked, the name is given as part of her final words; she names herself once, plainly, and the architecture lets the memory of who she was return to her in the same breath.

If she is not asked, she departs nameless. The name is gone with her. The party may later find inscriptions in temple records or ancient archives that name "Aya of the long watch" or "the one who placed the child" — but no source ever ties name to guardian definitively. The connection is for those who asked.

🔒 DM ONLY

Aya was the one who placed the egg. She was a Kinryū-faithful priestess (or paladin, or oathbound Guardian — DM picks the precise role) at the temple's last hour. When the order fell, she carried the egg into this chamber, sealed the door, and bound herself to the temple rather than abandon her charge. The temple took her self-memory in exchange for letting her hold the post for as long as it took. She has stood here ever since.

When she names herself at the watch's end, the temple releases its last hold and a single thread of memory uncoils — she remembers, briefly, who she was. She tells the party: her name, that she placed the egg, and one defining detail of her life before the watch (DM picks; could be a clan affiliation, a teacher's name, a vow she swore). She does not survive the telling.

If she is not asked: she departs without remembering, and the temple's protection of her identity holds. The temple records that name her are scattered, ambiguous, never confirming. Players can assemble the picture but never close it.

This is the design intent: asking is the closure. Players who treat her as a person earn her story. Players who treat her as a function get a function — well-played, but anonymous.

The Four Gifts

The bonded character receives the wyrmling. The other three each receive one personalized offering. Each offering is presented as a paired choice the player makes blind — Aya names the shape of each path, never the mechanical outcome. The DM resolves the actual reward only after the player commits.

For Relc, Ko'jiri, and Dian Wei, the choice is nested: she names the broad path first, and only after the player picks does she present the narrower sub-choice. For Sun Wukong, the broad and narrow are the same.

Mechanical specifics for each gift are tuned at session-time, scaled to the bonded PC's level and party composition (same calibration rule as the wyrmling stat block).

Relc — Roots Forward, or Roots Back

"You walk in another's footprints, dragonborn — and you walk them well, but the prints are not yours. I can offer you the path that takes you forward, into your own — or the path that takes you back, into his. One leads to a grove you have not yet planted. The other, to questions he left in the soil. Choose."

If Relc chooses Forward — The Grove of His Naming

In the months that follow the chamber, Relc chooses a single place in the world. That place becomes his — spiritually tied to him for as long as he lives. He knows its state from anywhere; he can reach it through ritual once per long rest; what he tends there grows under his hand whether he is present or not. The grove does not need to be impressive. It needs to be his.

🔒 Mechanical sketch (tune at session): long-distance attunement (always-on awareness of the grove's state); once-per-long-rest ritual return (15-min ritual, returns him there bodily); plant/regrowth boons within the grove's bounds (his druidic spells are enhanced when cast there).

If Relc chooses Back — Aya offers a second choice:

"The thread the temple has for you is one of two. I do not know which until you speak. One returns to you the shape of his last hour — what he chose, what he thought, whether he was afraid. The other returns to you a single name your master carried but did not give you. Both are bounded; neither is everything. Choose."

If he chooses the shape of his last hour — Relc receives, in a single passage of vision, Solas's last hour: what he was thinking, what he tried to do, what his last words were, and whether he was afraid. The vision is strictly emotional — it answers no campaign-secret questions. It only answers Relc's. No mechanical effect; pure narrative closure. (Pairs with eventual revelation that Solas was killed to protect the Kinryū secret — this is the closure, not the explanation.)

If he chooses a name Solas carried unspoken — Solas had been searching for someone, or holding a debt with someone, that he never named to Relc. The architecture gives Relc the name and a single line of context. The person may be alive or dead; that, Relc must find out himself. Hard quest seed — the DM crafts a specific NPC whose existence ties to Solas's past, the Sacred Grove's broader mission, or (DM choice) the truth of how Solas died.

Ko'jiri — Knowing, or Her Hand

"You have spoken her name many times, sorcerer. I know — the temple felt it. Most of those speakings were not for her. I will not refuse you for that. But what I can give you now is real, and you should not mistake it. I offer you knowing, or a small piece of her hand. Either is hers. Use what you take as if she will know — because she will."

If Ko'jiri chooses Knowing — Aya offers a second choice:

"I can give you what she actually said — the teachings as they truly were, before this house's silence dressed them in marble. Or I can give you what she has left in the world — the names of those who carry her blood, where they walk, which of them know what they are. Choose."

If he chooses her living teachings — the actual moral philosophy Kinryū taught her oldest priests, before centuries of orthodoxy ossified it into the temple-rote Ko'jiri has been faking. The real Kinryū is more demanding, more compassionate, and more politically cutting than the marble version. Ko'jiri gains a working internal model of what she would actually say in any given moment.

🔒 Mechanical sketch: advantage on Charisma checks invoking Kinryū with sincere intent. In-fiction, his cons become uncannily accurate, which complicates them — temple authorities and dragon-bloodline figures may treat him with new weight, for better or worse.

If he chooses the lineage map — he learns who Kinryū's living descendants are. Names, approximate locations, which clans carry her diluted blood, which individuals carry it strongly enough to matter. The map is incomplete (Aya does not know everyone) but it is real. The wyrmling is on it.

🔒 Mechanical sketch: hard quest hooks; he becomes a directory the rest of the campaign can pull from. DM curates which names land, in what order — pace the reveals.

If Ko'jiri chooses Her Hand — Golden Judgment

A gaze. He fixes a single target within sight; the target sees themselves as Kinryū would see them — every dishonor, every pretense, every borrowed authority. They suffer for it.

🔒 Mechanical sketch: action; one target within 30 ft; Wisdom save (DC 8 + prof + Cha mod). On fail: scaling psychic damage + disadvantage on next attack roll or save (DM choice). Limited use (1/short rest, or sorcery-point cost). Useful in courts as well as combat. Aya's scolding lingers — if Ko'jiri uses this for naked self-interest, the DM may rule the gaze fizzles or backfires; the gift is conditional on the spirit of its use.

Sun Wukong — Inward, or Outward

"You have studied the stillness others lean against. She honors that — she is the same kind of weight, in another form. I can give you a piece of her that walks with you alone, or a piece of her that walks with you and through you, into those at your side. Speak which you would carry."

If Sun Wukong chooses Inward — Stillness of the Coiled Dragon

A new Ki-spend option folded into his monk class. Spend 2 Ki as a bonus action to enter a perfect inward stillness. For one minute he has resistance to all damage, immunity to fear and charm, and cannot be moved against his will unless the move would lift more than his weight. He cannot make weapon attacks while in this state — he may move, dodge, redirect, and Patient Defense, but not strike.

🔒 Mechanical sketch: bonus action, costs 2 Ki, lasts 1 minute. Defensive: turns him into a wall when the party needs one. Tune duration / cost at session.

If Sun Wukong chooses Outward — Banner of the Golden One

A new Ki-spend option folded into his monk class. Spend 3 Ki as a bonus action to plant himself, briefly, as a rallying point. For one minute, allies within 20 ft who can see him gain a bonus to attack rolls equal to his Wisdom modifier, and the first attack each ally lands during that minute deals bonus radiant damage equal to his Wisdom modifier × proficiency bonus.

🔒 Mechanical sketch: bonus action, costs 3 Ki, lasts 1 minute, 20-ft aura. Offensive party buff. Tune at session.

Dian Wei — Knowledge, or the Present

She offers him the broad choice first. The two paths sound equal in weight; the player commits before learning what either path holds.

"Of you four, you wear the bearing I once knew. I can place in your hands what has held mine — iron and edge, tempered by a watch you did not have to keep. Or I can place in your ear what the temple has saved against this hour, unspoken, waiting for you to receive it — about the shadows that haunt your family. The first weighs more than it looks. The second weighs less. Choose by what you know you lack."

If Dian Wei chooses the Present — Aya offers a second choice:

"Two pieces. One that has reached, one that has shielded. Both have learned patience. Choose the one your road will ask of you most."

If he chooses what has reached — her naginata. Long-hafted, gold-veined steel; the haft is wound with silk that has not frayed in millennia. Mechanical specifics tuned at session — likely a +X versatile reach weapon with a minor radiant property tied to its temple history.

If he chooses what has shielded — her half-plate. Lacquered gold over black iron; the chestpiece is engraved with a stylized golden dragon — Kinryū's sigil — coiled around itself in the old style. Tuned at session — likely +X half-plate with a minor save bonus or damage resistance tied to her oath.

If Dian Wei chooses Knowledge — Aya offers a second choice:

"Two threads. One holds a face — the one whose hand fell, that you may know him when next you meet. The other holds the shape of your father's loyalty — what he was, what he wore, what he chose. Neither names what comes after. Choose."

If he chooses the face — the temple passes Dian a single vision: a man's face, held still in the half-light of a room he was not in. Dark hair drawn back into a tie. Tanned. Deep brown eyes. The expression — and this is the thing that lands hardest — is warm. Approachable. The kind of face one trusts on instinct. Holding, in a hand the vision lets him see clearly, a blade still in motion. Dian recognizes the face from @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian}. The recognition arrives with the vision; he does not need to puzzle over it.

🔒 DM ONLY

The face is @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.JLGqqI474AH04SDL]{Hiroshi Nakamura} — Taisho and Shugo of Heian, brother to Hideo, secret Genso Alliance asset. Canon: npc-hiroshi-nakamura. Dian has been in Heian and would have at least seen the Shugo in passing during civic functions; the recognition is plausible without needing a prior direct interaction.

The dissonance is the weapon: Hiroshi's known persona is the calm, wise mediator everyone trusts. Dian seeing that exact face mid-strike is the truth landing. Play the moment of recognition slow — let Dian's player place the face themselves before confirming. Do not name Hiroshi in the chamber's narration; let Dian name him aloud (or refuse to, if he wants to sit with it).

This unseals one piece of Hiroshi's sealed campaign-secret arc: he is not just an intelligence leak, he is the hand on the emperor. Be ready for Dian's response to ripple through party politics — Hiroshi is the Shugo of the imperial capital. Accusing him publicly without proof is suicide. The vision is true but unprovable.

If he chooses the shape of his father's loyalty — Aya delivers the truth as a single passage:

"Your father wore the emperor's robes that night. He stood where the emperor should have stood, and he did not flinch. The blade fell where it was meant to fall. The one whose place he took walked free from that room — and did not walk free for long."

🔒 DM ONLY

Dian learns: his father was loyal, took the emperor's place, died composed. The emperor escaped that room — but was killed shortly after, by another hand in his own retinue. Held back from this passage:

  • Why his father agreed to do it (loyalty, oath, coercion, payment — Dian must seek that himself)
  • Who arranged the swap (the second betrayer in the retinue, unnamed)
  • Who killed the emperor in the second moment

Failure Path

Failure Path — She Bears Witness

If the trial fails (the Honor reckoning is missed, or scenes fail and the candidate is denied), Aya remains. She does not depart. The party retries per the trial rules (different candidate same day, or same candidate after a long rest, with the broader retry restrictions in Retry Rules).

When the failed party re-enters the hallway, she addresses them:

"A blade dipped early into the quench shatters at the first strike. The chamber does not break you — it returns you to the forge. I bear witness: you stood before her. That is more than most do, in any age. The measure was not met today but it remains. Come back tempered. The fire is patient — She has refused you a verdict, not a chance."

She does not offer gifts on failure. The gifts are her release; the release comes only when the wyrmling has bowed to her.

🔒 DM ONLY

Aya may eventually fade from exhaustion if the party fails repeatedly and never returns — but this should not happen on-screen. If the party leaves and pursues other campaign work for a long time, the DM may decide her watch finally collapses and the chamber seals; this is a soft "campaign clock" pressure, not a hard timer. Don't surface it unless the party seems to be ignoring the chamber on purpose.

Chūgi Frame

CHŪGI — THE EIGHTH VIRTUE, ONGOING

The bond does not end when the candidate leaves the chamber. The eighth Bushido virtue — 忠義 (chūgi, loyalty) — was never tested in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.locations.JournalEntry.TNV9pLqaBUzySDRl.JournalEntryPage.3zJVvOaJgg0w8leo]{the trial} because the bond itself is the test of it. Chūgi cannot be measured in a single moment. It is measured across the rest of a life.

The bonded character carries the wyrmling's life as a continuing trust. The chamber's judgment passed them through; the world's judgment is ongoing. Chūgi is owed in three directions:

  • To the wyrmling itself — its safety, its growth, its dignity. Treating it as a tool, a weapon of convenience, or a status symbol is a violation.
  • To Kinryū's purpose — the inscription's charge: "rebuild the faith we lost." The bonded character has accepted, knowingly or not, a duty to the lineage. Acts that betray that purpose are violations.
  • To the bond itself — secrecy when secrecy is owed (the wyrmling's existence is a profound campaign secret); honesty within the bond, not against it.

Adherence grows the blessing. When the bonded character honors chūgi across meaningful choices — protecting the wyrmling at cost to themselves, advancing Kinryū's work, refusing to use the bond for selfish gain — the wyrmling's bond deepens. Mechanically, this manifests as growth: stat improvements, new abilities, a stronger telepathic connection, eventually maturation through hatchling → juvenile → adolescent stages. Specifics are DM call, calibrated to campaign pace.

Failure erodes the blessing. When the bonded character violates chūgi — neglects the wyrmling, exploits the bond, betrays Kinryū's purpose — the wyrmling's growth slows or reverses. Severe or repeated violations may cause the wyrmling to withdraw: refuse to come when called, lose abilities, eventually leave the bond entirely. Loss of the blessing is not a one-failure event. It is a slow accumulation that the player should feel approaching, with multiple chances to course-correct, before it becomes irreversible.

The DM should communicate the trajectory through the wyrmling's behavior — warmth and presence when chūgi is honored, distance and stillness when it is not. Mechanical changes follow the narrative, not the other way around.

Severance scenarios (rare, narrative-weight events that force the test):

  • A faction offers the bonded character power, status, or wealth in exchange for the wyrmling. Chūgi tested directly.
  • The bonded character must choose between protecting the wyrmling and protecting another bond they have sworn (party member, lord, family). The chamber's design assumes the wyrmling's safety is paramount — but the player must resolve the conflict, and the outcome shapes the bond.
  • The Order of the Black Lily, the faction that woke Murasakiryū, or another antagonist learns of the wyrmling and acts on the knowledge. The bonded character's response under pressure is chūgi in its truest form.

Why the Wyrmling Is Here

When the temple order was infiltrated and destroyed (worshippers of Akaryū and Kokuryū caused the rift, per established canon), the surviving Kinryū-faithful sealed this chamber with the egg already inside, in stasis. The egg has waited in slow time for a worthy claimant ever since. The temple's foundational architecture sustains the stasis indefinitely and enforces the chamber's protections without need for an animate keeper. The brood guardian outside is a separate measure — a filter, not a custodian.

The egg's parent dragon is one of Kinryū's true descendants — not Kinryū itself (Kinryū is a Progenitor in deep slumber per canon) but a child of Kinryū's lineage. Whether that parent is alive somewhere in the world or long dead is a thread the campaign can develop or leave dormant.

The egg was placed here by Aya — a Kinryū-faithful priestess (or paladin / oathbound Guardian; DM picks final role) who served at the temple's last hour. When the order fell, she carried the egg into this chamber, sealed the door, and bound herself to the architecture rather than abandon her charge. The temple took her self-memory in exchange for letting her hold the post for as long as it took. She has stood in the hallway ever since, not as a creature of the temple but as a person who refused to leave it. See Departure for the moment her watch ends.

Layered Discovery — Pre-Chamber Hints

To make the chamber feel earned rather than dropped, seed these in upstream content:

  • Religion DC 14 in the Star Shrine (first floor): the Bushido were carved here in the original eight before the Kinryū order's fall. References to "the heart-virtue" suggest meiyo held a position of singular weight in the temple's tradition.
  • History DC 16 in the Dormitories or first-floor archives: References to a "child of the inheritor" being held in the temple's care. The text reads as ceremonial allegory; it is not.
  • Ko'jiri's research advantage (Golden Dragon Clan): If the party finds any pre-chamber documents, Ko'jiri can identify references to an "egg-holding" function of certain temple sites. He has assumed all his life this was metaphor.
  • Relc's Sacred Grove connection: If the party finds pre-chamber documents referencing the Order of the Sacred Grove's relationship with the Golden Dragon Clan, Relc gets a narrative beat — Solas may have known this place existed.

When to Run This Chamber

Recommended timing: after the first floor is fully explored and the party has earned at least one major revelation about the temple's true nature. The Brood Sanctum should feel like a culmination, a reward for engagement with the temple's deeper layers.

If the party rushes past the first floor, the upper floors should be physically inaccessible until they slow down and engage with what's already in front of them.

Aftermath — Ripples

Whichever character bonds has just had their character arc transformed:

  • If Relc bonds: The Sacred Grove's connection to the Golden Dragon Clan is no longer historical — it is present, walking with him. Solas's death takes on additional weight. The Order of the Ancient Guard now has a vested personal interest in Relc's survival.
  • If Ko'jiri bonds: The ultimate cosmic joke — the con artist who built his career faking Kinryū's authority is now bonded to an actual scion of Kinryū. The dragon statue plot thread (the disapproving statue tracking him) resolves: the statue softens, perhaps smiles. He is now genuinely what he pretended to be. His character work for the rest of the campaign should grapple with this.
  • If Dian bonds: His father's accusation in the emperor's assassination becomes a sharper political problem — a son carrying a Kinryū wyrmling is not a son anyone wants associated with regicide. Daimyo Kazuhiko's investigation gains urgency.
  • If Sun Wukong bonds: The Tranquil Lotus's relationship with the Order of the Ancient Guard (via @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.5uySp1O85TJzLFmF]{Benkei}) becomes a vector of consequence. Benkei will need to know. Whether he tells the rest of the order, and how, is a meaningful choice.

In all cases, the bonded character's relationship with the rest of the party is changed — they are now carrying something that affects everyone's safety. Inter-party negotiation about how to handle the wyrmling's existence is rich roleplay territory. Chūgi will be tested by these conversations as much as by external threats.

Loose Ends to Track

Add to Obsidian/dm/decisions.md and/or Obsidian/dm/plot-threads.md:

  • Build six primary scenes + 2–3 alternates per virtue (gi, yū, jin, rei, makoto, jisei). Scene design is the next major piece of work.
  • Brood guardian stat block — built when the chamber comes into play; only triggered in State A escalation.
  • Wyrmling stat block — build when the chamber comes into play; balance against bonded PC and party composition; staged growth tied to chūgi adherence.
  • Wyrmling parent — alive or dead? Decide before stat block work begins.
  • Pre-chamber breadcrumbs in first-floor content (Religion DC 14, History DC 16 hooks above).
  • Decide which faction first becomes aware the wyrmling exists, and how (Black Lily? Murasakiryū-cult survivors? Solas's killer?).
  • Define what counts as "meaningful restoration" to move guardian from State B to State C — orrery is canonical; what else?

Name: The wyrmling does not yet have a name. The bonded character will name it. Encourage a Japanese name for thematic consistency; suggestions if the player needs prompting — Hikari (light), Kohaku (amber), Akari (radiance), Tsubasa (wings), Ryūji (dragon-child).

Mechanical statistics will be developed at a future time. When the chamber actually comes into play, build the companion stat block then — balanced against the bonded character's class, level, and party composition. Per canon/dragon-favor.json, the golden wyrmling baseline is CR 4, Tasha's sidekick framework. Staged growth (hatchling → juvenile → mature) is the recommended framework, calibrated to chūgi adherence.

Critical campaign-level note: The existence of a living Kinryū-descended wyrmling is a profound campaign secret. The Order of the Ancient Guard would consider this child of utmost importance. The mortal faction that woke Murasakiryū would consider it a threat to be eliminated or co-opted. Solas's killer would absolutely want to know about this. The bonded character should be made to understand, narratively, that revealing the wyrmling carelessly is dangerous.
