Disguising it as a more mundane creature (a large lizard, an exotic pet from Tatara) will eventually become a real concern.

The Hidden Archives. Accessed via the south-wall portal from the Tenkairō. Foundational warding extends through floor, ceiling, and outer walls — no other entry exists.

This file is a starting framework. The archive's specific contents will be flushed out in detail; what follows is canonical structure and the documents the archive is known to hold.

Physical Description:

The portal deposits the supplicant in a short anteroom hallway — 10 ft wide, 20 ft long, plain dressed stone — that terminates at a single open archway leading into the archive proper. The hallway is lit by two cold-flame sconces. The receiving end of the portal is the back wall of the hallway; turning around after arrival shows a smooth blank stone wall with no portal evidence on this side. Travel is one-way except via the Tenkairō activation, which the party must repeat to depart (the portal opens both ways for the ten-minute activation window, but resealing requires re-performing the seven-plate rite if the party leaves and returns later).

The Archive Proper:

A rectangular chamber, 40 ft wide × 60 ft deep, ceiling 14 ft. The chamber is dry — markedly so, the kind of dryness that has been engineered rather than weathered. The air is still and cool, slightly cold to the touch. Faint, clean cedar scent — the smell of kiri and sugi wood used in Japanese archival practice to repel insects and absorb humidity.

The walls are lined with tall lacquered cabinets — black-lacquered cedar, brass-fitted, doors closed, each cabinet roughly 12 ft tall × 4 ft wide × 3 ft deep, fronted with paper fusuma panels behind the outer doors. Cabinets are arrayed along the north, east, and west walls in unbroken rows; the south wall (the entrance side) holds a long reading table and three zaisu — low backed seats — facing the room.

A central display plinth, 6 ft tall, holds a single cradle for a scroll under sei-lacquered glass. The cradle is empty. (What was meant to live there is itself a sealed thread — see DM Notes.)

Lighting:

Four cold-flame sconces, one at each corner of the chamber. The light is bright, even, and unwavering. The archive was built to be read in.

The Cabinets:

Each cabinet is labeled at its top in gold leaf with a category glyph. A character with knowledge of the Golden Dragon order's archival conventions (DC 13 History; DC 10 for Ko'jiri) can read the categories at a glance:

  • Reishiki (礼式 — Rites and Liturgy)
  • Yakushi (薬師 — Healing Arts)
  • Tenmon (天文 — Astronomy and Calendar)
  • Hihō (秘法 — Secret Methods)
  • Keizu (系図 — Lineages and Records)
  • Bunsho (文書 — Correspondence and Edicts)
  • Other categories present, several damaged or empty.

The cabinets and their contents are intact. The archive's foundational warding has preserved everything inside it for thousands of years, exactly as it was the day the order fell.

This list is the framework — specific scroll-by-scroll detail is intentionally TBD and will be expanded as the campaign requires. The categories below are canon; the precise wording, count, and arrangement of individual documents are open.

  • The Vigil-Oath Dismissal Rite (Reishiki cabinet; DC 12 Investigation in the cabinet) — full text in old liturgical Draconic, with phonetic gloss. Resolves mon-tachibana-akiyo.
  • Pool Ritual Documentation (Reishiki and Yakushi cabinets; DC 12 Investigation) — the full DC-18 Religion content for the Hiroba pools (healing rite, condition rite, blessing of Kinryū). Equivalent to rm-grand-hall § The Pools' DC 18 Religion result.
  • Star Shrine Purification Rite (Reishiki cabinet; DC 12 Investigation) — the full DC-18 Religion content for lifting the Star Shrine darkness. Equivalent to rm-star-shrine § The Darkness' DC 18 Religion result.
  • The Gekkō Reversal Documentation (Hihō cabinet — Secret Methods) — the Golden Dragon counter-work to the Onyx transformation ritual. The crossed-out entry from the Zasu's index (see rm-zasu-ritual-scrolls) refers to this document. It exists. The infiltrators tried to destroy it with fireballs. The wards held. The reversal is here. Specific contents — methodology, prerequisites, the three components (site of origin, counter-work, convergence of three lights) — are TBD pending the party's progression.
  • Order of the Black Lily Correspondence (Bunsho cabinet) — late-period letters between the Tenkū-ji order and the Black Lily monastery, documenting awareness of the Onyx transformation ritual and early countermeasures. Cross-reference for the party's later Black Lily encounter.
  • Lineage Records of the Vigil-Sworn (Keizu cabinet) — Tachibana Akiyo's name appears here, with her sworn date and the Kinkkō chamber as her assigned threshold. The record confirms she was never released.
  • The Brood Activation Protocols (Hihō cabinet) — instructions for activating each of the seven brood-portals throughout the temple complex (the Kinkkō disc is one of seven; the others are TBD across the temple, the buried city of Kinkokyou, and the cavern system). Each activation requires its corresponding token.
  • Pre-Aphelion Astronomical Records (Tenmon cabinet) — millennia of star-position data. Pairs with the orrery's projection sequence. Provides the Great Aphelion timeline (already canon in core/great-aphelion.md).
  • The Order's Final Records (multiple cabinets, late-dated) — Head Priest Kinjiro's external correspondence in the order's last years, parallel to his personal journal in the Jushoku no Ma. Together, the two sources resolve much of what is missing from the operational ledger's fall-period gaps.

Each entry above is a slot. Specific document content will be drafted as the campaign approaches relevance.

  • The Foundational Warding — From The Inside (DC 14 Arcana)
  • The Empty Plinth (DC 13 Investigation or History)
  • The Cabinet Categories (DC 13 History; DC 10 for Ko'jiri)
  • The Reading Table — Last Use (DC 13 Investigation)
  • Time-Logged Entry Records (DC 14 Investigation)

The Foundational Warding: From inside the archive, DC 14 Arcana confirms what was inferred from outside — the wards are construction-level enchantment, woven into the masonry itself. The teleport prohibition extends through floor, ceiling, and all four walls. The portal in the south wall is the singular breach, designed and authorized by the temple's builders. Dispel Magic, Antimagic Field, and similar effects do not affect the foundational warding (it is not a sustained spell but a structural property). The party can read here freely. They cannot easily leave with everything they find — the archive contains far more than they can carry, and the portal's ten-minute window limits any single visit.

The Empty Plinth: DC 13 Investigation or History identifies the central display cradle as designed for a single scroll of significant ceremonial weight — the kind of plinth used to display a charter, a foundational sutra, or the order's most prized text. Whatever was here is gone. The cradle itself is undamaged; the scroll was removed deliberately, by someone who knew what they were doing, and left no trace of how. (DM: see DM Notes.)

The Cabinet Categories: DC 13 History (DC 10 for Ko'jiri) reads the gold-leaf labels as the standard archival categories of the Golden Dragon order's preservation tradition. A character familiar with the system can locate any document type efficiently. Without the system, finding specific documents becomes a slow Investigation grind.

The Reading Table — Last Use: DC 13 Investigation. The reading table holds, on its surface, the very faint impression of a book that lay open on it. Dust has settled around the impression but not within. Someone was reading here when the order fell. Whatever they were reading, they took with them — or were taken with it. The impression's dimensions match the standard format of Head Priest Kinjiro's journal (currently in the Jushoku no Ma).

Time-Logged Entry Records: DC 14 Investigation. The archive maintained an entry log — visitors and the documents they consulted, recorded by the chief archivist. The log is in the Bunsho cabinet, near the entrance side. The final entries record Kinjiro's name, repeatedly, in the weeks before the fall — he was here daily, consulting the Hihō (Secret Methods) cabinet. He was looking for the same Gekkō-reversal documentation the party now seeks. He found it. He was preparing to use it. Time ran out.

(No combat encounters. The archive is undisturbed and uninhabited. The wards have held everything — including the absence of intruders — for thousands of years.)

Atmospheric note: The archive is silent in a way the rest of the temple is not. Even the orrery chamber's acoustic dampening is dynamic — it has a sound, the sound of stillness. The archive has no sound. The wards extend to acoustic insulation. A character who speaks here hears their own voice and nothing more. Players may find this uncomfortable; that is intentional. The archive is a place where the temple's last thoughts are kept, and it does not echo.

Pacing — when to open this room: The archive is the second floor's reward. It is also, deliberately, an exposition dump risk — there is more material here than any single session should surface. Pace the discoveries:

  1. First visit should land 1-3 documents the party most needs for what they currently face. The Vigil-Oath dismissal rite (if Akiyo is unresolved). The Gekkō reversal framework (if they have made the connection from the Zasu's scrolls). The pool ritual content (if pool charges are tight). Other documents are visible but not surfaced — the cabinets exist; the categories are legible; the party knows what is here even if they have not read it yet.
  2. Subsequent visits can surface secondary documents as campaign needs arise. The party can return — the Tenkairō ritual is repeatable.
  3. Documents the party never reads: Some archive contents are background canon only. Not every document needs in-fiction surfacing.

The Empty Plinth — Sealed Thread: The plinth held the Charter of Kinryū's Mandate — the founding document of the Tenkū-ji order, signed by Kinryū herself in the era when the seven Progenitors physically gathered. The charter is not destroyed. It was removed before the fall by Head Priest Kinjiro and placed somewhere safer — either in the Hoko (currently TBD), or with another fragment of the order who escaped before the temple closed. Recovery of the charter is a deep-cut campaign thread; do not surface unless the party pursues it.

The Gekkō Reversal — Specifics Still TBD: The reversal documentation exists and is in this archive. Its specific procedural form is intentionally not yet written, so the campaign can shape it to fit what the party's path actually surfaces. Constraints (already canon, see rm-zasu-ritual-scrolls):

  • It requires the site of origin (a location in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} province, with acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, hollow stone).
  • It requires the counter-work itself (this archive contains it).
  • It requires the convergence of three lights (a Miyosai trinary alignment).
  • The procedure is bounded by these three. The exact ritual structure, material components, and casting requirements are open — establish before the party performs it.

The Brood Activation Protocols — Setup For Later: The seven brood-portals are a campaign-scale system. The Kinkkō disc in rm-vigil-hall is the only one in this temple proper. The other six are scattered; some are in the buried city of Kinkokyō, some elsewhere. The protocols document is the master key to the system. A party that recovers it gains the ability to activate any brood-portal they later find — provided they also recover the brood's specific token. This is meta-content; do not surface mechanically until the structure of the brood-portal arc is decided.

Note on Murasakiryū: The archive does not contain documentation of Murasakiryū as a Progenitor. The Golden Dragon order maintained the public seven-Progenitor framework but treated Murasakiryū's existence as discoverable-tier even within their own archives — the Keizu cabinet's lineage records list six broods, not seven. A character who specifically searches for Amethyst material (DC 16 Investigation, sustained search) finds one document — a sealed letter from an Ancient Guard correspondent to Head Priest Kinjiro, undated, advising him that the seventh dragon's name should not be inscribed in the lineage records. The letter does not explain why. Kinjiro complied. (This is the campaign's deepest archive breadcrumb toward the Order of the Ancient Guard's existence and Murasakiryū's masquerade. Surface only if the party is ready for the next layer.)

Connected entries: rm-tenkairo (only access route via south-wall portal), mon-tachibana-akiyo (dismissal rite held here), rm-zasu-ritual-scrolls (Gekkō reversal cross-reference), rm-grand-hall and rm-star-shrine (DC-18 Religion content equivalents).

"Chamber of the Star Mirror"

The Golden Dragon Clan built the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — mechanical and arcane, capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell in 13088. The Great Aphelion — the nadir of the sei drought — occurred approximately 1,256 years later (~14344), long after the last operator walked away.

What It Is

A circular domed chamber on the second floor of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji. At its center, a mechanical-arcane orrery — a system of bronze armatures, gear tracks, and arcane projection lenses that together model the full Miyosai system:

Type Bodies Armatures
Stars Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi 3
Moons Aokiba, Kagetsu, Nagikumo, Ryugetsu 4

The mechanical layer uses precision bronze gearwork to model orbital periods. The arcane layer projects illusory light around each armature — color, scale, atmospheric effects — transforming the bare mechanism into a functioning planetarium. A control interface at the base allows an operator to set a date, and the mechanism advances or rewinds to show the celestial configuration at that moment.

Miyosai System — Orbital Structure

The Miyosai system is a gravitationally bound trinary stellar system. All three stars orbit a common barycenter. Amaterasu is the most massive and carries its planetary family as it orbits. Seizan, as one of those planets, travels with Amaterasu.

The three stars travel on different orbital inclinations, producing a three-dimensional dance rather than a flat disc. The named astrological events — Nagorikaze, Long Shadow — are routine expressions of this dance.

Critical for the orrery: The seven planets orbit Amaterasu and do not participate in the Great Aphelion. The four moons orbit Seizan and are similarly unaffected. In the orrery, the sei drought is visible as exclusively a two-star withdrawal — Susanoo and Tsukuyomi receding while everything else continues its ordinary motion. The machine keeps working, the planets keep moving, and two of the three stars are simply not where they should be.

How It Connects to the Tapestries

The orrery is integrated with the temple's foundational magic. When the orrery reaches full operational status (all 9 components restored), its sei resonance propagates through the construction-level enchantment that permeates the entire structure. On the first floor, the ori-kioku tapestries — fabric woven with the Golden Dragon order's memory-recording technique — respond to the restored sei field by activating simultaneously.

In play: Full orrery restoration triggers all four surviving tapestries at once. The scenes do not loop or replay — they run continuously as sustained living images, the way a fire is sustained rather than the way a torch is lit and guttered. The woven figures move, the stitched landscapes shift, color deepens and flows. The tapestries remain active for as long as the orrery is operational.

The physical separation between the orrery and the tapestries still matters — the party must descend from the second floor to the South Entrance to witness the result. The first descent after restoring the orrery is a dramatic beat: they have been in this room before, they know these walls. Now the tapestries are alive.

The orrery's date-display function — its ability to model celestial configurations across millennia — is a separate capability, independent of tapestry activation. The party can use the orrery to explore the Miyosai system's history (including the dramatic approach of the Great Aphelion) without affecting the tapestries, which respond to the orrery's operational state, not its displayed date.

The 11 tapestry positions in the South Entrance correspond to 11 moments in the temple's history. Four survive intact. Seven are destroyed or removed. The observatory can only activate what physically remains — no tapestry, no scene.

Component System

The observatory requires 9 components to reach full operation. Seven are found on the first floor (five in the rooms the party visits during regular exploration, two in the Scriptorium); two remain on the second floor, both in the orrery itself (Amaterasu lens still mounted, stellar drive still in place). Components fall into four repair categories.

Repair Sequence

Repairs happen in stages as the party acquires components and makes checks. The observatory does not need all 9 components for partial function — it can be brought online incrementally.

Stage 1 — Assessment (No components required)

When: The party first enters the observatory. What happens: The room is visually impressive even damaged — the armature framework is visible, the dome's inner surface is etched with constellation guides, the central mechanism is clearly a device of extraordinary complexity. A character can assess the damage without tools:

  • DC 12 Investigation or Arcana: Identifies this as an astronomical device; recognizes missing/broken components
  • DC 14 History (DC 11 for Ko'jiri): Connects it to Golden Dragon Clan records of a celestial observatory; understands its purpose
  • DC 14 Tinker's Tools or Smith's Tools: Identifies what specific repairs are needed and in what order

DM note: If the party has already found components on the first floor, this is the "aha" moment — the mysterious crystals and bronze rings suddenly have context.

Stage 2 — Mechanical Restoration

Requirements: Planetary gear assembly (#2), stellar drive mechanism (#7, freed in place) Checks:

  • Free the seized stellar drive: DC 12 Athletics to break the main shaft loose, then DC 13 Tinker's Tools or Smith's Tools to clean and realign
  • Install planetary gear assembly: DC 13 Tinker's Tools (the bent outer ring must be straightened first — DC 12 Smith's Tools or improvised)

Result: The mechanical layer begins to move. Armatures track, but without lenses the movement is bare bronze — functional but producing no light or projection. The party can see the shape of celestial motion without the detail. This is still impressive and demonstrates the mechanism works.

Stage 3 — Arcane Restoration

Requirements: At least one projection lens (#1, #4, or #6 repaired), sei conduit filament (#5) Checks:

  • Install sei conduit filament: DC 14 Arcana — thread the filament through the conduit channel running from the mechanism's base to the projection mounts. A character attuned to sei (Ko'jiri, Relc) has advantage.
  • Mount projection lens(es): DC 12 Tinker's Tools per lens. Each lens seats into a specific mount — Susanoo (blue-white) in the inner ring, Tsukuyomi (deep red) in the outer ring, Amaterasu (golden) in the central position.
  • Repair cracked Amaterasu lens: DC 15 Arcana combined with Tinker's Tools (two characters can work together). Failure does not destroy the lens but leaves its projection dim and incomplete.

Result per lens:

  • Amaterasu only: The primary star projects — golden light fills the dome, warm and steady. The mechanical armatures are now illuminated. Beautiful but incomplete.
  • Susanoo added: Blue-white companion star appears; ghost-light effects play across the dome walls when its orbit draws close. Water magic ambient effects become faintly perceptible.
  • Tsukuyomi added: Deep red dwarf star appears on its elongated orbit. Shadows in the room shift subtly as it moves. The full stellar system is now operational.

Partial function note: With even one lens installed and the sei conduit connected, the orrery begins producing sei resonance — the room comes alive with partial projection. However, tapestry activation requires full orrery restoration (all 9 components). Partial restoration produces no tapestry response. The orrery's sei output at partial stages is sufficient for the observatory's own projection effects but not for propagating resonance through the temple's foundational magic to the South Entrance.

Stage 4 — Lunar Arms

Requirements: Lunar armature set (#8) Checks:

  • Install four lunar arms: DC 13 Tinker's Tools (single check for all four — they mount as a set into pre-built receivers)

Result: The four moons appear in the projection — each with its canonical character (Aokiba crystalline, Kagetsu shadow-absorbing, Nagikumo softly glowing, Ryugetsu color-shifting). Tidal calculations become visible. The compound stellar + lunar alignments that produce the named astrological events (Nagorikaze, Tatsunami, Hikarisho, etc.) are now trackable.

Stage 5 — Calibration

Requirements: Calibration disc (#3), operator's manual (#9) Checks:

  • Seat the calibration disc: DC 12 (automatic if a character understands its purpose)
  • Read the operator's manual: DC 14 History to read Old Imperial technical text (DC 11 for Ko'jiri; advantage if Comprehend Languages is active)
  • Set the reference date: DC 14 Navigator's Tools or Arcana — using the Star Shrine's fixed etching of the Great Aphelion as a known reference point (if the party studied it). Without the Star Shrine reference, DC 17.
  • Alternative calibration method: A character who meditates in the Star Shrine under moonlight and then returns to the observatory has advantage on the calibration check — the shrine's projected sky provides the "current" reference, and the orrery can be wound backward from there.

Result: The control interface is operational. The operator can set any date and the orrery advances or rewinds to display the celestial configuration at that moment. The tapestry activation reaches full clarity — but the party must descend to the South Entrance to witness the result.

Setting a Date

The operator turns the calibration disc to advance or rewind time. The mechanism moves smoothly — the room fills with light and shadow as centuries pass in minutes. Watching the Great Aphelion approach is dramatic: Susanoo's blue-white dims and vanishes from its armature; Tsukuyomi's deep red bleeds away even earlier. The planetary and lunar armatures continue their ordinary motion — the machine keeps working while two of its three stars go dark. The light dims to Amaterasu alone. The room grows cold. Then it passes, and the slow return begins — Susanoo first, then Tsukuyomi, centuries apart.

Orrery Projection Sequence

What the party observes when scrolling through the dial. Mechanical armature motion continues normally throughout — only the arcane projection layer responds to sei availability. See core/great-aphelion.md for the full detailed sequence with individual star profiles.

Pre-Decline (pre-~12605): All three stars at full intensity. The dome warm and fully lit — the room functioning as designed. When the party scrolls to a Golden Age date, they understand for the first time what they have been looking at in its damaged state.

Early Decline (~12605–12700): Tsukuyomi's deep red begins to bleed at the edges. Subtle. Susanoo holds full brightness. The dome is visibly but not dramatically wrong.

Deepening Decline (~12700–12806): Tsukuyomi's red is clearly diminished. Susanoo still holds. The first star crosses below visibility threshold at approximately 12806. Dark ages begin.

Late Decline (~12806–14264): Tsukuyomi's arm is dark. Susanoo still holds but dimming. The dome is Amaterasu's gold, Susanoo's fading blue-white, and one silent arm.

Susanoo's Failure (~14264–14344): Susanoo's projection dims and goes dark. The dome is Amaterasu alone. All planetary and lunar armatures continue their ordinary motion. The room does not feel like an observatory.

Great Aphelion (~14344): All three stars at maximum mutual distance. Three separate arms on three separate planes, all pointing away from each other. The geometry is legible before the party processes the darkness. Amaterasu alone in the dome. The nadir.

Post-Nadir (~14344–15883): Scrolling forward changes nothing visible. Amaterasu holds. The two secondary arms remain dark. Advancing centuries in seconds and seeing no change has its own effect at the table. The absence is not passive.

Dawn (~15883): Susanoo's armature shows the first ghost of blue-white. A character with sei sensitivity may feel warmth in their sternum before the light is visible to anyone. The dark ages end.

First Talents (~15883–15962): Susanoo's blue-white strengthens slowly. Tsukuyomi's arm remains dark. The match between star position and magical accessibility is legible if they think to look for it.

Return Arc (~15962–16693): Susanoo continues strengthening. Tsukuyomi's deep red begins its slower return. The return does not feel like restoration — it feels like recovery from a very long illness.

Great Awakening (~16693): Tsukuyomi's red crosses into clear visibility. All three stars present.

Current Date (16744): The orrery shows the present sky. All three stars lit. A comparison against a Golden Age date reveals Tsukuyomi's projection carries slightly less intensity than its pre-decline readings. The return is real. It is not yet complete.

This is the only moment in the orrery sequence where the party is looking at their own world in real time.

Tapestry Activation

When the orrery reaches full operational status (all 9 components restored), sei resonance propagates through the temple's foundational magic down to the South Entrance. All four surviving tapestries activate simultaneously.

  • Intact tapestry: The woven scene comes to life on the fabric itself. Stitched figures move within the weave, colors deepen and flow, the static image becomes a sustained living state. Faint sound — not words but the ambient texture of the recorded moment (wind, fire, distant voices) — emanates from the fabric. The scene does not loop or replay. It runs continuously, the ori-kioku sustaining the recorded moment as a living state rather than a playback.
  • Damaged tapestry: The surviving portions animate; damaged sections remain static or flicker with partial, distorted motion. Where the fabric is torn, the scene cuts off at the tear edge. Information is partial, shaped by what physically remains.
  • Destroyed tapestry: The position is dark. If the frame is still mounted but the fabric burned or decayed beyond recognition, a faint pulse of warmth and the ghost of color ripples across the ruined surface — the ori-kioku is trying to activate in material that can no longer carry it. Nothing readable comes through.
  • Missing tapestry (cut down and removed): Nothing at all. The empty wall shows no response. But a character standing at the empty position during activation (DC 12 Perception) feels a brief pulse of warmth in the stone behind the mounting brackets — confirming the system expected something here. The missing tapestries exist somewhere, if they can be found.

Tapestry III — Architectural Distinction

Tapestry III is architecturally distinct from the other three. Where Tapestries I, II, and IV hold fixed historical moments in their ori-kioku, Tapestry III was built as a monitoring surface — its ori-kioku records ongoing network state rather than a single event. When the orrery activates it, it does not play back the past. It shows the current state of the sanctuary network as of the moment of activation.

This distinction is discoverable: the motion quality of Tapestry III is subtly different from the others. Historical ori-kioku playback has a smoothness — complete, consistent, rendered the way memory renders the past. Tapestry III has the slight irregular quality of a live feed. The tidal motion does not loop. It follows an actual current. DC 14 Arcana to identify the distinction formally; observant players may notice it without a check.

This property means that Tapestry III's value is not fixed at the moment of orrery restoration — it continues to reflect the network's actual state. If a site changes status after the party restores the orrery, Tapestry III will show the change.

Ruling: The Tapestry Is the Medium

The ori-kioku technique records into the fabric. The fabric is not a screen — it is the recording. What was physically destroyed is gone. Cut sections, gouged faces, missing panels — the activation animates what remains, nothing more. Destroying a tapestry destroys the record. Removing a tapestry removes the record from this location.

This means:

  • The destroyed tapestries' content is permanently lost unless the physical fabric is recovered from wherever it was taken
  • The deliberate damage matters — the infiltrators who gouged the first head priest's face and cut sections from multiple tapestries successfully erased that information. Their act of destruction holds weight across millennia.
  • Finding missing tapestries becomes a potential quest thread — several were cut down and removed, not destroyed. They exist somewhere. Returning them to their positions and activating the orrery would reveal their scenes.
  • The activation rewards thorough exploration without cheapening the physical damage — the party sees four living moments of Golden Dragon history, each one powerful but incomplete. The incompleteness is the point.

Ko'jiri

The observatory is the genuine article of everything he has performed knowledge of. Working on the real mechanism — reading the operator's manual, recognizing the planetary notations from his research — is a moment where the con artist's scholarly knowledge proves to be real expertise. His Golden Dragon Clan advantage applies throughout. The orrery doesn't judge him the way the statue does; it just needs someone who knows what it is. He does.

Relc

The calibration process benefits from druidic celestial attunement. Relc can feel when the mechanism is correctly aligned — not through calculation but through the same instinct that connects him to natural cycles. The Star Shrine meditation path (advantage on calibration) is his contribution. The sky is a text he already reads.

Sun Wukong

The mechanical precision required for armature installation and lens mounting rewards steady hands and disciplined focus. Ki-guided fine motor work — the monk's equivalent of Tinker's Tools. The monastery's emphasis on patience and precision maps directly onto the repair work.

Dian Wei

The seized stellar drive requires physical strength (Athletics DC 12) before the fine work can begin. The structural assessment — identifying load-bearing cracks, ensuring the mechanism's frame is stable — is practical, martial knowledge applied in a new context. Dian holds the room together while the others do the delicate work.

Pacing Across Sessions

The observatory repair is designed to be prepared for on floor 1 (where seven of the nine components live, including the Scriptorium-stored lunar armatures and operator's manual) and executed on floor 2 (where the remaining two components stay in place inside the orrery itself). The repair work itself is concentrated in the orrery chamber; floor 2's other rooms — Tenkairō, Vigil Hall, Hidden Archives — carry the floor's exploration weight independently.

Suggested flow:

  1. First-floor preparation: Party gathers components across regular floor-1 exploration (Grand Hall, Star Shrine, Mess Hall, Dormitories, Inner Sanctum) and the Scriptorium. By the time they reach the stairs up, they may hold up to seven components without yet understanding what they are for.
  2. Discovery: Party reaches the Tenkairō, then the Orrery. Assessment checks. "Aha" moment lands hard if they have most of the components — the puzzle resolves.
  3. Other floor-2 exploration: The seven-plate ritual at the Tenkairō, Akiyo in the Vigil Hall, the warded north wall and its archives. The party can engage these in any order.
  4. First repair session: Mechanical restoration (Stage 2) — free the seized stellar drive, install planetary gear assembly. The mechanism moves. Brief, satisfying.
  5. Second repair session: Arcane restoration (Stage 3). Repair the cracked Amaterasu lens in place; install the Susanoo and Tsukuyomi lenses; thread the sei conduit filament. Light fills the dome. Major atmospheric moment.
  6. Final repair session: Lunar arms (Stage 4), calibration (Stage 5) using the operator's manual and calibration disc. Full activation.
  7. The descent: After full restoration, the party goes back downstairs to the South Entrance — the very first room they entered. They have been here before. They know these walls. Describe the South Entrance differently now. The moment they see the first tapestry moving, the room they thought they understood becomes something else entirely. Let that beat land.
  8. The living tapestries: All four surviving tapestries are now active simultaneously. The party can move between them freely. Budget 45-60 minutes for the full experience. This is a sustained state, not a timed event — they can return to the tapestries whenever they want as long as the orrery is running.

Each repair session should take 15-30 minutes of table time. The tapestry activation scene is the big set piece. Budget 45-60 minutes.

The Shrouded Isles rise from the Raijin no Fukai sea beneath three stars. This is Kagekuni — an archipelago of mist-veiled mountains, bamboo forests that stretch beyond sight, and castle towns where paper lanterns sway above streets of packed earth. It is a land shaped by earthquakes and typhoons, by the pull of four moons on restless tides, and by the ancient hierarchies of emperor, shogun, and clan. Here, honour is not a sentiment but a currency — earned through duty, spent through sacrifice, and lost in ways that can never be recovered. The samurai who kneels before their daimyō, the merchant who bows lower still, the priest who tends a shrine at the edge of a forest where the trees have bark of burnished bronze — each knows their place in an order older than memory, and each carries the weight of what that place demands.

For three thousand years, the world forgot magic. The energy called sei — once woven through every living thing, every river, every breath of wind — fell silent, and with it the knowledge, the institutions, and the traditions that had shaped civilisation for millennia. That silence ended fifty-one years ago. Sei has returned. The stars burn bright again in unfamiliar constellations, and across Kagekuni a generation is learning to wield power that their grandparents believed was myth. But the world that magic left behind did not stand still. Old rivalries hardened into new hatreds. Sacred places fell to ruin. Things that slumbered in the dark ages have begun to stir. You arrive in this world at the edge of what comes next — when the questions of what was lost, what survived, and what is waking matter more than they have in living memory.

The archipelago of Kagekuni — the Shrouded Isles — rises from the Raijin no Fukai sea like the spine of something ancient and half-submerged. Five major islands and a scattering of lesser ones form a chain shaped by the collision of four tectonic plates, each island bearing the scars and gifts of the geology beneath it. Volcanic peaks trail smoke into skies where three stars wheel. Coastlines shift with the complex tides of four moons. Bamboo forests climb mountain flanks where the trees give way to pale crystal trunks that chime in the wind, and lowland rivers run faintly luminous at night through paddies of indigo grass.

This is a land that moves. Earthquakes shake its foundations. Typhoons rake its coasts. Monsoons swell its rivers and drown its roads. The people of Kagekuni have never known a still world, and their architecture, their agriculture, their faith, and their politics all reflect it. Castles are built to flex rather than resist. Villages relocate rather than rebuild. Shrines stand where the earth is quietest, and the earth is rarely quiet for long.

The pages that follow describe the islands, provinces, and settlements of Kagekuni — the places where power concentrates, where trade flows, where clans hold their seats, and where the spaces between destinations are as important as the destinations themselves. The roads of Kagekuni are not empty connective tissue. They are where travellers encounter the world as it actually is: the weather, the terrain, the people moving between places with purposes of their own. A three-day journey through the mountains is three days of the world revealing itself — not a gap to be skipped.

Hokori is the largest island in the Kagekuni archipelago — approximately 237,000 square miles, stretching 750 miles long and 600 miles wide. Seen from above, the island is X-shaped, its form carved by the collision of four tectonic plates that converge beneath it. The geology is restless. Earthquakes are frequent. Volcanic peaks trail smoke from the northern highlands. Tsunamis reshape the coastline. The people of Hokori have built their civilisation not despite this instability but in conversation with it — their architecture flexes, their settlements relocate, and their culture carries the pragmatic resilience of people who know the ground beneath them is never truly still.

Hokori is divided into eight provinces, each with its own geography, climate, political allegiance, and character. Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana} occupies the eastern coast of Hokori and is the seat of imperial history. It stretches along the island's eastern seaboard, bounded to the northwest by the mountainous interior of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} province for the majority of its inland border, with @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.qODDmax1GHoTx3fx]{Tsuchi} and Hi to the west, and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} to the north.

The province's defining feature is the Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea), a vast inland sea covering more than a thousand square miles, fed by twenty-five rivers and thirteen waterfalls cascading from the Tenchusan Ren and the central highlands of Hokori. Its surface shifts color with the seasons. The tidal rhythms driven by Kagekuni's four moons make its edges unpredictable; the shoreline can retreat several hundred meters during low compound tides.

To the west, the Seidorin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) stretches for miles -- an ancient woodland where the trees grow with bark of burnished copper-bronze that catches sunlight like armor. Their leaves shed entirely in one night when the temperature drops below a certain threshold. The wood itself is extraordinarily hard and is harvested under strict clan license for weapons and structural reinforcement.

To the northeast, the land rises sharply toward the Tenchusan Ren. The pass through this range is the primary land route north. The mountains are sacred in Hana's religious tradition; several peak-top shrines are maintained by hermit monks.

Shirogane Yama (Silver Mountain), the highest peak on Hokori, dominates the northern skyline -- a pale peak streaked with natural mineral deposits that catch moonlight. At its summit sits the Hoshino To (Tower of Stars), an ancient astronomical observatory built during the Golden Age. The city of Kumoji sits at its base.

Key Waterways: Kinryugawa (Gold Dragon River), Midorikawa (Green River), Sutariba (Star River)

Points of Interest:

  • Seidorin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) -- Ancient woodland with metallic-barked trees. Harvested under strict Clan Kaminari license. The interior is unnervingly quiet -- sound behaves strangely under the canopy. Unlicensed logging is a capital offense.
  • Serenia-kai (Selenia Sea) -- The great inland sea. Major artery for trade and travel. The most dangerous tidal event is Ryugetsu's Embrace, when three moons align over the sea simultaneously.
  • Hoshino To (Tower of Stars) -- Ancient observatory on Shirogane Yama summit. Still operational; maintained by a small order of seimasters. Instruments calibrated to all three stars and four moons simultaneously.
  • Kodan no Jinja -- Ancient roadside shrine. Grants divine boons to supplicants for a period of days equal to three times the recipient's experience level (maximum sixty days). Only one boon at a time.
  • Shadowfen Bridge -- Stone bridge near @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.eUCVLOrFBBpO7dHx]{Sakura Mura} crossing into marsh forest. Legend claims a river spirit demands one honest secret spoken aloud; liars find the far bank leads somewhere unintended.
  • Tenchusan Ren (Heavenly Pillar Mountains) -- The mountain range forming Hana's northwestern boundary. The pass is treacherous in autumn and impassable during winter storms. Significant ruins exist within the range.

Culture & Trade

Hana's culture is the closest to the old imperial ideal -- formal, ceremonially rich, and deeply aware of its historical weight. The proximity to Heian means merchants, scholars, monks, and diplomats pass through constantly, and even small villages carry themselves with a certain civic dignity uncommon in frontier provinces.

The Bronze Wood trade defines the province's economy. Seidorin timber commands extraordinary prices across the archipelago -- weapons and armor crafted from it are status symbols as much as tools. The licensing system for harvesting creates significant corruption opportunities at every level of local administration.

Fishing on the Serenia-kai and the Kinryugawa sustains much of the rural population. The Gold Dragon River runs fat with a fish called @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.items.Item.aAVMPjIVMn92MoHV]{kinuo} (gold-tail) that is considered a delicacy in Heian and commands premium prices at market.

History

Hana is the oldest continuously inhabited province in the archipelago. The Golden Dragon Clan held dominion over these southern highlands long before human settlement -- their capital Kinkokyo is believed to have stood somewhere in or beneath the Tenchusan Ren, buried by the avalanche triggered during the Onyx Rebellion. The province's rivers still run faintly gold at dawn -- a phenomenon locals call Kinryu no Namida (the Golden Dragon's Tears).

Heian was chosen as the imperial capital by the First Emperor Tenryu no Mikado for strategic and spiritual reasons -- it stood at the convergence of three rivers, on a defensible peninsula, and was reportedly the site of a vision in which Kinryu declared the land under divine protection.

The province suffered heavily during the Dark Ages -- Heian was sacked twice -- but its infrastructure proved resilient. The Emperor's Highway remains largely intact through Hana.

Clan Kaminari has governed Hana for the past several centuries. The clan rose to prominence when @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.1J9hy9Hs6EVuYjyz]{Raijin no Kazuhiko} unified the province under a single authority following a period of fractious minor-clan governance.

Details

The Bronze Wood Forest's metallic quality has a deeper origin than simple mineral runoff -- connected to the buried city of Kinkokyo beneath the Tenchusan Ren.

The Shadowfen Bridge exhibits genuine sei resonance that produces mild disorientation in those who speak falsehoods while crossing.

A seimaster from Hoshino To has gone missing after reporting an unusual celestial alignment that matches nothing in the records.

The Buried City of Kinkokyo

The Golden Dragon Clan's capital is not simply buried rubble. Significant portions survived structurally intact, sealed beneath hundreds of feet of rock and earth. The gold doors the party currently stands before are an outer entrance to this buried complex, exposed by a recent earthquake. The temple above is connected to Kinkokyo below. Ko'jiri's research is essentially correct.

Kinryu no Hikari

The artifact exists. It is held in a sealed vault deep within the temple, in the farthest underground section of Kinkokyo. It is not a weapon or a key. It is a communication device: a golden mirror that allows direct communion with Kinryu, the living Golden Dragon, wherever she is hidden. She will answer if called by someone she deems worthy.

The Bronze Wood Secret

The Seidorin Mori grows over a second branch of the buried Kinkokyo canal system. The metallic quality of the trees is caused by trace mineral content in the groundwater -- water flowing through golden veins in the buried city's infrastructure for thousands of years. @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.YSPRToQNBVq5NJFZ]{Ren Nakamura} (Shicho of Kikyo) knows this. The merchant guild he is allied with wants to find the source and exploit it directly.

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.JLGqqI474AH04SDL]{Hiroshi Nakamura} -- Traitor in Place

As Shugo of Heian, Hiroshi controls the administrative heart of the province. His access to Clan Kaminari intelligence is nearly total. He has been feeding information to an outside party (undeveloped) for at least three years. His warm, approachable public persona is his most effective weapon -- even his brother Hideo does not suspect how deep the betrayal runs.

Plot Hooks

Unlicensed Bronze Wood poaching tied to a merchant guild front operation in Kikyo -- Ren Nakamura's faction or a rival?

Strange behavior reported in Shadowfen Bridge area -- a traveler arrived at the wrong destination and has no memory of the crossing

A seimaster from Hoshino To has gone missing after reporting an unusual celestial alignment that matches nothing in the records

Geography & Terrain

Hi is the most geologically violent province on Hokori -- a region of active volcanism, fumarole fields, obsidian plains, and mountains that periodically tear themselves apart. It encompasses the majority of the island's western side, surrounded by mountains and the sea. @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.qODDmax1GHoTx3fx]{Tsuchi} borders it to the southeast, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana} shares a small stretch of its eastern border, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} encompasses its northern boundary, and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.M72zAjYRdrTCan30]{Mizu} sits along its western edge. Earthquakes are ambient. Residents learn to read tremors the way sailors read wind.

The province takes its name -- Hi, meaning fire -- from the volcanic peaks that define it. The largest, Enshiyama (Flame Peak Mountain), is the third highest peak on Hokori. It last erupted in full approximately two hundred years ago.

The terrain is dramatic and hostile. Black obsidian fields stretch for miles where ancient lava flows cooled and cracked. Fumarole vents release sulfurous steam. Soil, where it exists, is extraordinarily fertile -- volcanic ash enriches it beyond anything in the southern provinces. Terraced farming on the slopes between active zones produces crops of startling quality. This contradiction -- death and abundance in tight proximity -- defines Hi's cultural character.

Rivers here run fast and hot from thermal sources. The Honogawa (Flame River) originates from a thermal lake near Enshiyama's base and is warm to the touch for its entire upper reach.

Points of Interest:

  • Enshiyama (Flame Peak Mountain) -- Dominant volcano of Hokori's north. Currently active at low levels. Crater contains a mineral-rich lake that glows faintly orange at night.
  • Honogawa (Flame River) -- Warm thermal river. Upper reach near the source is hot enough to scald. Runs through a narrow volcanic gorge.
  • Obsidian Fields of Kuroso -- Vast plains of black volcanic glass. Obsidian of exceptional quality, ideal for blades and lenses. Seismically active and hazardous.
  • The Crimson Shrine -- Deep in the volcanic highlands, predating the empire. Torii of natural red stone. Local tradition holds Akaryu's presence can be felt during major eruptions. Never absorbed into the imperial religious system.
  • Onsen-machi Hot Springs -- The only genuinely comfortable location in Hi. Natural hot spring pools developed into a resort town maintaining political neutrality.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes

Kurokawa Village Black river settlement; obsidian crafting; trade in volcanic glass
Onsen-machi Town Hot spring resort town; wealthy visitors; nominal neutrality

Culture & Trade

Hi's culture is defined by proximity to death. The people are laconic, practical, and possess a dark humor about their circumstances. They do not flee volcanic activity -- they have developed sophisticated systems for reading, mitigating, and living alongside it. Hi's volcano-guides, engineers, and evacuation specialists are prized across the archipelago.

Primary exports are obsidian, volcanic sulfur (used in alchemy and sei-related preparations), hot spring minerals, and surprisingly excellent agricultural products from volcanic terraces. The Onsen-machi resort draws wealthy visitors from across Hokori and beyond.

History

Hi was long considered a backwater -- too dangerous and too remote. The Crimson Dragon Clan had their true stronghold here before unification, and the western reaches refused submission to Tenryu no Mikado. That refusal left a cultural legacy: Hi's people are fiercely independent and deeply skeptical of imperial authority.

During the Dark Ages, Hi was almost entirely abandoned by formal authority. Small communities developed their own governance structures, spiritual practices, and martial traditions largely divorced from the broader empire.

The province is currently in contested administration. The previous governing clan was wiped out in the opening engagements of the Arashi-Genso war, and neither alliance has installed a replacement. Several smaller clans are vying for the position.

Details

The Crimson Shrine's keeper, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.oACSZZYBMIV9sr54]{Tsubaki}, has served for sixty years and communicates with something through the shrine's ember-bowl.

The western territories of Hi are home to descendants of the Crimson Clan faction that refused unification, organized into loose tribal confederacies preserving forgotten traditions.

Seimasters debate whether Enshiyama's current activity signals a major eruption building.

The Crimson Dragon Clan's Hidden Presence

Akaryu, the Crimson Dragon, is still alive and hidden. She maintains a tenuous connection to Hi through the Crimson Shrine. The shrine's keeper Tsubaki is an Initiate of the Order of the Ancient Guard. She does not know Akaryu's location, but knows the dragon is alive. Offerings burned in the shrine's ember-bowl reach something that responds.

The Western Territories

The western reaches are effectively a separate entity. Descendants of the Crimson Clan faction that refused Tenryu's unification live there in loose tribal confederacies that have preserved traditions the rest of the empire forgot. They are fiercely territorial and know things about the volcanic highlands that no imperial map captures.

Enshiyama and the Coming Eruption

The current low-level activity is the precursor to a significant eruption -- within one to three years. The seimasters who know this are divided on whether to publicize it; the political vacuum means there is no coordinating authority capable of organizing evacuation. This is an unlit fuse.

The Contested Administration

The three clans competing for Hi's governance are being quietly manipulated by a fourth party -- a merchant consortium that wants provincial administration too weak to enforce trade regulations. The current chaos is, to some degree, manufactured.

Plot Hooks

A volcano-guide from Kazan Mura has seen something in the upper reaches of Enshiyama -- something that moved against the wind -- and is too frightened to go back alone

The Crimson Shrine's ember-bowl responded to an offering in a way it never has before; Tsubaki needs discreet help interpreting what it means

A seimaster studying the eruption precursors has disappeared; her notes suggest she found something in the obsidian fields that was not geological

Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} is a province of shadows and mist. It occupies the eastern side of Hokori's northeastern leg -- the X-shape's upper-right arm. @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.ijGHvVOlw9tFpBo8]{Nami} sits to the north, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.EPAWGqYCrUzYfngV]{Kusa} to the west, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana} to the south, and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} shares a brief stretch of its southwestern border. Sheltered from direct coastal weather by mountain ranges, it has a microclimate of cool, damp air that never fully clears. The province averages fewer clear days per year than any other on the island. Its forests -- dense stands of dark cedar and ancient black pine -- grow so thickly that the canopy blocks most sunlight even in summer. Locals navigate by landmark and feel rather than by sun or stars.

The terrain is mountainous, cut by deep river valleys and narrow gorges. The Kazeyama Ren (Wind Mountain Range) runs along the province's southern border, channeling wind up the valleys in complex, disorienting patterns. Sounds carry strangely here, seeming to come from the wrong direction.

The Kagero River (Shimmer River) is the primary waterway -- named for the heat shimmer visible over its surface on rare warm days, caused by thermal differential between the water temperature and the cool air.

The town of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.ow3AGqlvFevncAwN]{Akatsuki} (Dawn) occupies a peculiar position -- its name suggests emergence and new light, but it is one of the most shrouded settlements in the archipelago. The name predates the current settlement.

Points of Interest:

  • Tsukikage (Moonlit Shadow) -- Abandoned former capital of Clan Gekko. Not destroyed or obviously fled in panic -- it simply emptied gradually over several months. Personal belongings remain in homes. The daimyo's residence is locked from the outside.
  • Monastery of the Black Lily -- Above Akatsuki village, accessible by stone staircase cut into rock. Dark stone and iron construction; austere; forbidding. The Order of the Black Lily operates here -- Kagekuni's most skilled infiltrators and intelligence operatives.
  • The Kagero Gorge -- Narrow river gorge with complex, disorienting acoustics. The gorge wall contains numerous carved reliefs depicting serpentine figures that do not match any known iconographic tradition.
  • The Hollow Peaks -- Three mountains in the Kazeyama Ren that are demonstrably hollow. Cold air vents from fissures at their bases year-round. Sei-sensitive individuals report a powerful residual presence.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes

Akatsuki Village De facto administrative center; above it: Monastery of the Black Lily
Kazetani Village Deep valley settlement; largely cut off; residents haven't left in months

Culture & Trade

Kaze's culture is inward-facing. Primary exports have historically been information -- Clan Gekko's intelligence networks and the Order of the Black Lily's trained specialists. In tangible terms, Kaze produces excellent black pine lumber, rare mountain herbs for medicine and alchemy, and distinctive lacquerware using naturally sourced pigments from mineral-rich soil.

The people of Kaze are not cold -- they are careful. A culture of watching and listening developed naturally in a province where visibility is limited and sound behaves unreliably. They form deep loyalties within small groups and extend trust to outsiders only after extended familiarity.

History

Kaze was historically the domain of Clan Gekko, an independent clan that maintained careful neutrality through successive political upheavals. The Gekko were notable for producing seimasters specializing in shadow and illusion magic -- linked to the province's physical character and lingering influence from the Onyx Dragon Clan.

The province was never fully subdued -- even Tenryu no Mikado secured Gekko cooperation through negotiation rather than conquest. This arrangement eventually crystallized into the Order of the Black Lily, Kagekuni's premier infiltration school.

Clan Gekko's recent disappearance has plunged the province into deep unease. Trade has slowed. The provincial administration has stopped communicating with @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian}. Small communities have reported strange encounters -- serpentine figures glimpsed on mountain trails, abandoned buildings showing signs of violent disturbance, livestock found dead in unnatural ways.

Details

Clan Gekko's disappearance was not caused by an outside force -- the senior seimasters attempted something that went catastrophically wrong.

The Order of the Black Lily knows the truth about what happened and has made a calculated decision about when to reveal it.

The Hollow Peaks were structures of the Onyx Dragon Clan -- hollow mountains used as nesting and storage spaces.

The gorge carvings depict something connected to the transformation that befell Clan Gekko.

The Nagaji Truth -- Core Campaign Revelation

Clan Gekko's disappearance was not caused by an outside force. The clan's senior seimasters, searching for a way to elevate their shadow magic capability, discovered fragmentary texts describing an Onyx Dragon ritual -- a transformation rite tied to Kokuryu. It transformed those who underwent it into Nagaji -- serpentine humanoids driven by new instincts they cannot fully suppress. The transformation spread. Masota no Gekko himself underwent the ritual last, in a desperate attempt to maintain control. He is now Nagaji as well -- somewhere in the Kaze highlands.

The Order of the Black Lily -- What They Know

The Order knows the truth about the Nagaji transformation. Several operatives witnessed the early stages. The Order has made a calculated decision: the information is too dangerous to release without a reversal plan. They will share the complete truth with parties who reach them -- but only the complete truth, no partial admissions.

Is the Transformation Reversible?

Yes -- but the answer lies in the Temple of Kinryu, specifically in the clan's records about Kokuryu's original ritual and the countermeasure that the Golden Dragon Clan developed. This creates a direct link between the party's current location (the gold doors) and the Kaze storyline.

Masota no Gekko -- Current State

He is alive, in the Kaze highlands. He retains fragments of his original identity but the transformation suppresses rational thought during stress or combat. He is not a villain. He is a leader who made a terrible decision in desperation. A potential redemption arc exists if the party can find a reversal.

The Hollow Peaks

These were Onyx Dragon Clan structures. The interior of at least one is accessible from the gorge. What remains inside is ancient and significant: Onyx Clan cultural artifacts, including documentation of the transformation ritual.

Plot Hooks

The Order of the Black Lily sends a message via an intermediary: "Come to Akatsuki. Come alone. Come before the moon is full."

Masota no Gekko leaves something behind at a ransacked site -- something a transformed being could not have done deliberately unless part of him was still trying to communicate

A scholar in Mikazuki has been studying the gorge carvings for years and has just realized what they depict

Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.EPAWGqYCrUzYfngV]{Kusa} is Hokori's verdant interior -- a province of dense forests, wide river floodplains, and grasslands so deep and tall that travelers on foot are hidden from view within a hundred paces. It occupies the western side of Hokori's northeastern leg, with @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} encroaching on its southeastern border, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.M72zAjYRdrTCan30]{Mizu} to the southwest, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.ijGHvVOlw9tFpBo8]{Nami} to the north, and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} to the east. Drainage from surrounding mountain ranges converges here, creating a network of rivers, oxbow lakes, and seasonal wetlands that makes the land extraordinarily fertile and difficult to traverse without knowing the paths.

The forests are ancient and immense, dark-trunked hardwoods with canopies that diffuse light into a permanent green twilight. The forest floor grows in luminous violet and deep blue hues -- murasaki-gusa (purple grass) and aoi-koke (blue moss) -- endemic to the interior lowlands and giving the province a distinctive visual character unique in Hokori.

The Midori River is the primary artery -- wide, slow-moving, navigable for flat-bottomed vessels. The capital Midoriko sits at the junction of the Midori and its largest tributary, the Futago-kawa (Twin River).

The Kusayama Ren (Grass Mountains) forms the province's northern boundary. Notable for the Yosei Mori (Forest of Spirits), a region of ancient woodland where sei activity is consistently elevated and unusual phenomena are reported year-round.

Points of Interest:

  • Yosei Mori (Forest of Spirits) -- Sei-active ancient woodland. Navigation is genuinely unreliable. The Forest of Spirits faction maintains sanctuaries within. Unusual creatures in deeper reaches exhibit significantly elevated intelligence.
  • Heiwa-mizo (Peace Ditch) -- Old defensive trench in Midoriko, now a long public garden with cherry trees. Hosts the Sakura no Nagori (Lingering Cherry Festival) -- a political event as much as a cultural one.
  • The Whispering Flats -- Unusual terrain in Kusa's central lowlands where violet grass grows to chest height and wind creates complex auditory patterns that some claim carry intelligible whispers. Local tradition says the dead speak from the Flats during the Long Shadow season.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes

Kusamoto Town Northern gateway to Kusayama Ren; staging point for forest expeditions

Culture & Trade

Kusa's economy is built on agriculture, river trade, and the unique resources of its forests. The Midori River supports extensive barge commerce connecting the interior to coastal trade routes. The Forest of Spirits faction, which publicly revealed itself during the Plague Campaign, operates from sanctuaries within the Yosei Mori and represents a significant if unusual economic and cultural presence.

History

Kusa was a battleground during the War of Fractured Banners. The Defense of Midoriko was one of the war's early major engagements -- the provincial capital was besieged and nearly fell before a relief force broke through. The scars of that siege are still visible in Midoriko's architecture.

During the Dark Ages, the Forest of Spirits became a refuge -- its elevated sei activity, present even when magic was absent everywhere else, drew survivors. The communities formed there eventually became the Forest of Spirits magical faction that publicly revealed itself during the Plague Campaign.

Details

The Forest of Spirits faction holds research and findings from the Dark Ages that they have not shared publicly -- discoveries about sei behavior during the magic-absent era that would upend current seimaster orthodoxy.

The Whispering Flats produce sounds that are not random and not the dead -- they are sei resonance from a buried structure beneath.

The Forest of Spirits

The faction's sanctuary in Yosei Mori is more significant than their public profile suggests. During centuries in the forest, they didn't just survive -- they studied. They have records, experiments, and findings from the Dark Ages that would upend current seimaster orthodoxy.

Midoriko's Garrison

The city's military infrastructure is controlled by a Genso Alliance-aligned clan. Its strategic location in the center of Hokori makes it a key pressure point -- control of Midoriko means control of Hokori's interior road network.

The Whispering Flats

The sounds are sei resonance from a buried structure beneath the flats -- a pre-imperial site, possibly connected to the Emerald Dragon Clan (Midoryu). The structure has not been rediscovered. The violet grass grows most densely directly over it.

Plot Hooks

The Forest of Spirits has a problem they cannot handle internally -- related to something their research during the Dark Ages disturbed that has recently become active again

Someone in Midoriko is passing military intelligence to the Arashi Alliance; the Genso governing clan needs quiet investigation

Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.M72zAjYRdrTCan30]{Mizu} is a province of water in all its forms -- crashing coastal surf, wide navigable rivers, reed-choked estuaries, tidal flats that stretch for miles at low compound tide, and interior lakes fed by reliable rainfall. It wraps around the northwestern string of mountains on Hokori, with Hi to the southeast, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} along its eastern and southern borders, and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.EPAWGqYCrUzYfngV]{Kusa} to the northeast. The Raijin no Fukai sea drives against its western and northern coastline with consistent force. The Kōri-no-Mori forest occupies its northern shores.

The coastline is irregular and complex -- carved into headlands, sheltered coves, sea-stacks, and natural harbors. The Shirakawa Estuary (White River Estuary) at the province's center is one of the largest navigable estuaries in the archipelago. The city of Minato-jo occupies a raised headland at the estuary's mouth.

Inland, the terrain transitions through agricultural floodplains and into the foothills of the central Hokori ranges. Rice production in Mizu's river valleys is among the highest in the archipelago -- the combination of reliable rainfall, mineral-rich alluvial soil, and excellent river irrigation infrastructure makes the province's farming output disproportionately important to regional food security.

Relc's home village of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.glkgG2E8eJWrxCrm]{Koriwara} is located in Mizu province's interior, in a foothills region where the climate shifts from maritime to montane.

Points of Interest:

  • Shirakawa Estuary -- The great river mouth. At compound low tide, the tidal flats extend so far the estuary looks almost dry. Channel navigation is complex; experienced local pilots are required for larger vessels.
  • Koriwara and the Sacred Grove Elder -- The village is unremarkable on its surface. What makes it significant is Elder Sato Hideaki, whose connection to the Order of the Sacred Grove gives Koriwara significance disproportionate to its size.
  • The Tidal Caves of Umigakure -- Sea caves accessible only during compound low tides. The caves extend far back into the coastal cliffs. Internal airflow suggests a significant interior cavity somewhere behind the accessible chambers.

Shirakawa Town Estuary trading town; river barge terminus; fishing fleet base
Koriwara Village Relc's home village; Elder Sato Hideaki; Order of the Sacred Grove connection
Umigakure Village "Sea-hidden"; small cove settlement; smuggling history
