Culture & Trade

Mizu's economy is built on maritime trade, fishing, and rice agriculture. Minato-jo serves as the primary western port of Hokori, handling trade routes across the Raijin no Fukai sea. The province's rice production is a strategic asset, and its river systems support extensive barge commerce connecting the coast to the interior.

History

Mizu has long been one of Hokori's most strategically important provinces due to its western coastline and natural harbors. The province's current alignment with the Arashi Alliance reflects its maritime orientation and the naval capabilities centered at Minato-jo.

Details

Elder Sato Hideaki in Koriwara is more than a village elder with nature connections -- he has deep ties to the Order of the Sacred Grove.

One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is near Koriwara.

The Tidal Caves of Umigakure have started showing light from deep within during night compound tides -- a new phenomenon.

The Order of the Sacred Grove -- Koriwara Connection

Elder Sato Hideaki is a mid-rank member of the Order of the Sacred Grove. He has interacted with Order of the Ancient Guard agents, including @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.Tpou815uKS3CU4HS]{Solas Evergreen} directly. He knows Solas was Ancient Guard (not just Sacred Grove). He has not told Relc because he was following Solas's instruction to let Relc develop organically.

The Cipher Poem's Connection to Koriwara

One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is near Koriwara -- in the foothills. Elder Sato knows this stone and knows, vaguely, what the Warden's Wisdom is: protected knowledge about the locations of the living dragons.

Arashi Naval Presence

Minato-jo's Arashi Alliance-aligned clan has been quietly building naval capacity beyond defensive requirements. Someone is planning an offensive operation involving the western sea. The scope of construction suggests something significant.

Plot Hooks

Sato Hideaki has sent word through a traveling merchant -- he needs to speak with Relc urgently; something happened near the sacred grove he tends

The Tidal Caves of Umigakure have started showing light from deep within during night compound tides -- a phenomenon not present three months ago

Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.ijGHvVOlw9tFpBo8]{Nami} sits on the northeastern tip of Hokori and faces the unabated ocean without shelter. @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.EPAWGqYCrUzYfngV]{Kusa} lies to the southwest and @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} to the southeast. Its shores receive the full force of oceanic weather systems -- storms that have built across open water for thousands of miles. The province's coastal architecture reflects this: every structure is built low and heavy, walls thick, roofs angled away from prevailing winds, shutters reinforced with iron.

The coastline is rugged and often spectacular -- dramatic sea cliffs dropping directly to churning water, narrow beaches of black volcanic sand between rocky headlands, sea arches and stacks in the offshore shallows. During Tatsunami season, storm swells overwash lower coastal roads entirely, and some villages are evacuated to higher ground as standard annual precaution.

The interior rises quickly from coastal cliffs into the eastern slopes of Hokori's central highlands. The terrain is less hospitable than the island's interior -- thinner soil, more exposure, colder -- but fishing and maritime trade make the province economically significant.

Fujisato, one of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana} province's northeastern ports, sits at the provincial boundary -- a natural gateway between the two provinces' maritime economies.

Points of Interest:

  • The Eastern Lighthouse Chain -- Signal towers and lighthouses along Nami's coast, serving as navigational aids and early warning systems. Some stone bases predate recorded history. During wartime, the chain serves as a communication relay.
  • The Stormwatch Cliffs -- The highest sea cliffs in Hokori, at Nami's northern reach. On clear days, Kawa island is visible in the distance. Seimasters come here to study weather sei during Tatsunami.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Kogarashi City Provincial capital; fortress-port; commands the northern strait
Namigashira City Major eastern port; fortified against storm and invasion
Takaiso Town Clifftop town; lighthouse; navigation services
Kurojima Village Black sand beach settlement; fishing cooperative; storm-weathered
Arashizaki Village Headland village; name means "storm cape"; considered lucky to survive the name

Culture & Trade

Nami's culture is shaped by its exposure to the open ocean. The people are resilient, practical, and accustomed to living with the constant threat of powerful storms. Maritime trade and fishing form the economic backbone, with Namigashira serving as Hokori's primary eastern port.

History

Nami has historically served as Hokori's eastern gateway, its ports connecting the island to maritime trade routes across the open ocean. The province's current alignment with the Arashi Alliance reflects its strategic naval importance.

Details

The oldest lighthouse foundation at Takaiso was not originally a lighthouse -- it was built atop something much older.

Nami's Arashi-aligned governing clan is coordinating with @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.M72zAjYRdrTCan30]{Mizu}'s Minato-jo for a joint naval operation.

Arashi Alliance Naval Operations

Nami's Arashi-aligned governing clan is coordinating with Mizu's Minato-jo -- together, the eastern and western ports are being positioned for a joint naval operation. The target is unknown, but intelligence suggests it involves a landing rather than a sea battle.

The Ancient Lighthouse Foundation

The oldest lighthouse foundation in the chain -- at Takaiso -- is built atop something much older. The original structure was not a lighthouse. Excavation work decades ago stopped abruptly when workers reported the foundation stones were warm to the touch and something moved in the space beneath. The site was sealed and built over. The sealed space is still there.

Plot Hooks

A vessel arrived at Namigashira from the open ocean with no crew -- cargo intact, navigation logs ending mid-sentence, cook fire still warm

The lighthouse at Takaiso went dark for three consecutive nights; the keeper is missing; locals won't go near it

Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.OgpA5KI2G94uYoN7]{Sora} -- Sky -- is the highest-altitude province in Hokori and encompasses the majority of the lightly populated mountainous interior at the island's center. It is often the most dangerous region to traverse. Much of it sits above the cloud ceiling. A traveler ascending from lower provinces will emerge through dense cloud into a world of startling clarity: thin air, intense sunlight, vast visibility, and a profound silence broken only by wind.

The province occupies the central mountain ranges that form the connective barrier between most of Hokori's other provinces. It borders nearly every other province in some capacity -- a sprawling, thinly governed wilderness between centres of population. The plateau itself is high grassland -- silvered grasses that catch light differently, giving the landscape an almost lunar quality. Standing water freezes for months; the ground is rocky and thin-soiled.

The Hoshimori Plateau (Star Keeper's Plateau) is the defining feature -- wide, flat, and high enough that stars are visibly brighter than anywhere else in the archipelago. This made it the site of observatories and sei-research installations during the Golden Age, several of which still stand.

The province has few settlements relative to its area, but the routes through it connect northern Hokori to the central, and controlling them carries strategic importance disproportionate to population.

Points of Interest:

  • Hoshimori Plateau (Star Keeper's Plateau) -- Exceptional astronomical observation site. The sky here behaves slightly differently -- star density appears higher and moons seem slightly larger. Whether this is optical illusion or something else has not been resolved.
  • The Golden Age Observatories -- Three of seven observatories built during Emperor Kinryu no Mikado's reign remain structurally intact. Their instruments -- large bronze mechanisms -- are still functional and oriented to alignments no current seimaster fully understands. A fourth, largely collapsed, contains sealed records.
  • The Storm Road -- Mountain route through Sora connecting @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana}/Hi to the northern coast. Impassable in winter; deteriorating without central maintenance authority.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Kumo-no-Ue Town "Above the Clouds"; provincial capital; cold year-round
Hoshimori Village On the plateau; observatory town; seimaster community
Kanransha Village Mountain pass waypoint; transit community; temporary lodging industry

Culture & Trade

Sora's small population is centered around the observatory communities and the transit routes that cross the province. The seimaster community at Hoshimori represents a concentration of astronomical and magical expertise. The province's isolation and altitude make it a natural retreat for those seeking contemplation or research.

History

During the Golden Age, Sora was a center of astronomical research and sei study, with seven observatories constructed on the Hoshimori Plateau. The Dark Ages saw these installations abandoned. The province's strategic importance lies in controlling the mountain routes connecting northern and central Hokori.

Details

The functional observatories are producing readings that match a pattern the ancient seimasters considered significant -- the Ryushinki (Dragon Awakening).

A seimaster from Hoshimori has been trying to reach @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian} with urgent information for three months and has not arrived.

The Abandoned Observatory Records

The sealed records in the collapsed fourth observatory contain documentation of a celestial alignment the Kinryu-era seimasters considered dangerous. The alignment -- involving all three stars, two specific moons, and a specific planetary configuration -- they called Ryushinki (Dragon Awakening). Their records suggest this alignment is associated with the founding dragons becoming active, visible, or vulnerable. The next occurrence is calculable and is not far away.

The Silver Dragon Connection

Ginryu, the Silver Dragon, is connected to Sora through the province's astronomical nature. She has been known to spend time on the Hoshimori Plateau. The plateau's unusual stellar appearance is partly her influence. She has not been seen in decades, but her presence would explain the plateau's anomalous sei readings.

Plot Hooks

One of the functional observatories has started producing readings matching the Ryushinki pattern ahead of schedule -- something is wrong with the calculation, or something is accelerating

A seimaster from Hoshimori sent a letter ahead that references "something moving in the clouds that is not a cloud"

Geography & Terrain

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.qODDmax1GHoTx3fx]{Tsuchi} occupies the southern portion of Hokori -- a primarily mountainous province dominated by rugged terrain and the imposing bulk of Kurogane Yama, the second highest peak on the island. @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana} borders it to the northeast and Hi to the northwest. The mountains here are old and weathered, less volcanically active than Hi but no less formidable -- steep valleys, narrow passes, and ridgelines that catch storms rolling in from the southern sea.

The southern mountains are resource-rich -- mineral deposits, timber in the sheltered valleys, and stone quarried from exposed cliff faces. But the terrain resists large-scale settlement. Communities are small, isolated by geography, and accustomed to self-reliance.

The Tsuchikawa (Earth River) is the main artery -- wide, slow, navigable for cargo barge travel, and historically important as a trade route connecting the interior to the coast.

Tsuchimoto sits at the center of the provincial plains, connected by roads in every compass direction. It is not a dramatic city -- no spectacular geography, no great harbor. It is a city of markets, granaries, administrative buildings, and the quietly enormous power of whoever controls the food supply.

Points of Interest:

  • The Great Granaries of Tsuchimoto -- Immense storage structures capable of holding enough grain to feed Hokori's population through two years of failed harvests. One of the most strategically important sites in the archipelago.
  • The Buried Road -- An ancient paved road that farmers have plowed around for centuries. Predates the Emperor's Highway by thousands of years -- pre-imperial, possibly pre-human. Where it goes and why it exists is unknown.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Twagakure City Provincial capital; hidden mountain stronghold
Tsuchimoto City Agricultural center; granary city; market center; Genso-aligned
Tashiro Town River town; barge trade; grain export hub
Komugi Village "Wheat"; small farming commune; exemplary agricultural management
Inaka Village Meaning literally "countryside"; deliberately generic; culturally proud of it

Culture & Trade

Tsuchi's culture reflects its agricultural identity -- practical, organized, and deeply connected to the land and seasons. The province's grain production is a strategic asset that gives its governing authority disproportionate political leverage. River trade along the Tsuchikawa connects the interior to coastal markets.

History

Tsuchi has long been Hokori's breadbasket. Its strategic importance has made it a prize in every major conflict. The province's current Genso Alliance alignment gives the alliance control over a significant portion of Hokori's food supply -- a fact with profound implications for the current political crisis.

Details

The Buried Road leads somewhere significant -- it is far older than any known human construction in the region.

The Great Granaries' contents are being used as an economic weapon in the current conflict.

The Granaries as Political Weapon

The Genso Alliance-aligned governing clan has been quietly restricting grain sales to Arashi-aligned provinces while maintaining normal trade with neutral parties. This is a slow-moving economic siege strategy. It hasn't become visible yet. When it does, it will escalate the current conflict significantly.

The Buried Road

The ancient road leads eventually to a pre-imperial site associated with the Emerald Dragon Clan (Midoryu) -- a "green court" predating any recorded human settlement. Traceable sections exist at intervals. The site it leads to is in the @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.EPAWGqYCrUzYfngV]{Kusa} province border region, beneath what is now part of the Whispering Flats. Midoryu is alive and maintains a particular connection to this buried court.

Plot Hooks

A farmer plowing a new field in eastern Tsuchi has found an intact structure beneath the buried road -- a sealed room -- and reported it to local authorities; those authorities are now not responding to outside inquiries

The granary administrator in Tsuchimoto is receiving death threats; she has information about grain supply restrictions that she wants to share with someone she trusts -- which is no one, currently

Kawa is an island that breathes with the seasons. For most of the year, only its highest terrain rises above water — ridgelines, hilltops, and a handful of elevated settlements that persist as islands within an island. In winter, the waters recede and the lowlands emerge: vast, extraordinarily fertile floodplains that have been farmed for millennia using agricultural techniques found nowhere else in the archipelago. The annual cycle of submersion and emergence defines everything about Kawa — its architecture (built on stilts and elevated stone foundations), its economy (one explosive growing season), and its people (patient, methodical, and deeply attuned to tidal calendars).

Kawa lies to the east of Hokori, visible from the Stormwatch Cliffs in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.ijGHvVOlw9tFpBo8]{Nami} province on clear days. The waters surrounding it are navigable but treacherous — shifting sandbars and unpredictable currents created by the interaction of four lunar tidal patterns make piloting around Kawa a specialist skill.

Points of Interest

The Great Library sits at Nagisawa, on the shores of Seirei Mizuumi (Spirit Lake) — a body of water said to connect to the underworld. The library was built during the reign of the First Emperor, Tenryū no Mikado, and remains one of the most significant repositories of knowledge in the archipelago. It was partially destroyed by an earthquake during the Dark Ages and restored during the Jinshō Reformation (~15642–15691).

Seirei Mizuumi itself is a place of deep spiritual significance. The Battle of Seirei Mizuumi — fought during the era of imperial unification — secured Kawa for the empire and broke the Azure Clan navy. The lake's waters remain a site of pilgrimage and scholarly study.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Nagisawa City Home of the Great Library; shores of Seirei Mizuumi
**

Culture & Trade

Kawa is the agricultural heartland of the archipelago — its seasonal floodplains produce yields that dwarf anything achievable on permanently dry land. The island's economy revolves around the winter growing season and the export of grain, rice, and preserved produce to the other islands.

Fushichō burns. The northern island is dominated by the Hi no Toride (Fire Fortress) mountain range — a chain of volcanic peaks, some dormant, some merely sleeping, and at least one actively erupting as of Hachigatsu 29, 16744. The Akaho Sanmyaku range is currently sending ash high enough to be visible from Hokori's central mountains, hundreds of miles to the south.

The island's terrain is hostile and spectacular — lava fields, fumarole plains, obsidian cliffs, and valleys where thermal vents keep the air warm even in winter. The soil in sheltered valleys between active zones is extraordinarily fertile, enriched by centuries of volcanic deposition, and the communities that farm there produce crops of remarkable quality. But the land gives and takes in equal measure. Settlements on Fushichō are built to be abandoned quickly.

Points of Interest

The Hi no Toride mountains are the island's spine — ancient and geologically violent. The Akaho Sanmyaku eruption is ongoing, and its consequences for the settlements and peoples of Fushichō are still unfolding.

The Siege of Fushichō during the War of Fractured Banners was one of that conflict's most brutal engagements. The island's defenders used the volcanic terrain itself as a weapon — collapsing lava tubes, redirecting thermal vents, and forcing invading forces through kill zones of natural geological hazard.

Settlements

**

Culture & Trade

Fushichō has always resisted outside authority. The western territories are home to descendants of the Crimson Clan faction that refused submission to Tenryū no Mikado during the era of imperial unification. These populations are organised into loose tribal confederacies that preserve traditions the rest of the empire has forgotten. They are fiercely territorial and know things about the volcanic highlands that no imperial map captures.

The island's primary exports are volcanic minerals, obsidian, and geothermal resources. Its people share the laconic practicality of Hi province on Hokori — unsurprising, given the shared geological character.

Yurei is avoided. The island lies somewhere in the archipelago — its exact position known to navigators but rarely marked on maps sold to the public. Sailors alter course to keep it below the horizon. Fishermen who drift too close report unease that builds to physical nausea before they've sighted land. The island is barren, cursed, and home to things that do not welcome the living.

An ancient catastrophe — its nature lost to the Dark Ages — left Yurei scarred in ways that have not healed. The land itself is blighted: grey soil, dead trees standing like bones, coastlines of sharp black rock where nothing grows. Spectres, undead, and creatures of unknown origin inhabit the interior. The few expeditions that have attempted to chart the island's geography have returned incomplete, or not at all.

Points of Interest

Kuroshi Temple is the most significant known site on Yurei — a dark temple whose origins predate the catastrophe. It was here that Takeda Arata found the necromantic tome that transformed him into Kuroyami no Akuma and set in motion the Plague Campaign of 16609–16616. What else the temple contains, and what other structures survive on the island, is largely unknown. Few have gone looking. Fewer have returned to report.

Settlements

None known. If anyone lives on Yurei, they are not living in any conventional sense of the word.

Culture & Trade

There is no trade with Yurei. There is no culture on Yurei — not anymore. The island serves as a cautionary reference in the folklore of every other island in the archipelago. "Yurei's shore" is a common idiom for a place of no return.

Tatara is the second largest island in the archipelago — mountainous, heavily fortified, and defined by a conflict older than the empire itself. The island is the heartland of two peoples: the Zirak (dwarves) and the Glimfyr (gnomes), whose rivalry predates human settlement and has outlasted every attempt at permanent resolution. When the emperor commands peace, they comply. When the emperor dies, they resume. There is no emperor now.

The island's terrain is rugged — dense mountain ranges, deep valleys, and fortified passes that have been fought over so many times the stone itself shows the scars. The Adamanzan Ren mountains contain the great Zirak fortress complexes — engineering achievements carved into living rock over millennia. The Glimfyr hold their own territory through ingenuity, traps, misdirection, and a willingness to fight asymmetrically that the Zirak find deeply offensive.

Points of Interest

The Kokuyō Ryūkyūjō is an imperial fortress built during the Golden Age — one of the most significant military constructions in the archipelago. Kuroi Yama (Black Mountain) was destroyed during the Onyx Rebellion (8238–8611), a four-hundred-year guerrilla war waged by Kokuryū against imperial forces. Kokuryū escaped when Kuroi Yama fell, and the mountain's ruins remain a place of dark reputation.

Regions

Region Governance Notes
Mizuho Clan Tsuchiura Genso Alliance-aligned
Shūgyoku Clan Shirotsuru Arashi Alliance-aligned
**

Settlements

**

Culture & Trade

Tatara's economy is built on mining, metalwork, and fortress construction. Stone quarried from the Adamanzan Ren was used to build the Great Library on Kawa. Zirak weaponry and armour are prized across the archipelago. The Glimfyr produce precision instruments, alchemical components, and mechanical devices of extraordinary sophistication.

The recent escalation — gnomes deliberately sabotaging a dwarven relic site — represents a dangerous provocation. Without imperial authority to impose restraint, the conflict is intensifying in ways that may eventually draw in outside powers.

Beyond the five major islands, the Kagekuni archipelago is scattered with smaller landmasses — some inhabited, some sacred, some simply too small or remote to support permanent settlement. The waters between them are shaped by the complex tidal patterns of four moons, and the currents that connect them serve as trade routes, pilgrimage paths, and, for those with reason to disappear, refuges.

Unmeijima — Island of Destiny

Unmeijima is the most significant of the minor islands — home to the city of Seishin, the premier magical research institution in the archipelago. Seishin was founded during the Era of Subtle Awakening as a refuge for persecuted Talents — individuals born with innate magical ability in a world that had forgotten magic existed. What began as a sanctuary grew into a city, and the Seishin Enclave is now the most important centre of sei scholarship in Kagekuni.

The town of Kazehama also occupies the island, along with the monastery of the Order of the Tranquil Lotus — a nature-based monastic order led by Elder @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.5uySp1O85TJzLFmF]{Benkei}, a Guhuza of 198 years.

Shizukajima

A quiet island, rarely visited, with little to recommend it to traders or settlers. Its name means "quiet island," and those who have been there report that the name is accurate — an unusual stillness that is not quite peaceful and not quite unsettling.

Other Minor Islands

The remaining minor islands — Gyoshima, Kakujima, Shukajima, Ryūhajima, Takarajima, and others — are referenced in navigational charts and historical texts but remain largely undeveloped in the current record. Some support fishing communities. Some are sacred sites visited only during specific festivals or lunar alignments. Some are simply rocks in the sea, named by sailors who needed a word for a landmark.

**

Dragonborn (Black) Clan Kurohana Daimyo of Clan Kurohana st-utsuroi

Daimyo of Clan Kurohana

Appearance

Black scales with a glossy sheen; glowing red eyes; intricate dragon tattoos on his back.

Public Role

Daimyo and supreme leader of Clan Kurohana, one of the three independent clans. Commands significant military resources and political influence. Issued the Imperial Seal of the Kurohana Clan calling upon the independent Kaminari Clan to investigate the Gekkō Clan's unexplained silence.

Personality

Stern, commanding; values loyalty and discipline; enjoys battle and strategy; unforgiving of betrayal.

Relationship to Party

Indirect. The party carries the Imperial Seal of the Kurohana Clan, issued by Lord Kurohana Tatsuya on behalf of the clan. The seal requests assistance investigating Gekkō Clan's silence. Both independent clans (Kurohana and Kaminari) are invested in the Gekkō situation — Gekkō is the third independent clan.

True Nature

Doubts the accusations against Dian's father regarding the emperor's assassination. Actively investigating the true culprits behind the emperor's death. Has allies in rival clans who are sympathetic to his cause.

Connections

Allied with sympathetic elements across clan boundaries in pursuit of the truth behind the emperor's assassination. His investigation parallels that of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.1J9hy9Hs6EVuYjyz]{Raijin no Kazuhiko} (Daimyo of Kaminari).

Quest Seeds

[QUEST SEED] May send the party to gather evidence exonerating Dian's father; can provide strategic resources and insights for the investigation.

Campaign Secrets

The convergence of both independent clan daimyo independently doubting the official assassination narrative is politically explosive. If this alignment became public, it would fundamentally shift the political landscape.

Plot Threads

Emperor's assassination investigation — active; truth unknown

Connection to Dian Wei's personal arc

Gekkō investigation — initiated the cross-clan seal requesting cooperation

Succession crisis implications

Elf Clan Kaminari Hyōrō Bugyō (Provisions Commissioner) Heian

Hyōrō Bugyō (Provisions Commissioner) — Clan Kaminari

Appearance

Long silver hair; piercing green eyes; kimono with leaf and vine patterns.

Public Role

Hyōrō Bugyō (Provisions Commissioner) of Clan Kaminari. Responsible for logistics, supply chains, and resource management across the clan's operations. Present alongside @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.Iul8ZsyqNrfhL4XZ]{Hideo Nakamura} when the party received their mission briefing at the Tensho no Mon district.

Personality

Exceptionally intelligent, organized, calm, authoritative; values order and efficiency; compassionate beneath stern exterior; integrity and fairness renowned.

Relationship to Party

Present at mission briefing in Tensho no Mon. Met the party alongside Taisho Hideo Nakamura.

True Nature

Dragonborn Clan Golden-dragon-clan Brood Guardian, Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji upper floor loc-tenkuji-temple

The Brood Guardian — Architecture-bound watcher of the Brood Sanctum

Appearance

A Dragonborn woman of the Golden Clan, scales the color of dulled old gold — paler than a young Kinryū-blooded Dragonborn, weathered in the way of bronze that has stood a long time in still air. Tall but not heavy. She wears lacquered half-plate over a black temple robe, the chestpiece engraved with Kinryū's sigil — a stylized golden dragon coiled around itself in the old style. A naginata stands at her side or rests across her lap. Her eyes are quiet and watchful; her expression does not move when the door opens.

Public Role

Sole guardian of the upper-floor hallway leading to the Brood Sanctum within Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji. She does not patrol; she does not leave her post. She speaks only to those who step fully into the hallway, and only after the temple's architecture has measured them.

Personality

Procedural. Not warm, not hostile by default — a judge with a specific mandate. Her tone shifts among three states (Hostile / Neutral / Welcoming) determined by the party's record of conduct in the temple. She is courteous within each state, unyielding across states. She does not bargain. She does not threaten beyond what duty requires.

Relationship to Party

First contact is at the second-floor landing of Tenkū-ji. The party finds a pile of arranged Nagaji bodies outside an unlocked, well-kept door. Beyond is a pristine hallway and the guardian at its far end. Her response — challenge, denial, or passage — depends on whether the party has plundered, ignored, or honored the temple's lower floors. She gates access to the Brood Sanctum and its trial.

Records & References

Several scattered references in temple archives and Golden Dragon Clan oral tradition gesture at the guardian's identity without confirming it. A party that asks her name receives the connection cleanly; a party that does not may piece it together but never close the loop.

  • Reliquary inventory, lower archives (Investigation DC 14): a list of binding rites references a Hoshimori-class oath — a ritual class specific to Brood Sanctum guardians, named for the star-keeper surname taken upon entry. Indicates the role exists; does not name an individual.
  • Devotional poem, Star Shrine archives (Religion DC 14): a fragmentary verse mentions "Aya, who refused the door." Context is ambiguous. The poem could be metaphor — could be biography.
  • Temple genealogy, Dormitories (History DC 16): a roster of priestesses present at the temple's last hour lists Hoshimori Aya among them. The entry is struck through; a note in a different hand reads, see also: the long watch.
  • Golden Dragon Clan oral tradition (Ko'jiri's research advantage): surviving family stories reference "she who placed the inheritor" — gendered, never named, treated as half-mythical.
  • Plinth inscription, Brood Sanctum: the temple's last faithful speak in a collective "we entrust to this place our greatest treasure." The "we" includes a person who did not leave.

Quest Seeds

[QUEST SEED] Asking the guardian her name is the gate to unsealing her identity. If she is asked at any point during the chamber's events, she gives her name and a single self-defining truth at her watch's end. If she is not asked, her name is lost — the party may collect breadcrumbs but never confirm the connection. The asking is the closure.

[QUEST SEED] Hoshimori-class oaths (per the lower-archive inventory) imply other Brood Sanctum sites — other guardians, other charges. None are confirmed to exist. If the campaign develops the Progenitor / dragon-bloodline arc further, additional Hoshimori-bound guardians could surface as long-dormant allies or cautionary mirrors.

True Nature

Aya is the priestess who placed the wyrmling's egg in the Brood Sanctum at the temple's last hour. When the Kinryū order fell during the War of Fractured Banners (~13088), she carried the egg into the chamber, sealed the door behind her, and bound herself to the temple's foundational architecture rather than abandon her charge. The architecture took her self-memory in exchange for letting her hold the post for as long as it would take a worthy claimant to arrive. She has stood in the hallway ever since — present without being awake, watching without seeing, waiting without remembering why.

Campaign Secrets

Her awareness model. She does not actively perceive what passes in the temple. The architecture relays positive or negative impressions to her based on how those it watches treat the place; she acts on those impressions, not on knowledge. Time has not collected in her — she does not remember faces, conversations, or events. In State C she is openly apologetic about this; in State B she does not feel the gap.

The egg-placer reveal. Her role as the woman who placed the egg is the chamber's deepest narrative truth and is gated entirely behind the party asking her name. If asked, she names herself at the watch's end and acknowledges placing the child. The architecture's hold on her memory releases in the same breath; she remembers, briefly, who she was — and tells the party one defining detail of her life before the watch (DM picks: a teacher's name, a vow she swore, a clan affiliation). She does not survive the telling.

The four gifts. When the wyrmling bonds and the watch ends, she gives one personalized offering to each of the three non-bonded party members. The bonded character receives the wyrmling. The gifts are her release; their giving is what lets her fade. Full offering structure documented in the chamber writeup (Obsidian/dm/brood-sanctum-redesign.md).

On failure. If @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.locations.JournalEntry.TNV9pLqaBUzySDRl.JournalEntryPage.3zJVvOaJgg0w8leo]{the trial} fails, she remains. She does not depart. She bears witness without bitterness and waits for the next attempt. She does not offer gifts on failure — the gifts are tied to the wyrmling's bow, which only happens on success.

Combat, last resort. If the party crosses into State A and persists in destructive behavior, she fights. Stat block TBD — calibrated at session-time to the party's level when the chamber comes into play. She will not pursue beyond the hallway; she does not leave her post.

The archipelago's recorded history stretches back more than eight thousand years — and its unrecorded history stretches back further still. What follows is the account as it is understood by scholars, priests, and the educated classes of Kagekuni. Some of it is reliable. Some of it is myth layered over truth. Some of it is truth layered over something deeper that no one alive fully remembers.

Period Years Name
Pre-Imperial Before ~8000 Age of Dragons
Imperial Founding ~8000–8611 Era of the First Emperors
First Golden Age 8611–13050 The Golden Age
Age of Strife 13050–13088 War of Fractured Banners
Dark Ages 13088–15642 The Long Dark
Recovery 15642–15691 Jinshō Reformation
Second Golden Age 15691–15757 Era of New Discovery
Subtle Awakening 15757–16620 Return of Talents
Great Awakening 16620–present Magic Restored
Current 16744 Post-Imperial Crisis

Before there were emperors, before there were clans, before there were borders drawn on maps or roads cut through mountains — there were dragons.

Seven dragon clans ruled the archipelago of Kagekuni, each sovereign over its own island or territory. Their domains were not kingdoms in the human sense but spheres of influence, shaped by the nature of each dragon and the land they inhabited. The Crimson Clan held the volcanic island of Fushichō. The Azure Clan commanded the waters around Kawa. The Emerald Clan tended the forests and plains of Hokori. The Onyx Clan ruled from Tatara in shadow and cunning. The Golden Clan mediated from the highlands of central Hokori. The Silver Clan kept the cold northern waters and the island of Fuukajima. The Amethyst Clan studied the arcane from Shizukajima.

The earliest mortal settlers arrived in this world and found it already governed. They did not conquer — they integrated. The first communities paid tribute to their local dragon clan, adopted their customs, and in time became part of the social fabric the dragons had built. Intermingling between dragonborn, humans, and the founding clans produced the near-immortal Arcadian leaders who became the first daimyō — mortal rulers who carried draconic blood in their veins and governed with the implicit blessing of the dragons above them.

Over centuries, the dragons gradually withdrew from direct rule. Whether this was a deliberate abdication, a slow retreat into contemplation, or something else entirely depends on which account you trust. By the time the first emperor rose, the dragons had become figures of reverence rather than governance — still present in memory and tradition, but no longer sitting at the head of the table.

The age of dragons ended and the age of emperors began with a single figure: Tenryū no Mikado.

Tenryū ascended to power around the year 8000. He was already 852 years old — an Arcadian of mixed Crimson and Golden dragon lineage, carrying the blood of fire and justice in a single line. His unification of the archipelago was not achieved through war alone. Tenryū was a diplomat as much as a conqueror, binding clans through marriage alliances, trade agreements, and appeals to shared identity as often as through force of arms.

Not all clans submitted willingly. The Crimson Clan fractured over the question of imperial loyalty. The eastern faction accepted Tenryū's authority and joined the empire. The western faction, loyal to the dragon Akaryū, refused submission and withdrew into the volcanic ranges of the Akaho Sanmyaku on Fushichō. Their descendants live there still — loose tribal confederacies preserving traditions the rest of the empire forgot.

The Battle of Seirei Mizuumi secured the island of Kawa and broke the naval power of the Azure Clan, bringing the eastern waters under imperial control.

The gravest threat to the young empire came from Tatara. Kokuryū — the Onyx Dragon — refused to accept Tenryū's authority and launched the Onyx Rebellion in 8238. What followed was not a war in the conventional sense but a four-hundred-year guerrilla campaign fought across the shadowed mountains and tunnels of Tatara. The rebellion ended only with the destruction of Kuroi Yama — the Onyx Clan's fortress mountain — though Kokuryū himself escaped. The dragon was never captured, never killed, and never seen again.

Tenryū no Mikado died in the year 8694. His son, Ryūhiko no Mikado, was already 794 years old when he ascended the throne. The imperial dynasty was established, and the long peace began.

For nearly four and a half thousand years, Kagekuni flourished.

Eight emperors reigned across the Golden Age: Tenryū, Ryūhiko, Seiryū, Byakuryū, Kinryū, Shoryū, Inaryū, and Kōryū. Under their rule, the archipelago achieved a level of civilisation, artistic refinement, and magical sophistication that has never been equalled.

The great constructions of the Golden Age defined the physical landscape of the empire. The Imperial Palace in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian} became the architectural heart of the nation. The Great Library at Seirei Mizuumi on Kawa gathered the accumulated knowledge of civilisation under one roof. The Grand Canal of Mizushima connected inland waterways into a navigable system spanning provinces. The Hoshino Tō — a grand observatory — rose on the slopes of Shirogane Yama, and the Kokuyō Ryūkyūjō fortress on Tatara brought order to the Onyx Clan's former territory. The Emperor's Highway, completed in 11248, extended from Heian in three directions, and to this day everything important in Hokori is measured by its distance from that road.

Sei — the magic energy flowing through all living things — was fully accessible and deeply understood. Seimasters studied with the rigour of astronomers, supported by institutions whose traditions stretched back to the dragon clans themselves. Architecture incorporated magical principles. Agriculture was enhanced by sei-attuned cultivation. The boundary between the natural and the supernatural was not a line but a gradient, and the educated classes moved through both with fluency.

It could not last. Nothing built on that scale ever does.

The Golden Age ended in blood.

The spark was Tatara. The eternal feud between the Zirak and Glimfyr — dwarves and gnomes sharing an island neither was willing to surrender — had been managed for millennia through imperial intervention. When that intervention weakened, the feud spread. What began as a regional conflict metastasised into empire-wide war as clans chose sides, old grievances resurfaced, and the bonds that had held civilisation together for four thousand years snapped one by one.

Emperor Kōryū no Mikado was slain on the battlefield in 13053 — the first emperor to die in combat in the empire's history. His son, Ryūjin no Mikado II, ascended the throne and made the decision that would shape the next era: he established the Shogunate, appointing Kazutaka no Kazuhiko as the first Shōgun — supreme military commander with the authority to compel obedience from the daimyō.

The war raged across the archipelago. The Defence of Midoriko, the Pursuit to Kumoji, the Campaign in Tatara, the Burning of Shirotsuru, the Siege of Fushichō, the Ambush at Tatsumaki Gorge, and the Battle of the Thunder Plains — each left its mark on the land and the people who survived it. Two clans — the Seiryū and the Hagane — were destroyed entirely, their names erased from the rolls of the living.

The war ended in 13062. But something else ended with it — something no one understood at the time.

Magic vanished.

The disappearance of sei was not a sudden event but a slow bleeding that scholars only recognised in retrospect. By the time the war ended and the empire looked up from its wounds, the bleeding was catastrophic.

The secondary stars in the sky — Susanoo and Tsukuyomi — had been fading. Within decades of the war's end, both had crossed below naked-eye visibility. The night sky, which had burned with three stars for all of recorded history, now held only the golden light of Amaterasu. The other two were simply gone.

With them went the complex magical expressions that had sustained civilisation. Healing failed. Transformation magic fell silent. What remained was Amaterasu's baseline: enough sei to sustain life, agriculture, and the physical world, but not enough to power the institutions, the architecture, or the knowledge systems that the Golden Age had built.

The collapse was total. Famine swept the archipelago as sei-enhanced agriculture reverted to conventional farming on land that could not support the populations the Golden Age had sustained. Disease followed famine. The population of the archipelago fell by nearly half. The Temple of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji — one of the great institutions of the Golden Age — fell in 13088, its surviving worshippers departing into an empire that no longer had use for their knowledge.

The Dark Ages lasted approximately three thousand years. Little documentation survives. Entire cities were abandoned to silence and weather. The knowledge of sei, the scholarly traditions, the institutional memory of how magic worked and what it meant — all of it was lost. The world that emerged on the other side was not the same world that had entered the darkness.

Recovery, when it came, was not magic returning. It was a single emperor deciding that the empire would not die quietly.

Jinshin no Mikado ascended the throne in 15642 and enacted sweeping reforms that dragged Kagekuni back from the edge. Agricultural revival came first — new cultivation techniques, land redistribution, irrigation projects that did not rely on sei. Infrastructure followed — roads rebuilt, bridges repaired, harbours dredged. Trade stimulation reopened routes that had been abandoned for centuries. An educational revival rebuilt the scholarly institutions, and the Great Library — destroyed by an earthquake during the dark ages — was partially restored.

Jinshin also established the Kokushi Kyōkai in its recognisable modern form, creating the positions of Seimu Daijin (Minister of Administration) and Zaiumu Daijin (Minister of Finance) to manage the empire's civilian machinery. The framework he built — imperfect, incomplete, but functional — is the same framework that governs Kagekuni today, eight hundred years later.

The Jinshō Reformation stabilised the empire. What followed was the discovery that the empire was not alone.

In 15691, an expedition led by Admiral Taira no Akinori and General Tokugawa no Ryūji, with diplomat Hōjō no Kaoru as its political voice, sailed beyond the known waters of the Raijin no Fukai sea and discovered lands beyond Kagekuni. They returned with slaves, precious metals, new knowledge, and the unsettling revelation that the world was larger than anyone had imagined.

Over the next sixty years, more than 150 expeditions followed. The discoveries were transformative — and destabilising. New wealth poured into the archipelago, but it flowed unevenly. Clans with naval reach grew rich. Clans without it watched their neighbours outpace them. Rivalries that had simmered for centuries found new fuel.

The Emperor responded by appointing Minamoto no Katsuro of the Tenshiko Clan as Shōgun around 16012. Katsuro enacted a series of regulatory acts — the Expedition Regulation Act, the Resource Distribution Act, the Peace and Mediation Act, and the Defence Enhancement Act — that imposed order on the chaos. When the crisis passed, the Shogunate retired voluntarily. Hōjō no Kaoru was appointed the first Gaikō Daijin (Minister of Foreign Affairs), extending the Kokushi Kyōkai to five ministers.

The stars were coming back. No one knew it yet.

Around 15757, a child was born in Kagekuni with the ability to call lightning from clear air. His name was Hikari no Kenta, and he was the first known Talent — an individual born with innate magical ability in a world that had not seen magic in over three thousand years.

The reaction was not welcoming. Kenta was feared, studied, and eventually persecuted. He was not alone for long — other Talents emerged across the archipelago, each manifesting different abilities without training, without teachers, and without a society that had any framework for understanding what they were. Many were hunted. Many formed underground communities for survival.

Notable Talents of this era included Mizuki no @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana} of Clan Gekkō, who manifested shadow magic, and Fujimoto no Aiko of Clan Ryū@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{kaze}, who could manipulate wind. The Seishin Enclave was founded on the island of Unmeijima as a place of study and refuge for Talents — it eventually grew into the city of Seishin, the premier magical research institution in Kagekuni. Hikari no Shizuku, a healing and light magic tradition, established itself within the imperial capital of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian}.

The return of magic coincided with a period of intense political reorganisation. Over two centuries, the clan structure of Kagekuni was remade.

The Hōjō Clan tore itself apart in civil war, and the survivors merged with the Minamoto Clan to form Clan Kaminari — named in honour of Raijin, the spirit of thunder. Clan Ryū@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{kaze} absorbed smaller clans and became dominant in the northwest. The Yamamoto Clan splintered. The Ishikawa Clan dissolved entirely, and from its remnants the mercenary Clan Tetsujin emerged.

The political map that exists today — the alliances, the rivalries, the independent clans — was drawn during this period.

Not all upheaval came from above. In 16442, a crackdown in Midoriko village sparked a peasant uprising that spread across multiple provinces. The emperor appointed Takeda no Hiroshi as Shōgun in 16443 to restore order. But this was not a rebellion that could be solved by swords alone. In 16453, the emperor created the position of Fukushi Daijin (Minister of Welfare) and appointed Hayashi no Haruto to address the underlying grievances — healthcare, education, and public assistance for the common people.

A combined military and diplomatic approach ended the uprising in 16461. The Shogunate again retired when its purpose was fulfilled.

The defining trauma of the post-Awakening era.

Kuroyami no Akuma — born Takeda no Arata — discovered a necromantic tome in the cursed Kuroshi Temple on the haunted island of Yūrei. What he found there transformed him. He established the Eikyū Yami Clan — a cult of death — and raised armies of the undead. For seven years, his legions waged war across the archipelago, leaving devastation and plague in their wake.

The response united unlikely allies. Shōgun Minamoto no Katsuro was appointed in 16610 and made the unprecedented decision to recruit Talents — magical individuals the empire had spent centuries marginalising — into the war effort. The magical enclaves of Seishin, the Raimeiin, and the Forest of Spirits revealed themselves publicly for the first time, stepping out of the shadows to defend the world that had persecuted them.

Kuroyami was defeated. He was never captured or killed. His cult, the Eikyū Yami Clan, persists in some form. The question of where Kuroyami is — and what he has been doing for the last 128 years — is one that very few people ask aloud.

Magic officially returned to the world around the year 16687, though the process had been building for decades. The Great Awakening was not a single moment but a threshold — the point at which sei became reliably accessible to trained practitioners rather than appearing only in rare Talents born with innate ability.

The daimyō moved quickly. Every clan began recruiting mages into their service. The magical institutions that had emerged during the era of Talents suddenly found themselves courted rather than feared. Seishin expanded from an enclave into a city. Magical study became a path to advancement rather than a mark of suspicion.

But the world that magic returned to was not the world it had left. The institutions, the knowledge, the scholarly traditions of the Golden Age were gone. The current generation of practitioners is rebuilding from fragments — studying sei with the tools of a civilisation that lost three thousand years of progress. They are learning fast, but they are learning without teachers, and the gaps in their understanding are significant.

The current crisis did not begin with war. It began with a reform.

In 16732, Emperor Ryūjin no Mikado — the eighteenth emperor, the last of the near-immortal Arcadian line — decreed that the Kokushi Kyōkai could no longer appoint a Shōgun without imperial approval. It was a safeguard. It may also have been a warning.

Seven years later, in 16739, Ryūjin died. The official cause was old age. He was the final link to an unbroken chain of rulers stretching back over eight thousand years. No confirmed successor has emerged. Multiple claimants have presented genealogical proof of varying credibility. None has secured recognition.

The Shogunate — the military authority that has historically held the empire together during periods of crisis — is legally frozen. There is no emperor to approve a Shōgun, and no Shōgun to impose order.

In 16742, war erupted between the Genso Alliance and the Arashi Alliance. Two years of escalating hostility have produced no decisive outcome. Three independent clans — Kaminari, Kurohana, and Gekkō — hold the balance of power, and every faction knows it.

The year is 16744. The throne sits empty. The war grinds on. Magic has returned to a world that does not fully understand it. And somewhere in the archipelago, things that slumbered during the long dark have begun to stir.

The world of Seizan exists within the Miyosai system — a trinary stellar system governed by three stars, orbited by seven planets, and watched over by four moons. It is a world where magic energy called sei flows through all living things, shaped and amplified by the celestial bodies that wheel overhead.

The archipelago of Kagekuni — the Shrouded Isles — sits within the Raijin no Fukai sea, shaped by competing celestial influences and the restless geology beneath its shores. Earthquakes, tsunamis, typhoons, and volcanic eruptions are regular features of life here, not catastrophes to be survived but rhythms to be understood. Architecture, agriculture, and culture have all adapted to a world that moves.

Above, the three stars of the Miyosai system trace their ancient paths. Their movements drive named astrological events that overlay the standard four seasons, influencing weather, tides, the flow of sei, and the behavior of the spirit world. The four moons compound these effects — their own cycles creating tidal patterns, omen windows, and subtle magical resonance that those attuned to sei can feel in their bones.

Seven planets share the system, each with its own character and influence. From molten Akahoshi burning close to Amaterasu to distant Yamiyo trailing in permanent shadow, the planetary family marks time on scales both human and cosmic.

The people of Kagekuni have watched these skies for millennia. Their calendar, their festivals, their understanding of magic and the natural world — all of it is rooted in the dance of light above them. What follows is what is known of that dance.

DM Note — The Great Aphelion

The Miyosai system's three stars orbit a common barycenter on independent orbital inclinations. Once in recorded history, all three reached maximum mutual distance simultaneously — the Great Aphelion (14344). This event caused the sei drought and the dark ages (12806–~15883). The connection between stellar position and sei availability is the campaign's deepest cosmological secret. No living scholar has assembled the complete picture. See the individual section entries for details on how this manifests in each celestial body's behavior.

sealed

The name is a historical fossil from the earliest age when the seven Progenitor dragons did physically gather during the tenth month. The tradition outlived the practice by millennia. The Ancient Guard recognizes the irony — the "Month of No Gods" was originally the month when all the gods were present in one place. The Great Aphelion and the Sei Drought

sealed

The sei drought began with the stellar decline of the War of Fractured Banners era (~12605). As Susanoo and Tsukuyomi entered their long retreat from the barycenter of the Miyosai trinary system, sei accessibility diminished gradually. The first secondary star crossed below naked-eye visibility around ~12806, marking the beginning of the dark ages. The Temple of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji fell in 13088 — a consequence of the drought, not its cause.

The three stars of the Miyosai system orbit a common gravitational center (barycenter) on different orbital inclinations. Planets orbit Amaterasu and travel with it; moons orbit Seizan directly. Neither participated in the Great Aphelion — only the three stars reached maximum mutual distance. The Great Aphelion itself (~14344) was the absolute nadir: Amaterasu at one extreme of its barycentric arc carrying Seizan with it, while Susanoo and Tsukuyomi sat at opposing extremes on their own inclined planes. The geometry was not a uniform recession but a three-dimensional separation — the distances compounded geometrically.

Amaterasu never went dark. Its baseline sei sustained life, agriculture, and the physical world throughout the dark ages. The world retained normal day/night cycles. What was lost was the complex magical expression that depended on the full trinary system — Susanoo's contribution to water magic and healing, Tsukuyomi's contribution to transformation and energy manipulation. The dark ages were cultural and intellectual collapse rather than extinction.

The Progenitors entered their slumber during this same period. Whether the aphelion caused the slumber, the slumber caused the sei drought, or the aphelion caused both remains unknown — even to the Ancient Guard. The slow return of sei beginning 15962 (First Talents) correlates with Susanoo's partial orbital return after dawn (15883). The Great Awakening (~16693) marks the moment all three stars became clearly visible simultaneously — effectively the moment Tsukuyomi's return crossed the threshold of reliability. The orbital correction is still ongoing — the current celestial configuration has not yet fully returned to its pre-Aphelion state.

This connection is not understood by any living scholar. The data exists in fragmentary astronomical records across multiple institutions, but no one has assembled the complete picture. The Golden Dragon Clan's observatory at Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji contained the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — mechanical and arcane, capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell.

See also: core/great-aphelion.md — full canonical timeline, orbital mechanics, and orrery projection sequence.

sealed

The sei drought was not caused by the War of Fractured Banners — it coincided with the Great Aphelion, a once-in-millennia event in which all three stars of the Miyosai trinary system reached maximum mutual distance from their common barycenter simultaneously. The planets, which orbit Amaterasu and travel with it, did not participate — nor did the moons, which orbit Seizan directly. The true timeline: stellar decline began 12605; dark ages started ~12806 (first star lost to visibility); the temple fell in 13088; the Great Aphelion nadir occurred ~14344; dawn (first star returned) ~15883; First Talents ~15962; Great Awakening ~16693. Amaterasu — The Golden Anchor

Type: Primary star, golden-yellow Character: Stable and foundational. Amaterasu is the most massive of the three stars and carries the entire planetary family — including Seizan — with it as it moves. Its warmth sustains life, agriculture, and the physical world. Magical Influence: Core life energy; baseline sei. The foundation upon which all other magical expression rests.

Susanoo — The Blue Storm

Type: Smaller blue-white dwarf Character: Complex and variable orbit. Susanoo produces both the closest stellar approaches and meaningful retreats. When it draws near to Seizan, the skies fill with blue-white atmospheric phenomena — ghost rainbows shimmer across the horizon and the air takes on a crystalline quality. This close approach is the celestial event known as Nagorikaze. Magical Influence: Water magic, healing, and purification. Susanoo's proximity intensifies all water-aspected sei. Coastal communities, healers, and maritime practitioners track its position closely.

Tsukuyomi — The Red Shadow

Type: Larger deep-red dwarf Character: Elongated orbit with the most dramatic near-far swing of the three stars. Tsukuyomi's routine orbital variation produces the astrological event known as Long Shadow — periods when transformation magic weakens and shadows behave strangely across the land. At perihelion (closest approach), its deep red light casts visible daytime shadows that move independently of Amaterasu's golden light. Magical Influence: Transformation magic and energy manipulation. When Tsukuyomi burns close, shapeshifting, transmutation, and raw sei channelling reach their peak. When it retreats, these disciplines falter.

DM Note — The Three Stars and the Great Aphelion

The three stars orbit a common barycenter on independent orbital inclinations, producing a three-dimensional dance rather than a flat orbital disc. The named astrological events (Nagorikaze, Long Shadow) are the routine expressions of this dance — individual stars reaching notable positions within normal orbital variation.

The Great Aphelion (~14344) was a singular event requiring all three independent orbits to peak simultaneously. The probability is the product of three separate low-probability alignments, and the distance compounds geometrically.

Amaterasu During the Drought

Amaterasu never went dark. Its baseline sei sustained life throughout the dark ages. The world retained normal day/night cycles. What was lost was the complex magical expression that depended on the full trinary system.

Tsukuyomi — First to Fade, Last to Return

Tsukuyomi's deep red began bleeding approximately 150–170 years before the nadir (14174–14194). Its elongated orbit meant early decline would have appeared as an unusually extended Long Shadow before the deeper pattern was recognized. Transformation magic became unreliable first. Tsukuyomi was the last star to return — its deep red crossing into reliable visibility defined the Great Awakening (16693).

Susanoo — Second to Fade, First to Return

Susanoo dimmed approximately 50–80 years before nadir (14264–14294). The order watched Tsukuyomi declining for nearly a century before Susanoo followed. Susanoo's failure was the loss that reached the general population — healers losing effectiveness, maritime practices becoming unreliable. Tsukuyomi's decline was a practitioner problem; Susanoo's was a human one. Susanoo was also first to return — the first Talents (15962) correlate with its partial recovery, consistent with healing and purification being among the earliest accessible sei expressions.

Four moons orbit Seizan directly, each with its own character, orbit, and influence on the world below. Together they are called The Sisters' Tears — a name whose origin has been lost to time, though folk tales offer a dozen contradictory explanations. Their combined gravitational pull creates complex tidal patterns that shape coastal life, maritime navigation, and the rhythms of agriculture across Kagekuni. Beyond the physical, the moons carry a subtler influence — secondary sei signatures that interact with the stellar field in ways that seimasters study but do not fully understand.

Aokiba — The Blue Fang

Translation: Blue Fang Orbital Period: 17 days Character: Crystalline in appearance with an elliptical orbit that brings it dramatically close to Seizan at perigee. When near, its surface catches Susanoo's blue-white light and scatters it — the moon appears to have teeth, jagged edges of refracted brilliance that give it its name. The shortest cycle of the four — Aokiba waxes and wanes faster than some journeys take to complete. Notable Influence: Aokiba drives the most violent tidal surges, particularly during Tatsunami — the four-moon alignment convergence. Coastal communities track its orbit with the same urgency that mountain villages track avalanche seasons. Sailors consider its close approach a navigation hazard; harbormasters adjust schedules around it.

Kagetsu — The Shadow Moon

Translation: Shadow Moon Orbital Period: 33 days Character: The largest of the four moons. Kagetsu absorbs light rather than reflecting it — a dark presence against the night sky, visible primarily by the stars it occludes and the faint luminous halo that surrounds it at full phase. It dominates the sky not through brightness but through absence. Its cycle runs slightly longer than a calendar month, so its full face drifts across the seasons — never quite falling on the same date twice in succession. Notable Influence: Dreams experienced under Kagetsu's full face carry mystical significance. Diviners, spirit-speakers, and those who work with the dream-world time their practices to its cycle. Common folk avoid sleeping in direct moonlight when Kagetsu is full — not from superstition, but from the unsettling vividness of the dreams that follow.

Nagikumo — The Gentle Cloud

Translation: Gentle Cloud Orbital Period: 23 days Character: The smallest of the four moons, yet it appears disproportionately large in the sky — an optical quality that astronomers at Seishin have debated for centuries without resolution. Nagikumo carries a soft inner glow, a perpetual luminescence that persists even when the moon passes through Seizan's shadow. It never fully darkens. Its three-week rhythm gives it a steady, reassuring cadence — the most intuitive of the four cycles to track without instruments. Notable Influence: Tranquility. Nagikumo's presence in the sky is associated with calm weather, settled seas, and restful sleep. Healers note that patients recover more steadily during its visible phases. Whether this is sei influence or cultural expectation is a matter of ongoing scholarly argument.

Ryūgetsu — The Dragon Moon

Translation: Dragon Moon Orbital Period: 41 days Character: The most complex orbit of the four — Ryūgetsu's path is gravitationally linked to the outer planet Shizukanami, creating a resonance that makes its position difficult to predict without sophisticated calculation. Its surface shifts color depending on which stellar light dominates: golden under Amaterasu alone, tinged blue when Susanoo is ascendant, deepening to wine-red under Tsukuyomi's influence. Its long, irregular cycle means weeks pass between phase changes — the color of Ryūgetsu shifts so gradually that only attentive observers notice the transition. Notable Influence: Ryūgetsu periodically enters what observers call Dragon's Rest — auspicious pauses in its orbital motion where it appears to hover. These pauses are considered favorable for weather magic, spirit communication, and ceremonial work. During the astrological event Hikarishō, Ryūgetsu's full phase alignment produces celestial auroras — curtains of light that ripple across the sky in colours that echo the dragon's own shifting surface.

Full Conjunction — Tatsunami

All four moons align every 529,023 days — approximately once every 1,448 years.

A true Tatsunami is not a storm but a convergence so rare that most civilizations experience it only once, if at all. The tidal forces compound catastrophically; the sei amplification reaches levels that no living seimaster has experienced. Historical records from Seishin describe the last full conjunction in fragmentary, reverential terms — the ocean withdrew beyond the horizon before returning as a wall of luminescent water, and sei-sensitive individuals reported hearing the world itself vibrate like a struck bell.

Lunar Sei Influence

The moons carry secondary sei signatures — subtler than the stars but meaningful in combination. Scholars at Seishin track three distinct channels of lunar influence:

  • Tidal — Physical effects on water, weather, and geological activity
  • Omen — Divinatory significance; dream potency; spirit-world permeability
  • Sei Amplification — Mild magical resonance that compounds with stellar alignment

When stellar and lunar alignments coincide, the compounded effects are meaningfully greater than either alone. A Nagorikaze event during a Tatsunami convergence, for instance, produces tidal and magical conditions that exceed what either event generates independently.

DM Note — Tatsunami Frequency and Campaign History

At ~1,448 years between full alignments, there have been roughly 11 true Tatsunami events since the founding year (year 0 of the Kagekuni calendar, ~16,744 years ago). The most recent would have fallen approximately 300–400 years before the current campaign year, placing it within recorded history but beyond living memory. The term "Tatsunami" is used colloquially for any severe multi-moon tidal event (particularly when three moons are in near-alignment), which is why coastal communities treat it as a recurring threat rather than a once-in-a-millennium catastrophe. The true four-moon convergence is something most scholars debate rather than fear.

DM Note — Moons and the Great Aphelion

The four moons orbit Seizan directly and were not affected by the Great Aphelion. Their physical tidal influence continued normally throughout the dark ages. However, with two of the three stellar sei sources absent, the moons' secondary sei signatures had nothing to compound with — their amplification channel was effectively inert for ~3,077 years. The return of stellar sei has reactivated lunar resonance, but whether the current lunar sei signatures match their pre-Aphelion intensity is unknown. Seishin's records do not extend that far back.

Seven planets orbit Amaterasu, travelling with the primary star as it traces its own path through the Miyosai system. Their positions relative to Seizan shift in predictable patterns — the movements of siblings sharing a common parent rather than independent wanderers. Astronomers at Seishin track their orbits with precision, and the agricultural, maritime, and spiritual calendars of Kagekuni all reference planetary positions for timing and omen-reading.

Our world. Seizan sits at the habitable heart of Amaterasu's planetary family — close enough for warmth, far enough for temperance. DM Note — Planets and the Great Aphelion

Because the planets orbit Amaterasu and travel with it, the seven planets did not participate in the Great Aphelion. Their positions relative to Seizan shifted only in their normal orbital patterns throughout the entire drought period. In the Tenkū-ji orrery, this is visible and striking: the planetary armatures continue their normal motion while the two secondary stellar arms go dark. The machine keeps working, the planets keep moving — two of the three stars are simply not where they should be.

Sei is the magic energy that flows through all living things on Seizan. It is not an external force to be harnessed or a resource to be mined — it is present in the blood, the breath, the roots of trees, and the currents of rivers. Sei is woven into the fabric of the world, expressed through celestial alignment and natural forces, amplified or diminished by the positions of stars and moons overhead.

The Nature of Sei

Sei responds to the Miyosai system's celestial bodies. The three stars provide its primary signatures — Amaterasu sustains the baseline, Susanoo governs water magic, healing, and purification, and Tsukuyomi shapes transformation and energy manipulation. The four moons contribute secondary resonance: tidal, divinatory, and amplificatory. When stellar and lunar alignments coincide, the effects compound beyond what either produces alone.

Sei is not evenly distributed. Certain places — ancient groves, mountain peaks, volcanic vents, river confluences — concentrate it naturally. Others are sei-dead, drained by catastrophe or corruption. Most people live their entire lives within sei's presence without consciously feeling it, the way a fish does not feel the water. Those with the talent to sense and shape sei are rare, and rarer still are those with the discipline to master it.

Seimasters

Seimasters are arcane scholars and researchers — though not necessarily practitioners. The title connotes scholarship over raw power. A seimaster studies sei as a discipline: mapping its flows, theorizing about its celestial dependencies, documenting the correlations between stellar alignment and magical expression. A non-casting seimaster may outrank a gifted practitioner socially, in the same way a physician who researches disease may outrank the healer who treats it.

Those who do manifest sei practically map to the familiar arcane traditions — wizards, sorcerers, monks — though in Kagekuni these distinctions carry different cultural weight than in other lands. Study typically occurs in mountaintop monasteries, removed from the noise of lowland life where the celestial influences can be observed more clearly.

The Sei Drought

Sei began declining during the era of the War of Fractured Banners (~12605). The decline was gradual — the first secondary star was lost to naked-eye visibility around ~12806, marking the beginning of what scholars now call the dark ages. By ~13088, when the last major sei institution — the Temple of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji — fell, sei was effectively inaccessible.

The period without accessible sei lasted approximately 3,077 years (12806–15883). During those millennia, the magical traditions of Kagekuni were extinguished. Knowledge was lost, institutions crumbled, and the cultural and intellectual life of the archipelago collapsed — though the physical world survived, sustained by Amaterasu's baseline energy.

Sei slowly returned through the emergence of Talents beginning 15962 — individuals born with an innate capacity to sense and shape sei, the first in over three thousand years. The process accelerated until the Great Awakening (16693), when sei was considered fully restored. The current campaign date of 16744 is just 51 years post-Awakening — living memory. The eldest practitioners remember a world without magic.

The drought's cause is officially unknown. Scholars debate whether it was a consequence of the War of Fractured Banners itself, a natural celestial cycle, or something else entirely. No consensus exists.

Kuroyami no Akuma and the Plague Campaign

Not all who shape sei do so in service of the living. Kuroyami no Akuma — formerly Takeda Arata — discovered a necromantic tome within Kuroshi Temple on the haunted island of Yurei. The knowledge within allowed him to wage the Plague Campaign (16609–16616), a war of undeath and corruption that scarred Kagekuni.

Kuroyami no Akuma was defeated but never captured or killed. He escaped, and his whereabouts remain unknown. His followers, the Eikyū Yami Clan, persist — a reminder that sei is a tool, and tools serve the hand that holds them.

DM Note — The True Cause of the Sei Drought

The sei drought was caused by the Great Aphelion — the simultaneous maximum separation of all three stars of the Miyosai system. The causal chain (aphelion → Progenitor slumber → drought, or aphelion → both independently) is unknown even to the Ancient Guard. The slow orbital return of the secondary stars correlates precisely with sei's gradual restoration, but the orbital correction is not yet complete. Tsukuyomi's projection, while present, carries slightly less intensity than its pre-decline readings.

No living scholar has assembled the complete picture. The data exists in fragmentary astronomical records across multiple institutions, but no one has connected stellar position to sei availability. The Golden Dragon Clan's observatory at Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji contained the most complete model of the Miyosai system ever constructed — the mechanical-arcane orrery capable of projecting celestial positions across millennia. It has not been operational since the temple fell in 13088.

DM Note — Murasakiryū's Sei Awareness

Every sei use in Kagekuni passes through the awakened Progenitor Murasakiryū's awareness. Every spell the party casts, every druidic invocation, every monk ability — all of it is potentially observed. Whether Murasakiryū actively monitors individual sei users or maintains passive background awareness is unresolved. Whether the party registers as notable is unknown.

Seizan experiences four standard seasons that mirror the familiar cycle of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These provide the foundational rhythm of agricultural life, festivals, and daily existence across Kagekuni. Overlaying these are the astrological events driven by the Miyosai trinary system — celestial phenomena that alter weather, tides, the flow of sei, and the behaviour of the natural and spirit worlds.

Astrological Overlays

The astrological events of the Miyosai system are not seasons in their own right — they are recurring celestial phenomena that overlay the standard four seasons, sometimes reinforcing their character and sometimes disrupting it. A Nagorikaze event during summer intensifies the monsoons; the same event during winter creates eerie blue-white frost patterns and unseasonal coastal surges.

Kagekuni follows a traditional twelve-month calendar rooted in the agricultural and spiritual rhythms of the land. Each month carries a name that reflects the character of its days — what grows, what changes, what is demanded of the people who live through it. The names are ancient, predating the dark ages, and their meanings have weathered millennia of use without losing their aptness.

The current year is 16744. The current date is Nagatsuki 1 — the first day of the ninth month, the opening of Aki (autumn).
