Notes on the Calendar

Mutsuki opens the year with the Month of Affection — a time for rekindling bonds, settling debts carried over from the old year, and renewing oaths of loyalty. Despite winter's grip, it is a month of warmth between people.

Kisaragi, the Month of Changing Clothes, marks the first tentative preparations for the season ahead. Heavy winter garments are aired and stored; lighter layers are brought out, though the cold has not yet released its hold.

Satsuki, the Month of Early Rice, is the agricultural pivot — the planting that determines whether the year will be one of plenty or hardship. Communities work together; even samurai households may contribute labour during Satsuki in rural provinces.

Minazuki is paradoxically named the Month of Water despite the kanji literally reading "month without water" — a reference to the rice paddies drinking the rains dry as fast as the monsoons deliver them.

Fumizuki, the Month of Letters, reflects the summer tradition of correspondence — poetry exchanges between allies and rivals, love letters carried by trusted messengers, and the formal diplomatic communiqués that shape the political landscape of the following seasons.

Kannazuki — the Month of No Gods — carries the common saying that "the gods are away" during the tenth month, though no one remembers where they supposedly go. The name is accepted without question by most, treated as folk tradition rather than literal truth.

Shiwasu, the Month of Running Priests, closes the year. Even the most contemplative monks are said to be running during the twelfth month — settling accounts, performing final rites, and preparing shrines for the new year. It is the busiest month for temples and the most frantic for merchants.

DM Note — Kannazuki's True Origin

The name Kannazuki is a historical fossil from the earliest age when the seven Progenitor dragons did physically gather during the tenth month. The tradition outlived the practice by millennia. The Ancient Guard recognizes the irony — the "Month of No Gods" was originally the month when all the gods were present in one place. Now, with the Progenitors slumbering, the name is accidentally accurate again for entirely different reasons.

Discovery path: Research in the Great Library of Kawa; conversations with Ancient Guard members; study of pre-Reckoning texts.

It has been fifty-one years since the Great Awakening. Within living memory, magic returned to a world that had forgotten it existed. The energy called sei — once woven through every living thing on Seizan — went silent for over three thousand years. When it returned, it returned to a world that had changed. Institutions built on magical foundations had long since crumbled. The knowledge, the traditions, the scholarly lineages that once sustained sei practice were gone. What emerged in their place was something rawer: individuals born with innate magical talent — Talents — appearing without warning, without teachers, and without a society that knew what to do with them.

The first Talents were persecuted. Later ones were tolerated, studied, and eventually recruited. Magical enclaves formed — Seishin on the island of Unmeijima became the premier research institution; Hikari no Shizuku established a healing tradition within the capital. By the time the Great Awakening made sei fully accessible again, the daimyo of Kagekuni were already competing to recruit mages into their service. Magic had returned. The question of who would control it had only just begun.

An Empire Without an Emperor

Emperor Ryūjin no Mikado — the eighteenth emperor, the last of the near-immortal elven line stretching back to the founding — died in 16739. The official cause was old age. He was the final link to an unbroken chain of rulers that began with Tenryū no Mikado over eight thousand years ago.

No confirmed successor has emerged. Multiple claimants have presented genealogical proof of varying credibility, but none has secured recognition from the Kokushi Kyōkai — the five government ministers who administer the empire. The ministers themselves are holdovers, functioning in constitutional limbo. They maintain taxation, law, infrastructure, and diplomacy, but they lack the authority to resolve the central crisis: who rules?

The problem is compounded by Ryūjin's final reform. In 16732, the emperor decreed that the Kokushi Kyōkai could no longer appoint a Shogun without imperial approval. The Shogunate — the military authority that has historically held the empire together during periods of crisis — is legally frozen. There is no emperor to approve a Shogun, and no Shogun to impose order.

The Caste System

Kagekuni's social order is rigid, ancient, and under strain. Three castes define a person's place in the world:

The Kugai — the elite — are primarily humans and dragonborn who claim descent from the imperial founders. Daimyo, courtiers, scholars, and high-ranking samurai occupy this tier. Below them, the Zokumin — the commonfolk — encompass everyone from samurai and ronin to peasants, artisans, and merchants. Merchants sit at the bottom of the Zokumin despite their often considerable wealth, a source of constant social friction. At the lowest rung, the Burakumin — the outcasts — are those whose occupations involve death: leather workers, butchers, executioners, undertakers. They live in segregated communities with limited civil rights and face systemic harassment.

Race compounds caste. Dragonborn and humans — particularly those of the locally dominant lineage — move through society with relative ease. Others do not. Characters who are not of the dominant race in a given territory find doors closed, prices raised, and suspicion constant.

The Ronin Surge

With the political vacuum, the frozen Shogunate, and open war between the alliances, the number of masterless samurai — ronin — has reached an all-time high. Former retainers of dead lords, warriors whose clans dissolved during the Epoch of Factional Flux, and samurai who simply walked away from service they no longer believed in — all of them crowd the roads, the teahouses, and the employment boards of every town. Some seek honourable service. Others have abandoned honour entirely. The roads of Kagekuni have never been less safe.

The Eruption of Akaho Sanmyaku

On Hachigatsu 29, 16744 — just days ago — the volcanic range of Akaho Sanmyaku on the northern island of Fushichō erupted. Ash is visible from as far as the Tenchūsan Ren mountains on Hokori. The eruption is ongoing. Fushichō has always been a land of fire and ancient secrets; what this eruption means for the settlements and peoples of that island remains to be seen.

Tatara — The Eternal Feud

On the southern island of Tatara, the ancient feud between the Zirak (dwarves) and the Glimfyr (gnomes) has escalated again. The conflict — which predates the War of Fractured Banners — has historically been held in check only by imperial decree. With no emperor to command restraint, old hatreds have resurfaced. Recent reports suggest the gnomes deliberately sabotaged a dwarven relic site, an act of provocation that the Zirak are unlikely to answer with diplomacy.

The Shadow of the Plague Campaign

The Plague Campaign of 16609–16616 remains the defining trauma of the post-Awakening era. Kuroyami no Akuma — once Takeda Arata, before he found a necromantic tome in the cursed Kuroshi Temple on the haunted island of Yurei — raised undead legions and waged a war that scarred the archipelago. The response united unlikely allies: the Shogun recruited Talents, and the magical enclaves of Seishin, the Raimeiin, and the Forest of Spirits revealed themselves publicly for the first time.

Kuroyami was defeated. He was never captured or killed. His cult, the Eikyū Yami Clan, persists in some form. The question of where Kuroyami is — and what he has been doing for the last 128 years — is one that very few people ask aloud.

The Magical Landscape

Magic is new. Not new to the world — new to the people living in it. Sei sustained civilisation for millennia before the dark ages, but the dark ages lasted long enough to erase nearly all institutional memory of how magic worked, who wielded it, and what it meant. The current generation of practitioners is rebuilding from fragments.

The major magical institutions known publicly are:

  • Seishin (Unmeijima) — The premier research institution, founded around the figure of Hikari no Kenta, the first known Talent. Now a city in its own right.
  • Hikari no Shizuku (Heian) — A healing and light magic tradition operating within the capital.
  • Raimeiin — Revealed during the Plague Campaign; methods and focus not widely known.

The Season

It is Nagatsuki 1, 16744 — the first day of the Month of Long Nights, the opening of Aki. Autumn has arrived. The harvest is underway across the lowlands. Violet grasses are darkening toward black on the hillsides. Crystal-barked trees have begun to chime in the cooling mountain winds. The goldtail fish runs have started in the rivers.

Above, all three stars of the Miyosai system burn in the sky — Amaterasu's gold, Susanoo's blue-white, and Tsukuyomi's deep red. Fifty-one years ago, that was not the case. The eldest among you remember a sky with only one star. The world is brighter now. Whether it is safer remains to be seen.

DM Note — The Emperor's Death

Ryūjin's death is not what it appears. The official story is old age, but foul play is suspected. Two independent daimyo — Raijin no Kazuhiko (Clan Kaminari) and Akihiko Kurohana (Clan Kurohana) — are both quietly investigating the circumstances of the emperor's death. Neither has shared their suspicions publicly. The 16732 reform that froze the Shogunate may have been motivated by Ryūjin's awareness of threats against the imperial line — a last attempt to prevent his enemies from consolidating power after his death.

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.JLGqqI474AH04SDL]{Hiroshi Nakamura}, Shugo (military governor) of Heian in Kaminari territory, is a traitor working with the Genso Alliance. He is using his position to feed intelligence to Genso — likely connected to the larger political destabilisation.

DM Note — Clan Gekkō

Clan Gekkō attempted a dark ritual with catastrophic consequences. The entire clan — including Daimyo Masota no Gekkō — was transformed into Nagaji (serpent folk). Masota retains fragmented awareness, but his mental coherence is degrading over time. The longer the situation persists, the less of him remains to reach.

The Order of the Black Lily (Monastery of the Black Lily, above @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.ow3AGqlvFevncAwN]{Akatsuki} village in Kaze province) knows the truth and has been monitoring the situation. The party has already encountered and killed several Nagaji without knowing they were Gekkō clan members. The moral reckoning is pending.

A reversal may be possible but requires rare materials, specific conditions, or Progenitor involvement. The details are TBD.

DM Note — The Order of the Ancient Guard

Behind the known orders lies the most secret organisation in Kagekuni: the Order of the Ancient Guard. Their purpose is the silent protection of the living founding dragons — the seven Progenitors who are believed dead but are in fact in deep slumber. The Ancient Guard maintains hidden sanctuaries, exerts subtle influence to prevent any single power from dominating, and guards the conditions under which the dragons remain safe and hidden.

Known members include Benkei (rank TBD) and the deceased Solas Evergreen (rank likely Protector or higher). Solas's murder means someone killed a member of the order protecting the dragons. The scope of the threat is unknown.

DM Note — The Progenitor Dragons

All seven founding dragons are alive, hidden in deep slumber across the archipelago. Their dormancy coincided with the Great Aphelion and the sei drought. Whether one caused the other, or both share a common cause, is unknown even to the Ancient Guard.

One exception: Murasakiryū (Amethyst Dragon, domain of arcane knowledge and divination) is awake — woken by dark mortals who believed they were awakening Kokuryū (Onyx). Murasakiryū is actively masquerading as Kokuryū. The Great Awakening (~16687) was not a natural restoration of magic — it was the consequence of waking a single malevolent Progenitor. Every sei user in Kagekuni draws power through Murasakiryū's waking awareness.

Solas Evergreen was killed to prevent the awakening of Kinryū (Golden Dragon, domain of honour and justice) — the natural counter-balance. Relc now holds Solas's mission: the Warden's Wisdom cipher that leads to methods for waking Kinryū.

Kagekuni is a civilisation built on hierarchy. It is not a suggestion, not a tradition that has softened with time — it is the architecture of daily life, enforced by law, reinforced by custom, and internalised by nearly everyone who lives within it. From the moment a child is born, their place in the order is known. What they may do, where they may go, how they must speak to those above and below them — all of it is governed by structures older than most of the buildings they live in.

Understanding this society is essential to moving through it. The adventurer who ignores social rank will find doors closed, prices raised, and patience exhausted long before any blade is drawn.

At the apex of Kagekuni's political structure sits the Emperor — or, more precisely, the empty throne where an emperor should sit. For over eight thousand years, the imperial line traced its descent from Tenryū no Mikado, the first emperor, who united the warring dragon clans and forged the archipelago into a single civilisation. The emperor's authority was absolute in theory and considerable in practice, tempered by the realities of governing a vast island chain through intermediaries.

Beneath the emperor, the Shogun served as supreme military commander — a wartime appointment granted by imperial decree, carrying the authority to mobilise armies, impose martial law, and compel obedience from the daimyō. The position was never permanent by design. In practice, some shoguns held power for decades.

The Kokushi Kyōkai — the Council of Five Ministers — administers the empire's civilian machinery. Five departments cover the essential functions of governance:

Title Role
Anzen Hoshō Daijin Minister of Security — intelligence, imperial protectorate
Fukushi Daijin Minister of Welfare — healthcare, education, public assistance
Gaikō Daijin Minister of Foreign Affairs — diplomacy, trade, foreign nationals
Seimu Daijin Minister of Administration — provincial governance, infrastructure
Zaiumu Daijin Minister of Finance — treasury, taxation, revenue

Below the national level, provincial administration follows its own chain: Chiji (Governor) to Gunji (County Magistrate) to Shi (Municipal Assembly) to Shichō (Mayor) to Sonchō (Village Leader). In theory, each level answers to the one above. In practice, local power depends heavily on who controls the samurai in the region.

The Teikoku Keisatsu — the Imperial Police — maintain order at a local level. Once an empire-wide institution, the police have retreated to a regional footprint in the absence of central authority. They cooperate with local clan forces where relations allow it and operate independently where they do not.

Kagekuni's population is divided into three castes. Movement between them is rare, difficult, and in most cases functionally impossible. A person's caste determines what occupations they may hold, who they may marry, where they may live, and how they are treated under law.

The ruling class. Kugai families claim descent from the imperial founders or the dragon clans that preceded them. In practice, the caste is dominated by humans and dragonborn, though other races with sufficient political connections have occasionally been elevated. The Kugai includes the daimyō, their courts, senior scholars, and the highest-ranking samurai — the hatamoto, or bannermen, who serve as personal retainers to clan lords.

Kugai families maintain genealogical records stretching back centuries. Some are genuine. Some are creative. All are taken seriously.

The broad middle of society, encompassing everyone from samurai to merchants. The Zokumin are not a single class but a gradient, and the distinctions within it matter enormously to those who live them.

At the top sit samurai in active service — warriors sworn to a lord, carrying the authority of their clan. Below them, rōnin — masterless samurai — occupy an uncomfortable middle ground: they retain the right to carry weapons but lack the social anchor of a lord's name. Below rōnin come peasants, who work the land and form the backbone of the food supply. Artisans follow — craftspeople whose skills are valued but whose social standing reflects the society's bias toward land and loyalty over craft. At the very bottom of the Zokumin sit merchants.

This last distinction is the source of chronic social tension. Merchants often possess considerable wealth — in some cases more than the samurai who look down on them. But wealth without rank buys comfort, not respect. A merchant who forgets this distinction will be reminded of it quickly and without sympathy.

Those whose work involves death or pollution. Leather workers, butchers, executioners, undertakers, gravediggers — anyone whose livelihood touches the boundary between life and death. The Burakumin live in segregated communities called buraku, subject to limited civil rights and systemic harassment. They are not enslaved, but the freedoms available to them are narrow and the prejudice they face is open.

The caste system predates the current empire. It survived the Dark Ages, the return of magic, and every political upheaval in between. It will likely survive whatever comes next.

Honour in Kagekuni is not an abstraction. It is a currency, a weapon, and a sentence.

A samurai's honour determines their standing within their clan, their right to speak in councils, the marriages their children may make, and the manner of their death. Honour is earned through service, loyalty, and sacrifice. It is lost through cowardice, betrayal, or failure — and once lost, it is extraordinarily difficult to recover. A samurai who loses their honour may face exile, ritual punishment, or the expectation that they will take their own life to restore their family's name.

The codes of bushidō — the way of the warrior — govern samurai conduct. Duty to one's lord supersedes personal desire. Courage in battle is expected, not celebrated. Loyalty is absolute until the moment it isn't, at which point it becomes treason. The tension between these demands — when duty conflicts with conscience, when loyalty to a corrupt lord meets personal honour — is the engine that drives much of Kagekuni's political drama.

Honour applies differently across the castes. Peasants and merchants are not bound by bushidō, but they live within its shadow. A merchant who shames a samurai may find their shop burned. A peasant who fails to show proper deference may be struck without legal consequence. The social codes are enforced not by law alone but by a pervasive understanding that hierarchy is the natural order — and that those who disrupt it invite consequences not just for themselves but for their families.

The archipelago is home to many races, though not all enjoy equal standing. Humans and dragonborn — particularly those claiming descent from the founding dragon clans — move through society with the fewest barriers. Other races face varying degrees of prejudice depending on the region, the local clan's attitudes, and the circumstances of their presence.

The Zirak and Glimfyr have maintained an eternal feud on their shared island of Tatara. They rarely stop fighting. Historically, only an emperor's direct command has imposed truces — and those truces have always ended sooner than intended. Their conflict once sparked the empire-wide War of Fractured Banners. With no emperor to restrain them, the feud has recently escalated again.

Characters who are not dragonborn, human, or the locally dominant non-human race will encounter prejudice in social situations. Doors close. Prices rise. Patience runs thin. This is not universal — individual NPCs may be more or less tolerant — but the systemic bias is real and pervasive.

War in Kagekuni is the domain of the samurai, but the dying is shared widely.

The military command hierarchy runs from the Shōgun (currently a vacant position) down through the daimyō, who command their clan's forces directly. Below the daimyō, the chain continues:

Sotaishō (Supreme Commander) → Karō (Chief Retainer) → Taishō (General) → Kumigashira (Squad Leader) → Kogashira (Corporal)

Samurai form the officer class, ranked from gokenin (housemen) through goshi (rustic warriors) to hatamoto (bannermen — the elite retainers of a daimyō). Below them, the ashigaru — peasant infantry — fill the ranks with sword, spear, and bow.

An extensive logistics corps of bugyō (commissioners) manages everything from weapons and armour to provisions, boats, and battlefield flags. War in Kagekuni is not simply a matter of warriors meeting on a field — it is an administrative enterprise requiring coordination across difficult terrain, unpredictable weather, and supply lines that stretch through mountains and across water.

The current political vacuum has produced a surge in rōnin — masterless samurai — at numbers not seen in living memory. Some lost their lords to the war. Others served clans that dissolved during the upheaval. Some walked away by choice, unable to reconcile their duty with their conscience.

Rōnin are a destabilising force. They retain the right to bear arms and the training to use them, but lack the social anchor of a lord's authority. Some seek new masters. Some sell their swords. Some turn to banditry. The roads of Kagekuni are significantly less safe than they were a decade ago, and rōnin are the primary reason.

Power in Kagekuni flows through clans. Each is a political entity unto itself — a family at its core, expanded over centuries into a network of vassals, retainers, allied families, and sworn samurai. A clan controls territory, maintains armies, administers justice within its borders, and pursues its interests through diplomacy, marriage, trade, and war. The daimyō who leads each clan holds authority that is, within their province, nearly absolute.

For most of the empire's history, the clans answered to the Emperor. With the throne empty and the Shogunate frozen, that restraint is gone. What remains is ambition, geography, and the alliances that clans have forged to survive what comes next.

Two years of open war have divided Hokori's major clans into opposing alliances, with three clans maintaining a precarious independence between them.

The Genso Alliance controls the verdant interior and the southern frontier. Its strength lies in agricultural wealth, ore from the mountains of Tsuchi, and the strategic depth that comes from holding the island's most productive farmland.

The Arashi Alliance commands the northwestern coast and the storm-battered northeast. Its advantages are naval — Minato-jō and Namigashira are the two great ports of Hokori — and its clans are hardened by generations of living where the weather itself is a combatant.

Two years of escalating hostility have produced no decisive outcome. Battles are fought, borders shift, villages burn, and the common people pay the price.

The three independent clans are the fulcrum on which the war may turn. Every faction knows this. The independents are courted, threatened, and watched. Their allegiance — or continued neutrality — could end the war overnight.

Kaminari controls the Province of Hana and with it the imperial capital of Heian — the most politically sensitive position of any clan in Kagekuni. They hold the seat of empire without the authority to claim it. Every decision Kazuhiko makes is scrutinised by both alliances, who see in Hana's independence either a potential ally or a threat that must eventually be addressed.

Kaminari's warriors are fierce and well-trained, known for discipline under pressure and a willingness to fight in conditions that would break lesser forces. Dragons Today — CRITICAL SECRET (DM Only)

The spiritual life of Kagekuni is layered, ancient, and deeply woven into daily existence. There is no separation between the sacred and the mundane — a farmer who plants rice in the spring does so with a prayer to the kami of the paddy. A samurai who draws their blade offers a silent word to their ancestors. A merchant who opens their shop at dawn bows to the small shrine beside the door, and means it. Religion in Kagekuni is not practiced in isolation; it is practiced in everything.

At the foundation of Kagekuni's faith is a single supreme divine being — an ultimate creator whose nature is understood to transcend mortal comprehension. This entity is not named in common speech, not depicted in art, and not the subject of direct worship in the way a familiar god might be. It simply is. The divine is the origin point from which all other spiritual beings descend, the source of the natural order, and the reason the world holds together rather than falling apart.

Beneath this supreme being, a hierarchy of venerated figures serves as intermediaries between the divine and the mortal world. These figures — historical heroes, legendary seimasters, mythologised rulers, and great spiritual teachers — occupy a role analogous to saints. Shrines and temples may be dedicated to specific figures without contradiction; a shrine to a legendary healer and a shrine to a dragon ancestor both point upward toward the same ultimate source.

This structure allows for enormous local variation. A fishing village on the coast of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.ijGHvVOlw9tFpBo8]{Nami} may venerate a storm-calming saint unknown in the interior of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.EPAWGqYCrUzYfngV]{Kusa}. A mountain monastery may honour a philosopher whose name has never been spoken in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian}. The faith accommodates these differences without strain — local devotion and universal truth coexist.

pages.name: Kami — The Spirits of the World

text.content:
Kami are the spiritual inhabitants of the natural world — beings of place, element, and phenomenon who exist alongside the mortal population. They are not gods. They are not saints. They are something else entirely: presences that dwell in rivers, mountains, ancient trees, crossroads, waterfalls, and any place where the natural world gathers unusual weight or beauty.

A kami may be benevolent, indifferent, or dangerous — and sometimes all three, depending on how it is treated. The kami of a river might bless the villages along its banks with clean water and good fishing for generations, then drown a child who wades too deep without offering respect. This is not cruelty. It is nature. Kami do not operate by human morality. They operate by their own logic, which mortals can learn to read but never fully control.

Shrines mark the resting places and territories of known kami. These range from grand structures maintained by dedicated priests to simple roadside markers — a torii gate, a stone basin, a length of sacred rope tied around an ancient tree. The distinction between a great shrine and a humble one is not a measure of the kami's power but of the community's resources. A village kami honoured with a mossy stone and a daily cup of rice may be every bit as potent as one housed in a lacquered hall.

Interaction with kami follows established protocols: purification before approach, offerings appropriate to the spirit's nature, prayers spoken with correct form, and gratitude expressed whether the request is granted or not. Disturbing a kami — through disrespect, pollution of its territory, or destruction of its shrine — invites consequences that can persist for generations.

The dead do not leave. Not entirely. In Kagekuni's understanding, the boundary between the living and the deceased is less a wall than a screen — translucent, permeable, and never quite solid. The ancestors watch. They listen. And they care, deeply, about the conduct of their descendants.

Every household of any standing maintains a butsudan — a family shrine where the names, images, and memorial tablets of the dead are kept. Daily offerings of rice, incense, water, and sometimes @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.items.Item.aWfQyc0LZGZ3GPk6]{sake} are made to the ancestors, accompanied by prayers that range from formal invocations to quiet conversation. A samurai may inform his grandfather's tablet of a promotion. A merchant may ask a deceased parent's forgiveness for a poor decision. A child may simply say good morning.

At the community level, temples maintain records of the dead and conduct ceremonies marking the anniversaries of passing, seasonal remembrances, and festivals where the boundary between worlds thins and the ancestors are believed to return briefly to the mortal realm. These are not sombre occasions — they are celebrations, feasts, and reunions with the dead conducted in a spirit of joy and gratitude rather than grief.

Ancestor veneration carries practical weight in Kagekuni's political life. A daimyō whose ancestors served with honour can invoke that legacy as a source of authority. A family whose ancestors committed shameful acts may carry that burden for generations. The dead vote, in a sense — their reputation shapes the living's standing in ways that no amount of present achievement can entirely overcome.

The founding dragons occupy a unique position in Kagekuni's spiritual landscape — elevated above saints, distinct from kami, revered as something closer to demigods. They are the seven Progenitors who ruled the archipelago before the first human emperor rose to power, and whose bloodlines, according to tradition, flow through the veins of the dragonborn elite and the imperial line itself.

Clan Dragon Color Domain
Crimson Clan Akaryū Red Fire, volcanic power, strength
Azure Clan Aoryū Blue Water, storms, coastal protection
Emerald Clan Midoryū Green Nature, earth, healing, balance
Onyx Clan Kokuryū Black Shadow, darkness, cunning, mystery
Golden Clan Kinryū Gold Honour, justice, nobility, mediation
Silver Clan Ginryū Silver Grace, purity, ice, moon and stars
Amethyst Clan Murasakiryū Purple Arcane knowledge, divination, mystical arts

Each dragon clan once ruled from a specific island or region of the archipelago, and the cultural memory of those domains persists in regional identity, local festivals, and the heraldry of the clans that claim descent from them. Temples and shrines dedicated to the founding dragons are found across Kagekuni — some grand and well-maintained, others ancient and half-forgotten, their stonework crumbling under moss and rain.

The first emperor, Tenryū no Mikado, is said to have descended from both the Crimson and Golden bloodlines — fire and justice united in a single line. His unification of the warring dragon clans approximately eight thousand years ago established the imperial dynasty and the political order that persists, in increasingly fractured form, to this day.

In the current era, the founding dragons are considered historical and mythological figures. The world at large believes them long dead or ascended beyond mortal reach. Dragon eggs — occasionally unearthed from ancient sites — are treated as fossils and collectibles rather than signs of living beings.

Dragonborn within the Kugai elite claim direct descent from the founding dragons, and this claim forms the bedrock of noble authority in many clans. Whether the genealogies are genuine or constructed, the social power they convey is real.

Purification is the most universally practiced spiritual act in Kagekuni. It crosses caste, clan, and regional boundaries. The principle is simple: contact with death, blood, illness, spiritual pollution, or moral transgression creates impurity that must be cleansed before a person can properly interact with the sacred.

In practice, purification takes many forms. Water is the most common agent — the ritual washing of hands and mouth at a shrine's temizuya (water basin) before entering. Salt is scattered at thresholds to ward off impurity. Incense smoke purifies spaces. Priests perform formal ceremonies of cleansing for individuals, buildings, and even weapons. Before a battle, entire armies may undergo purification rites — not for divine protection, but to ensure they enter combat in a state of spiritual clarity.

The most significant purifications mark life transitions: birth, coming of age, marriage, and death. A house where someone has died is purified before the living resume normal activity. A blade that has taken a life may be ritually cleansed. A warrior returning from battle washes not just the blood from their skin but the spiritual residue of killing from their soul.

This practice intersects with the caste system in uncomfortable ways. The Burakumin — whose occupations involve constant contact with death and spiritual pollution — are considered permanently impure by those who observe the strictest interpretations of purification law. Their segregation is, in part, a spiritual justification layered over social prejudice.

pages.name: Kannazuki — The Month of No Gods

text.content:
The tenth month of the calendar is called Kannazuki — the Month of No Gods. Tradition holds that during this month, the kami leave their shrines and territories to gather at a great convocation, leaving the mortal world temporarily unattended. Shrines see reduced attendance. Certain rituals are suspended. The month carries a faint unease — a feeling of being unwatched, which in Kagekuni is not a comfort but a vulnerability.

The name is ancient — far older than the current empire — and its origin has been debated by scholars and priests for millennia without resolution.

Monasteries serve as centres of learning, contemplation, and — not infrequently — political refuge. The monastic traditions of Kagekuni draw on a contemplative philosophy that emphasises mindfulness, detachment from worldly desire, and the cultivation of inner stillness. Monks and nuns withdraw from the hierarchies of secular life, though in practice monasteries are never entirely free from political entanglement.

Several monastic orders maintain influence across the archipelago:

The Order of the Tranquil Lotus on Unmeijima combines nature-focused spirituality with rigorous physical discipline. Their elder, @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.5uySp1O85TJzLFmF]{Benkei} — a Guhuza of 198 years — is among the oldest known living individuals in Kagekuni.

The Order of the Sacred Grove follows a druidic tradition devoted to protecting specific sacred sites. Their guardians tend individual locations for decades, maintaining a quiet vigil that most of the world never notices.

The Order of the Black Lily, based above @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.ow3AGqlvFevncAwN]{Akatsuki} village in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze} province, is less a spiritual order than a professional one — Kagekuni's premier infiltration specialists, operating from a monastery that serves as both temple and training facility.

The tension between worldly duty and spiritual withdrawal runs through all of these traditions. A monk who retreats from the world still lives in it. A monastery that claims neutrality still sits on land that someone claims to own. The spiritual life of Kagekuni is never purely spiritual — it is always, in some measure, political.

For most people in Kagekuni, religion is not a matter of doctrine but of practice. A farmer does not study theology. He maintains his family shrine, makes offerings to the kami of his fields, honours his ancestors at the butsudan, and visits the local temple on festival days. His faith is expressed through action — through the rituals that mark the rhythm of the year, the prayers that accompany daily work, and the quiet understanding that the world is populated by forces larger and older than himself.

This practical faith produces a population that is simultaneously devout and pragmatic. The people of Kagekuni believe in the spiritual world because they live in it — because the rivers glow faintly at night, because the fog sometimes carries incense from no source, because the trees in certain forests have bark of burnished bronze and no one considers this remarkable. The sacred is not separate from the ordinary. It is the ordinary, seen clearly.

Village Kaze Province Hokori Pop: Small
Clan: GekkoClimate: Cold; perpetual shadow from peaks; mist rarely lifts"The village that keeps secrets the way stone keeps cold -- completely and without effort."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.ow3AGqlvFevncAwN]{Akatsuki} -- Dawn -- is a village whose name contradicts its character. It sits in perpetual shadow from the peaks above it, reached by a winding stone path gaining significant altitude. The air is cold even in summer. Mist collects in the surrounding terrain and rarely lifts before midday, often not at all.

The village is modest -- terraced farming on steep slopes, stone-built houses with heavy roofs designed for snow load, a central well, a small shrine. Residents are not hostile but are compact -- words measured carefully, questions answered with just enough to satisfy without offering more. They have maintained this posture for generations because they live below the Monastery of the Black Lily.

Above the village, higher on the mountainside and accessed by a stone staircase cut into the rock face, stands the Monastery of the Black Lily.

The Monastery of the Black Lily -- Dark stone and iron construction; austere; functional rather than beautiful. The Order of the Black Lily operates here -- Kagekuni's premier training facility for infiltration specialists, covert intelligence operatives, and precision agents.

The Order's relationship with Clan Gekko was long and close. The disappearance of Clan Gekko has severed the primary institutional support structure. They are reassessing.

The monks and initiates know the truth about the Nagaji transformation. They have made a calculated decision to not release this information without a reversal plan. They will share the complete truth with parties who demonstrate they are positioned to actually address the situation.

None publicly documented. The village maintains deliberate anonymity.

Details

The Order of the Black Lily knows what happened to Clan Gekko and will share the truth with those who can demonstrate they are positioned to act.

The village is not simply a bystander community -- it functions as a support system for the monastery.

DM Secrets

The Order's Full Knowledge The Order knows: what ritual was used, who performed it first, approximately how many Gekko clan members were transformed, and that Masota no Gekko himself underwent the ritual. They do not know where Masota currently is. The transformed Gekko move in patterns that even their surveillance cannot consistently track.

The Reversal The Order has determined a reversal exists -- theoretical, not practical. It requires three elements: the original ritual documentation (in Kinkokyo, in the Golden Dragon Clan's records); a specific sei configuration present only during a particular celestial alignment (upcoming, within the next few sessions); and a practitioner capable of performing sei-based restoration at significant scale.

What the Order Wants from the Party The Order will propose a partnership: the party retrieves the reversal documentation from the Temple of Kinryu; the Order handles logistics of gathering the transformed Gekko; together they manage the political revelation on a controlled timeline. In exchange, the Order provides intelligence, resources, and full knowledge of the Gekko situation.

The Village's Role Several former Order members have retired to the village. Two of the village's farmers are active deep-cover agents between assignments. Visitors who threaten this arrangement will encounter more than agricultural resistance.

Plot Hooks

A message from the Order reaches the party: "Come to Akatsuki. Complete information will be provided. Bring nothing official."

The Order has been watching the party since the mountain pass and wants to know what was found beyond the gold doors

An Order initiate has broken protocol and is heading toward Heian with partial information -- needs intercepting before triggering political consequences

Town Hana Province Hokori Pop: Medium
Clan: KaminariClimate: Valley setting; sheltered; cold winters; brief warm summers; heavy spring snowmelt"Everyone coming or going through the mountains passes through Ayame. Everyone."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.O65fxIh1WZwEtwrf]{Ayame} occupies the valley at the base of the Tenchusan Ren pass -- the primary land route between @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana}'s southern lowlands and the northern provinces. Everything that travels overland between these regions passes through Ayame. This geographic chokepoint function defines the town's character: it is less a community than a transit organism.

The town is organized around the pass road. The main thoroughfare runs straight through parallel to the Kinryugawa, broadening into a market square at the center. Secondary streets branch off at intervals -- accommodation, services, and residential areas spreading outward in concentric zones of decreasing formality.

The military overseer structure means Ayame is administered by appointed officials with military backgrounds. This produces efficient governance but can feel impersonal; permanent residents are pragmatic people who work with whoever is in charge.

Chuo-ku (Central District) -- Main thoroughfare and market square. Most commercial activity. The Marketplace operates daily.

Tenchusan Chiku (Mountain District) -- The approach zone toward the pass. Stables, equipment rental, guide services, outfitter shops. Increasingly sparse toward the pass entrance.

The Marketplace -- Permanent covered market stalls along the main street. Serves local needs and traveler provisioning. Prices reflect the captive market.

Blacksmith's Forge -- Military-grade equipment maintenance and standard smithing. Works in cooperation with the garrison.

Weaver's Shop -- Mountain-weight textiles and cold-weather clothing. Genuinely excellent; mountain gear quality is a survival matter.

Kawabe no Tengaku (Riverside Haven) -- Inn along the river approach. Quieter; favored by travelers wanting rest over socialization.

Kin no Chochin Ryokan (Golden Lantern Inn) -- Main waypoint inn on the central street. Busy, efficient, well-run. The party stayed here during their @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.O65fxIh1WZwEtwrf]{Ayame} transit.

Ryu no Yasuragi Yado (Dragon's Rest Lodge) -- Secondary inn; the party stayed here after the wagon impoundment situation. Slightly more modest.

Ayame Temple -- Small temple in the residential quarter. Patron deity is a traveling spirit protector. Resident monk maintains the shrine to the pass spirits.

• @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.icm5k8ve4junatqN]{Takeda Yoshinobu} -- Town leader; competent administrator
  • Chief Inspector @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.Mly4i17grlghx2a2]{Oshiro Masahiro} -- Teikoku Keisatsu; confirmed party ally

Details

Oshiro Masahiro's intelligence network extends far beyond what his official position suggests.

The Tenchusan Ren pass approach is under more surveillance than it appears.

Mountain guides have been returning from upper-route jobs shaken and unwilling to specify what they saw.

DM Secrets

Oshiro Masahiro -- Intelligence Asset Oshiro's decision to assist the party was not simply a judgment about innocence. He had received information suggesting their mission was legitimate and the impoundment was creating an obstacle. He knows more about the Gekko situation than he has shared. He is a potential ongoing intelligence ally.

The Pass Road -- Surveillance The pass approach is watched more carefully than it appears. Oshiro has informants at both the waypoint inn and the outfitter district who log significant travelers and goods movements. The network also detected a group with no identifiable clan affiliation, moving fast and carrying unusual cargo, approximately three weeks before the party's transit.

Takeda Yoshinobu's Concerns Yoshinobu has been receiving reports from mountain guides about unusual activity in the upper pass -- disrupted trail markers, signs of large encampment at non-standard locations, and two guides who came back shaken and unwilling to specify what they saw. He has not reported upward because he has no official channels he trusts.

Plot Hooks

Oshiro sends a discrete message: he has information relevant to the party's mission that he couldn't share safely in Ayame; proposes a meeting at the next Michibata up the pass

One of the mountain guides who returned early is drinking heavily at the Dragon's Rest and muttering fragments of what they saw

City Hana Province Hokori Pop: Large
Clan: KaminariClimate: Temperate; cherry blossom springs; warm summers; brilliant autumns; mild winters"The city that outlasted every empire built within it."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian} is the oldest continuously inhabited city in the archipelago and the seat of imperial authority for over eight thousand years. It stands on a peninsula where the Nagisa Sea meets Lake Midoriko -- a position offering both a defensible landward approach and open water access in two directions.

The city is beautiful in the way that things shaped by deep time become beautiful -- through the accumulation of craftsmanship, care, and purpose. Ancient trees line the main avenues, their roots lifting paving stones that are reset around them generation after generation. The Imperial Palace complex dominates the skyline. Shirogane Yama is visible on clear days forty miles to the north and northwest.

The Emperor's Highway extends from Heian in three directions -- north through Tenchusan Ren toward @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze}, east along the coast, and west by ferry connection to Sakurano and the interior. With no emperor, the city is a center without a purpose -- the streets are still busy, the markets still active, but there is a quality to civic life: the posture of a city holding itself together while waiting for resolution.

Hikari Zon -- Knowledge District Libraries, academies, schools, and scholarly institutions. Low, wide buildings with sliding walls. The central library holds the largest collection in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.eAI9SnbW1RmsWOGw]{Hana}. Seimasters and scholars from across the archipelago spend time here.

Hinode-ku -- Eastern Residential Ward Mixed residential for artisans and merchants. Workshops opening onto narrow streets. A lively night market operates along the canal.

Ichiba Chiku -- Market District The economic heart. The largest open market in Hokori operates six days out of seven. The Market District never truly closes.

Inari Kyoku -- Religious District Temples, shrines, and spiritual institutions. Torii gates multiply inward from the boundary. A shrine to each of the seven dragon clans exists here.

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.D2VV9bFa1txuKDxB]{Kaze}-sho -- Wind District Open spaces, windmills, farming plots within the city boundary. The windmills power grain milling and workshop machinery.

Kinrin Chiku -- Palace Surrounding Quarter Residential and administrative district surrounding the Imperial Palace. Noble families and senior officials. Access is controlled. Streets are wider for ceremonial processions.

Kokyo Chiku -- Imperial Palace Complex Palace grounds surrounded by walls, gates, and a water moat. Centuries of accumulated construction. With no emperor, maintained by skeleton staff under the Kokushi Kyokai. Sections have been sealed.

Kurogane-sho -- Steel Precinct The forge district. Smiths, armorers, weapons specialists. Runs hot year-round. Home to Taro's Forge.

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.M72zAjYRdrTCan30]{Mizu}-gai -- Riverside Ward Along the water's edge. Water gardens, seafood restaurants, fish markets, fishing family residences. The morning catch market is a @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian} institution.

Ryu Jikuchiku -- Dragon Borough Nightlife, theater, teahouses, entertainment. Operates on a shifted schedule -- fully alive after dark. Hosts noh theater, storytellers, gambling establishments, and renowned teahouses.

Sakura-ku -- Cherry Blossom Ward Parks, public gardens, festival infrastructure. Famous cherry tree avenues. Hosts major seasonal festivals.

Tabibito Gai -- Traveler's Street Eastern gate neighborhood for transient visitors. Inns, stables, money changers, translation services. Character shifts constantly.

Tenku Zon -- Hilltop Ward Highest elevation residential area. Reserved for nobility and senior officials. Finest architecture in Heian.

Tensho no Mon -- Military District Barracks, command infrastructure, training grounds. Home to Taisho @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.Iul8ZsyqNrfhL4XZ]{Hideo Nakamura}'s command headquarters. Where the party received their mission briefing.

Taro's Forge (Kurogane-sho) -- Master blacksmith @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.2Mal6Uf7jgW1kLPg]{Taro Fukomoto}'s workshop. Renowned for quality and integrity. Produces exceptional weapons and armor. Taro teaches those who demonstrate genuine commitment.

The Moonlit Garden (Ryu Jikuchiku) -- Teahouse in the Dragon Borough with a garden famous for nighttime aesthetics -- white stone, silver-leaved trees, reflecting pool. The party first convened here. Renowned for discretion.

Hikari no Shizuku (Hikari Zon) -- Healing and light magic enclave in the Knowledge District. Provides medical services and trains healing-aligned sei practitioners.

• @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.JLGqqI474AH04SDL]{Hiroshi Nakamura} -- Shugo (Governor) of @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian}
  • @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.Iul8ZsyqNrfhL4XZ]{Hideo Nakamura} -- Taisho (General); military commander
  • @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.2Mal6Uf7jgW1kLPg]{Taro Fukomoto} -- Master blacksmith

Details

The Imperial Palace's sealed sections contain something found after the Emperor's death that the Kokushi Kyokai does not know how to handle.

The Moonlit Garden teahouse serves a deeper function as a neutral meeting ground for intelligence exchanges.

Multiple individuals have arrived in Heian with claims to imperial succession.

DM Secrets

Hiroshi Nakamura -- Traitor in Place As Shugo, Hiroshi has near-total access to Clan Kaminari's intelligence and administrative operations. He is feeding intelligence to an outside party and has been for at least three years. He is aware that Hideo is investigating and is actively monitoring that investigation. His public persona is a performance of exceptional consistency.

The Imperial Palace -- Sealed Sections Something was found in the imperial apartments after Ryujin no Mikado died that the Kokushi Kyokai administrators do not know how to handle. It is not evidence of murder -- it is evidence of something older and stranger.

The Moonlit Garden's True Function The owner is a retired intelligence operative who maintains it as a neutral meeting ground for the Elven Council, among other groups. Information exchanges here regularly under the social protection of tea ceremony neutrality. The staff are trained to notice and remember without appearing to.

Hideo Nakamura's Investigation Hideo is hunting a traitor he does not yet know is his brother. He has narrowed the leak to a small circle of senior staff. The question is whether he reaches the conclusion before Hiroshi learns how close Hideo is and takes action.

The Succession Crisis in Heian Multiple claimants with genealogical documents of varying plausibility. The Kokushi Kyokai handles them through administrative delay. Three serious claimants are being watched. Two are probably fraudulent. One may not be.

Plot Hooks

Hideo Nakamura asks the party to carry out intelligence work he cannot assign to his own staff -- suggests he suspects someone close

An unusual request arrives from the sealed section of the Imperial Palace: someone inside has sent a note requesting outside contact; the Kokushi Kyokai doesn't know how this happened

A succession claimant approaches the party specifically, wanting independent witnesses to a document verification

City Hana Province Hokori Pop: Large
Clan: KaminariClimate: Temperate; influenced by Seidorin Mori microclimate; slightly warmer and drier than coastal Hana"The city that built its fortune on something older than itself."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.8BPLYleAkYpmvX5a]{Kikyo} sits at the eastern edge of the Seidorin Mori -- the Bronze Wood Forest -- organized entirely around harvesting and trading a resource it did not create. The Bronze Wood is to Kikyo what a great mine is to a mining town, except the resource is renewable (slowly), carefully managed, and far more politically complicated.

The city's architecture uses Bronze Wood extensively -- older buildings have developed a patina of aged copper giving streets a warm metallic glow at sunset. Newer construction uses it more sparingly due to licensing restrictions, creating visible stratification between old-money establishments and newer buildings.

Kikyo's economy runs on the licensing system. Every piece of Bronze Wood leaving the forest passes through a licensing transaction administered by @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.YSPRToQNBVq5NJFZ]{Ren Nakamura}'s office. The paperwork is meticulous; the opportunities for licensed abuse are significant.

Commercial Quarter -- Trading heart. Merchant warehouses, guild offices, the commodity exchange for Bronze Wood contracts. Ko'jiri was caught performing here.

Administrative Quarter -- @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.YSPRToQNBVq5NJFZ]{Ren Nakamura}'s offices and civic administration. The licensing offices are among the most visited buildings in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.8BPLYleAkYpmvX5a]{Kikyo}.

Residential Quarters -- Mixed; older areas near the forest edge contain original families; newer development pushed outward.

Kikyo Guard Compound -- @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.42aqdLe3xEuuPScf]{Haruto Masashige}'s base of operations. Small but highly capable force focused on licensing enforcement and forest protection.
Notable establishments are primarily the licensing offices, merchant guild headquarters, and the Guard Compound -- all integral to the Bronze Wood trade that defines the city.

• @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.YSPRToQNBVq5NJFZ]{Ren Nakamura} -- Shicho (Mayor) and Daimyo of Clan Minato
  • @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.42aqdLe3xEuuPScf]{Haruto Masashige} -- Captain of the Guard; Gold Dragonborn

Details

Ren Nakamura has discovered the true source of the Bronze Wood's metallic quality and is working with a merchant guild to exploit it.

Haruto Masashige is building an informant network and has noticed irregularities in the licensing records.

Ko'jiri carries both a legitimate letter from Ren Nakamura and a forged version -- a ticking clock.

DM Secrets

The Bronze Wood Secret The Seidorin Mori grows over an underground branch of Kinkokyo's ancient canal system. The metallic quality is caused by trace gold and copper in groundwater flowing through the buried city's infrastructure for thousands of years. Ren Nakamura has discovered this. His allied merchant guild wants to locate and exploit the source directly, bypassing tree-harvesting -- requiring excavation that would destroy the forest.

Haruto Masashige's True Purpose Masashige suspects something significant about the licensing system. He has noticed irregularities -- specific harvesting zones consistently licensed to a single merchant entity with documentation that obscures the pattern. He is three to four months from a coherent accusation.

Ren Nakamura's Alliance The merchant guild is based in Heian with operations across Hana and beyond. The alliance provides financial support for Clan Minato's elevation ambitions and exclusive export contracts. Nakamura is not villainous by nature but has made compromises requiring further compromises to sustain.

Ko'jiri's Forged Letter -- Ticking Clock Ko'jiri carries a legitimate letter and a forged version requesting additional materials. The real letter has already been sent to Heian through official channels. When the discrepancy is discovered, Ko'jiri's Conditional Pardon will be immediately at risk. Estimate: 2-4 sessions.

Ancient Dragonborn Ritual Knowledge Haruto Masashige's knowledge of ancient Dragonborn rituals includes a purification and restoration rite preserved in his family's oral tradition -- directly applicable to the Nagaji situation if someone connected the dots.

Plot Hooks

Haruto sends word to the party in Heian: he has found something in the licensing records connecting to their mission

A merchant guild representative in Kikyo attempts to discourage the party from returning there with unusual vehemence

Ren Nakamura contacts Ko'jiri separately with an additional, unwritten request

Village Mizu Province Hokori Pop: Small
Clan: TbdClimate: Foothills; transitional maritime to montane"Not every important place announces itself."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.glkgG2E8eJWrxCrm]{Koriwara} sits in the foothills where @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.IxWbWZoFox1yoTDs.JournalEntryPage.M72zAjYRdrTCan30]{Mizu} province's maritime lowlands begin to rise toward Hokori's interior ranges. It is unremarkable by any visible standard -- small-scale farming and herding, modest architecture, a self-contained community with little need for outside contact. A traveler passing through would find nothing to distinguish it from dozens of similar villages.

What distinguishes it cannot be seen from the road: the presence of Elder Sato Hideaki, whose decades of accumulated knowledge, his connection to the Order of the Sacred Grove, and his quiet role as a node in networks extending far beyond a mountain foothills village give Koriwara significance disproportionate to its size.

The sacred grove that Sato tends is a small stand of ancient trees on the hillside above the village, reached by a foot path behind the northernmost homes. The grove is not marked, not fenced, not formally maintained -- it simply exists, and the village has always known to leave it alone.

This is Relc's home village.

• Sato Hideaki -- Choro (Village Elder); 78 years old

Details

Elder Sato knows far more than he has shared with Relc about the Order of the Sacred Grove, the Order of the Ancient Guard, and Solas Evergreen.

One of the three stones referenced in Solas's cipher poem is in the sacred grove above the village.

A stranger recently arrived in Koriwara asking questions about Relc.

DM Secrets

Sato's Full Knowledge Sato is a mid-rank member of the Order of the Sacred Grove. He has interacted with Order of the Ancient Guard agents, including Solas Evergreen directly. He knows Solas was Ancient Guard (not just Sacred Grove). He knows what the Ancient Guard is and broadly what it protects. He has not told Relc because he was following Solas's instruction and because he judged Relc was not yet ready.

The Cipher Poem One of the three stones is in Koriwara -- in the sacred grove above the village. A naturally occurring stone with unusual surface striations that, viewed from a specific angle at dawn, produce a visual pattern. Sato knows this stone. He knows what the Warden's Wisdom is: protected knowledge about the living dragons held by the Order of the Sacred Grove.

Solas's Murder -- What Sato Knows Sato does not know who killed Solas, but knows the category of entity capable of it. The killing required significantly superior capability or intimate familiarity -- someone Solas trusted. This points to either a very powerful practitioner or someone inside the Orders themselves.

Plot Hooks

Sato sends word through a traveling merchant heading toward Heian: he needs to speak with Relc; something has happened near the sacred grove

A stranger arrived asking questions about Relc and where they had gone; Sato gave nothing away but is concerned about whether Relc is being watched

Village Hana Province Hokori Pop: Small
Clan: KaminariClimate: Coastal; influenced by Serenia-kai tidal patterns"The sea gives and the sea takes. We have learned not to keep count."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.DGvk4sQTQAwvHUzg]{Natsumura} is a small fishing village at the point where the Star River empties into the Serenia-kai. The village has existed in essentially the same form for centuries -- a cluster of wooden thatched houses on the riverbank, a small port with drying racks and mooring posts. The Serenia-kai's tidal complexities make the approach navigable only during specific tidal windows; the village's fishermen know these windows intimately.

The @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.items.Item.aAVMPjIVMn92MoHV]{kinuo} (gold-tail fish) that commands premium prices in @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian} runs heaviest at the Sutariba's mouth in late spring and early autumn. During these runs, Natsumura's population effectively doubles with seasonal workers and traders.

The Seaside Teahouse & Inn -- The village's sole accommodation and primary social gathering point. The proprietor is the de facto news exchange.

Fisherman's Market -- Daily fish market at the dock. Operates at dawn.

Boatwright's Shed -- Repairs and maintains the village's fishing fleet.

Net Weaver's Workshop -- Produces and repairs fishing nets adapted to Serenia-kai conditions.

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.DGvk4sQTQAwvHUzg]{Natsumura} Shrine -- Small riverside shrine dedicated to a water spirit associated with the Sutariba. Receives offerings before gold-tail runs.

• Takeda Haruto -- Village leader

Details

The Star River has recently shown anomalies -- unusual turbidity, temperature changes, and dead fish with injuries inconsistent with normal predation.

A figure has been observed watching the village from the far riverbank at night.

DM Secrets

The Sutariba's Upper Reach The Star River has recently shown anomalies -- unusual turbidity, changes in water temperature, and dead fish floating downstream bearing injuries inconsistent with normal predation. This is a consequence of Nagaji activity in the upper pass.

Takeda Haruto's Observation The village leader has seen, twice, a figure watching the village from the far riverbank at night -- a figure that moved in a way that was not quite right. He has not reported it because he has no confidence that authority is currently functioning.

Plot Hooks

Investigation of the river anomalies could lead to discovery of Nagaji presence in the mountains above

The figure watching from across the river -- Nagaji scout, or something else?

Village Hana Province Hokori Pop: Small
Clan: KaminariClimate: Temperate; rolling agricultural hills"A good market draws people together. Everything else follows."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.7Th9c00d5oE1qbfi]{Nishihara} sits in the rolling hills west of the Kinryugawa, in the gentle agricultural country between @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Zk6QD9Sdfud4SuRV]{Heian} and the Tenchusan Ren foothills. It is a village that exists primarily to serve the farmers and herders of the surrounding area -- a focal point for exchange, news, and social connection in a landscape of dispersed homesteads.

The weekly market is Nishihara's defining feature. It draws traders from a surprising radius -- merchants from Heian, specialty vendors from neighboring villages, and itinerant traders whose routes include Nishihara. The market has a genuine village-fair quality; it is not purely transactional.

Market Hall -- Permanent covered structure hosting the weekly market. On non-market days it functions as a community gathering space and occasional shelter for travelers.

Temple of the Ancestors -- The largest structure in the village; a well-maintained ancestor-veneration temple serving the surrounding rural community. Seasonal festivals draw families from several hours' travel distance.

• Yukari -- Village leader

Details

Yukari has an unusually clear picture of broader regional events because she makes it her business to listen to the traveling traders.

The Temple of the Ancestors maintains records going back several centuries with documentation of unusual historical events.

DM Secrets

Market Intelligence Nishihara's market functions as an informal information exchange point for the rural interior. Yukari has an unusually clear picture of broader events because she listens attentively to traders. She is not an intelligence operative -- she is simply attentive. If the party passes through and asks good questions, she can provide regional context unavailable from official sources.

The Temple's Old Records The Temple maintains records going back several centuries. Among them is documentation of a regional event approximately 80 years ago -- a strange sickness affecting livestock and then people in a specific pattern before stopping suddenly. The documented symptoms, if examined by a seimaster, would match early stages of a sei-manipulation effect rather than natural illness. No one has looked at these records recently.

Plot Hooks

Yukari can provide regional context and rumors if approached with good questions

The temple records could be relevant to understanding historical sei phenomena in the region

Village Hana Province Hokori Pop: Small
Clan: KaminariClimate: Temperate; forested surroundings; along Emperor's Highway"It grew because travelers needed a reason to stop. Now they stop because it grew."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.eUCVLOrFBBpO7dHx]{Sakura Mura} did not begin as a planned settlement -- it accumulated around a single inn on the Emperor's Highway that proved well-positioned for a rest stop. Over generations, the inn attracted other services, the services attracted residents, and the residents built a community. The village retains its highway-dependent character.

A river runs east-west through the village, spanned at the north end by Shadowfen Bridge -- a stone bridge leading into a stretch of marsh forest. A secondary road path continues north from the bridge's far bank.

The village is surrounded by forest on three sides, with a lake visible to the southeast. The cherry trees that give the village its name line the Highway approach for a quarter-mile -- planted two centuries ago by a traveling monk as a gift.

Oka-tei Inn -- The original settlement's reason for existing. Large, well-run, designed for highway travelers. Stabling for horses and oxen; common room with a good fire; private rooms at premium rates.

Takahashi's Hunting Lodge -- Equipment, local guides, and hunting licenses for the surrounding forest. Serves both dedicated hunters and travelers wanting fresh game.

None specifically documented.

Details

The Shadowfen Bridge exhibits a genuine sei phenomenon -- a low-level resonance that produces mild disorientation in those who speak falsehoods while crossing.

The marsh forest north of the bridge contains remnants of an ancient, consumed structure.

DM Secrets

Shadowfen Bridge The local legend has a basis in actual sei phenomenon. A low-level sei resonance exists at the bridge, likely from the marsh forest on the far bank. It is not strong enough to genuinely redirect travelers, but sei-sensitive individuals feel a strong pull toward honesty when crossing. Someone who speaks a significant lie experiences mild but unmistakable disorientation.

The Forest North of the Bridge The marsh forest past Shadowfen Bridge contains remnants of a structure predating Sakura Mura by many centuries. Not accessible without knowing what to look for -- the marsh has largely consumed it. Local hunters know to avoid a specific area they describe as "wrong-feeling." The structure's origin and purpose are unknown.

Plot Hooks

Investigation of the Shadowfen Bridge sei phenomenon could reveal the ancient structure beneath the marsh

Local hunters' avoidance of the "wrong-feeling" area could lead to discovery of pre-imperial ruins

Village Hana Province Hokori Pop: Tiny
Clan: KaminariClimate: Mountain shadow; less direct sunlight; thin rocky soil"The mountain owes us nothing. We dig anyway."

@UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.Beldp2EHfpNljWTc]{Takamine} is a village of honest poverty. It sits in the shadow of Kinryuzan (Gold Dragon Mountain) at the head of the Star River, in a valley receiving less direct sunlight due to the mountain's angle. The small iron mine that sustains the village produces modest yields -- enough to keep the operation viable, not enough to generate real prosperity. Thin, rocky soil supplements mining income through limited farming.

The community is close-knit in the way that difficult circumstances produce -- people who depend on each other genuinely. Visitors are noticed. Help is offered and received as a matter of course. The village has a pride rooted in endurance.

Ryu no Tetsu Ryokan (Dragon's Iron Inn) -- The village's single inn. Comfortable by local standards. The innkeeper's family has run it for four generations.

Ryu no Iki Kajiba (Dragon's Breath Forge) -- The village forge, working primarily in local iron. The smith produces tools and hardware; technically capable of weapons work.

General Shop -- Combined general goods; also serves as the mine company store.

Village Temple -- Small and well-maintained despite the village's poverty. The community invests disproportionately in its upkeep as collective identity.

• @UUID[Compendium.kagekuni-assistant.lore.JournalEntry.bNLqG19qg46YyZzF.JournalEntryPage.sEqN73oesS19N5Xj]{Yamamoto Kenji} -- Village leader

Details

The mine has recently started encountering an unusual material in the deeper work face -- not iron, not gold, but something with remarkable properties.

Yamamoto Kenji has quietly sent a sample to Heian for identification.

DM Secrets

What the Mine Actually Contains The deeper work face has started encountering a dark, lustrous metal with unusual properties: it doesn't rust, is harder than anything the village smith has worked, and holds an edge that standard iron cannot match. Yamamoto Kenji has quietly sent a sample to Heian, but the political vacuum has slowed response.

The material is a trace deposit of an alloy associated with Onyx Dragon Clan presence. Kokuryu's domain was never here, but volcanic geology has carried the material far from its origin. The vein is small but uniquely suited for sei-conductive tools and weapons.

Yamamoto Kenji's Dilemma If the mine material becomes known, Takamine loses control. The village is too poor and too politically isolated to defend a valuable find. Kenji is trying to get information before events overtake him. He would respond warmly to trustworthy outsiders who could help.

Plot Hooks

The mysterious metal could draw unwanted attention from merchant guilds or military factions

Kenji needs help identifying the material and deciding how to protect his village's interests
